Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the member for Calgary Southwest on her remarks this morning.
In the area of disability pensions I welcome the changes in bringing the system back up to date.
I find that in most of the disability cases that we are presented with as members of Parliament, the people who are on disability pensions have very few resources and have great difficulty in the processing of these disability pensions.
Quite frankly from time to time I have found that the departments have been short in resources. It seems to me that in an area like disability we should make sure that particular division within the department is really given the kind of public service support so that those people who are applying get a sense of comfort and a speedy response.
When someone with a family of two or three children who is eligible for a disability pension has to wait sometimes two or three years to get it, it causes tension and frustration not only for a marriage but for the children and everything. It really causes a lot of pain.
I know that the act is not designed to cause that kind of frustration, but it would seem to me that we should somehow suggest to the public servants who process these claims that we have to go out of our way to make
Government Orders
sure those disability pensions are processed in an expeditious manner.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the comments of my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood.
I know that he has always in this House spoken very deeply and sincerely with regard to people in need and people at the lower end of the income scale. I certainly share his concerns for people with disabilities and the time lag with regard to the processing of the claims. I certainly will take his words to heart and through the minister discuss this with the department.
Claims of people with disabilities should be processed as quickly as possible. I think this is something that the department has been kept apprised of with regard to needing the medical evidence that is necessary. Sometimes it is slow for the disabled person to provide and get it through. It is perhaps a long appeal period and there are some delays, but that is why we have one amendment within the bill with regard to reducing that first appeal period of time from one year down to 90 days.
Unfortunately the disabled person may lag out that time and not appeal for the year. It hurts. Financially they are hurt, there could be marriage break-ups, and indeed the youngsters suffer.
One of the amendments within the bill is to reduce that appeal period down to the 90 days so we can process faster and get the funds into the hands of the disabled.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on second reading of Bill C-39.
Constituents of Winnipeg North would like to see me debate this very important piece of legislation, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act.
Why then would I the other night wake up from a sound sleep engulfed in a feeling of dread? Why have I been troubled for days about this upcoming debate which I, as critic for health and welfare for my Liberal caucus, am to lead?
On the surface this is a necessary bill. It will do two things. First, it will raise the Canada Pension Plan contribution rate which the government says is necessary to keep the plan solvent. Second, it will give more money to the survivors of the plan's participants.
Who could argue against it? Who could argue against good health for the Canada Pension Plan and for the

Government Orders
financial security of children whose parents have died? No one would argue against such objectives.
I still remained troubled for a while. The other night it fell into place as I was reading my clipping files. The London Free Press on June 30,1990 said: "Pension poker: The Canada Pension Plan is billions of dollars in debt. How much should you rely on it to support you in your old age? That depends on how much you trust governments".
The Ottawa Citizen on November 29 last year said: "Canada Pension Plan fund faces shortage". The St. John's Evening Telegram, February 1 this year, said: "Payroll tax big money raiser. The hike in Canada Pension Plan payments proposed by the finance minister won't likely produce the bellyaching that comes with most tax increases", indicating that this is a form of indirect taxation.
On February 10 of this year The Calgary Herald, a voice from the west said: "Tax in all but name". The Ottawa Citizen on October 25 of this year said: "CPP contributions to double. Levy rising over 20 years to prevent plan's insolvency".
As I read my clipping files on this issue I really remained troubled. Then on November 15 of this year The Globe and Mail said: "Panel", referring to the cross country video-conference panel, "pleads for survival of medicare. The cross-country video conference blasts government health care cuts". On November 15, this month, The Toronto Star said: "More federal cuts loom".
I truly remain troubled about this bill, about what this government has done.
Last year the government introduced Bill C-69 followed by Bill C-20. Both these bills froze transfer payments to the provinces. Bill C-32 put a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan. Furthermore, a Supreme Court decision determined that the government has carte blanche to further cap, cut and freeze.
It is my hope that the government does not take the Supreme Court ruling as an open door for its policy that truly has hit the social conscience of Canadians and has damaged the social conscience of this country.
Provinces are dying from lack of funds. They cannot pay their civil servants. Hospitals are running up record deficits. The future looks more grim than ever.
Last January the former Minister of Finance when meeting with his provincial counterparts in Toronto struck a provincial agreement on the Canada Pension Plan. We heard the parliamentary secretary tell us about it too. I believe there are two parts to that deal: to provide for the solvency of the plan and to raise the credit limit of the provinces. I repeat, to raise the credit limit of the provinces.
In light of the reduction in transfer payments the federal government would raise rates for the Canada Pension Plan. All or most of the surplus money in the pay as you go plan would be lent to the provinces on top of the $42 billion in plan money provinces already have in loans. The provinces in turn pay interest which pays for current needs of CPP participants.
It is no secret that the CPP is being used by the provinces for their own needs. Nor is it a secret that it is highly unlikely the provinces will ever be able to repay the money borrowed.
Is it right for the federal government intent on lowering its own federal deficit to aid the provinces in running up their deficits? Is it right for the federal government to cut funds to the provinces and then to throw another tax on workers and businesses because it has pushed the provinces into debt?
I fear this bill is not about the Canada Pension Plan and orphans per se. It is about taxing employers and employees in order to have more money to lend the provinces quietly. Will that money be safe in 10 years when transfer payments according to the health coalition called HEAL will have been reduced to zero? I fear this bill is about reducing the federal debt at the expense of Canadian businesses and our workers. It is about halftruths and money that rightfully belongs to the workers of our country. It is about holding the Canada Pension Plan and children for ransom.
Politicians come and go. How many of the people here today will be here in 20 years when the baby boom generation is ready to retire and needs pension funds? Who will they turn to when the coffers are bare and the provinces cannot return the interest much less the principal on massive CPP loans?
Bill C-39 is the act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act. These are three acts which even this government has said in debate define the commitment to care for the
November 18, 1991

majority of Canadians, children and parents, our workers and our seniors. How could anyone not reach out a hand to help these groups to keep the Canada Pension Plan in good health and to raise survivors' benefits?
If only it were that simple. I am frustrated with the workings of this government which makes bills like this necessary because of poor management. I feel as though I am in the middle of a war zone with Canada being attacked from within. If all Canadians could hide in bunkers underground until the end of this Tory rule, until the next election, I am sure we would all emerge to find they left us a country in ruin. But at least we would not have had to watch it happen, watch it dismantled piece by piece.
For all Canadians at least until November 1993 at the latest there is no escape from the Tory bungling and bruising of the Canadian economy and the Canadian people. Why is a bill like this necessary? Why must the government raise contributions to the Canada Pension Plan? This is the crux of this bill. Raising contributions is the crucial question.
I submit that the other clauses that affect children and benefit children are necessary. However I regret to say they are not the main concern of this government.
If the Tories really wanted to help children they would not have waited until one year or so before the federal election to dip into slush funds and flood news-rooms with press releases on their generosity toward the youth of this country.
Do not misunderstand me. I want survivors' benefits raised. I would like to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare for finally bringing this part of the amendment into the House of Commons.
Let us now deal with raising contributions to the Canada Pension Plan. That is the crucial question as defined in this bill. Departmental officials of health and welfare say that miscalculations were made on birth and death rates 20 years ago when the CPP was implemented. At that time it was estimated that six workers would be available to provide for each retired worker in the future. Because of declining birth rates, diminishing worker productivity and early retirement there will be only three workers supporting each retiree in the next 20 years.

By the government's own reckoning "short-term increases and expenditures are due to a higher than expected take-up of early retirement and lower than expected productivity increases in the Canadian economy". I would like to quote from an excellent document to paint the picture of poverty so that this government hopefully one day may truly feel and realize that it has failed to address this issue of child poverty. This document is called Beyond Rhetoric: A New American Agenda
for Children and Families, the final report of the National Commission on Children south of the border. It was published this year. Let me read the following:
Although many children grow up healthy and happy and strong in stable families, far too many do not. They are children whose parents are too stressed and busy to provide caring attention and guidance. They are children who grow up without the material support and personal involvement of their mothers and fathers. They are children who are poor, whose families cannot adequately feed and clothe them and provide safe secure homes. They are children who are victims of abuse and neglect at the hands of adults they love and trust, as well as those they do not even know. They are children who are bom too early and too small, who face a lifetime of chronic illness and disability.
They are children who enter school ill prepared for the rigours of learning, who fail to develop the skills and attitudes needed to get good jobs and become responsible members of adult society. If this government cannot act on a vital issue of child poverty with a national blueprint, I do not know whether I can ever say that this government has a social conscience. Before the government is tempted to make that argument public, let me say as I alluded to earlier that on October 27 to 30, 1991 the symposium "Canada's Children-The Priority for the 90s" was held in Ottawa by a coalition of people, a coalition of organizations, some 15 of them, all concerned for Canada's children. How many of today's youth, with an unemployment rate of 17 per cent and with over one million living in poverty, will become lasting contributors to the Canada Pension Plan? Is the government quizzical about lower birth rates? Let me explain some facts of life. In lean times people are afraid to have children. They fear not being able to raise them to a standard of decency because they are afraid of job losses, of rising taxes, of crime, of drugs, of environmental disaster and of poverty. I believe parents today are worried about the future. Many cannot afford

to have children, the most precious aspiration of humanity.
Men and women of my generation often had four children, as my wife and I do, but today most families can afford no more than two children on a middle class income. Why do I say that?
Why do I make this recommendation to the government? In February of last year the National Council on Welfare in its report entitled Pension Reform said: "We believe it is fundamentally wrong that a public pension program set up to cover the entire paid labour force is incapable of producing benefits large enough to keep most of its beneficiaries out of poverty". There are other aspects of this bill I do not like. The government has the perfect opportunity here to address the problem of people who have lost disability benefits because they waited too long to file a claim. My colleague from Broadview-Greenwood alluded to that in his earlier questions.
Most of these people with disabilities, those who may have suffered from cerebral palsy as a consequence of problems during birth, chronic fatigue syndrome, a

disease we are still trying to elucidate in the medical profession, environmental illnesses, migraines or other often little understood diseases, have refused to admit they are ill. Therefore the province looks to British Columbia as an example or to Quebec. British Columbia charges medicare premiums for health care and Quebec charges user fees for emergency room services.

Some of the things that we see as parliamentarians are really discouraging. To see a family member, the breadwinner of a family, come into the office in some cases with arthritis so bad that he or she can hardly move, using a cane and being denied and having to go through the appeal process is discouraging. After lengthy appeals

I feel that term must be looked at. We must look at it in very serious terms. In real terms the interpretation has often disqualified people working on a very part-time basis or people attending a training program or pursuing other educational opportunities.
What we are left with is a system in which people are penalized for making any attempt to remain independent and self-sufficient following their disability. The second test currently used is that the disability must be prolonged. I see cases daily in which people are legitimately disabled through serious accidents or illness and are caught in a trap. Their unemployment insurance sickness benefits run out after four months and they do not qualify for CPP disability benefits.
I would like to suggest that the definition of disability be changed in three ways to help the system work better. First, the definition should be changed from "severe" and "prolonged" to "significant" and "extended". Second, "significant" should be defined in such a way as to allow for limited employment opportunities as a first step to reintegration back into the work force.
Finally "prolonged" should be defined as at least four months so people are not impoverished because of unfortunate circumstances. There is another major flaw in existing legislation not addressed in Bill C-39. I

Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to rise on this debate and add a few comments to the discussion of Bill C-39, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Securities Act.
Before starting to talk specifically in this debate, I just want to add an observation. I had a meeting with some nurses on the weekend. They were discussing why when legislation comes up individual members of Parliament do not get out and discuss the ramifications of that legislation with absolutely everyone who is directly involved in it. It makes a lot of good sense, because philosophically that is what we should be doing as members of Parliament. Our job is to get out and talk to our constituents and let them know what is going on, solicit feedback and reflect their feelings to this House.
I thought this morning as I prepared a few notes on what to say on Bill C-39 what a difficult task it would be to talk to absolutely every worker in our constituency and ask how the changes to Bill C-39 affect them. It is something that we do have to reflect on people. I share the comments of the previous speaker that it is something we should be talking about to as many Canadians as possible.
I have appreciated a lot of the comments I have heard this morning so far in the debate from both sides of the House. It is very obvious from the tones of the comments that members of this House on both sides share a concern for the welfare of Canadians and for the fiscal viability of our national programs. However like all
November 18, 1991

programs everyone seems to find it easy to support improved benefits, but unfortunately it is a little more difficult to find support for the necessary mechanisms to pay for those improved benefits. The same thing holds for all government programs and today it is illustrated by the changes proposed for the Canada Pension Plan.
Since 1966 Canadian workers have contributed along with their employers into the Canada or Quebec pension plans. The Canada Pension Plan has provided workers and their families with income for retirement and with financial help if the workers die or become disabled. From the debate this morning it is obvious that there is considerable sympathy for the disabled and concerns in some cases over the bureaucratic hurdles that those people have had to face in applying for those benefits. Like the previous speakers, I am very sympathetic but I want to direct my comments to how the Canada Pension Plan is funded.
This plan is financed primarily by contributions: equal contributions from workers and their employers and from interest on the accumulated plan reserves. As expenditures under the plan have risen and continue to rise, the federal government, working in close co-operation with the provinces, has taken steps to ensure that Canadians will always be able to rely upon their Canada Pension Plan for retirement, survivor or disability benefits which they have earned or will earn.
The Canada Pension Plan was established in 1966 after extensive consultation and negotiation with the provinces. Many times in this House I have heard members of Parliament refer to a specific year as significant. I have often wondered how they can remember dates and years. I remember 1966 and the introduction of this plan very well. It was my first year in the work force and my first year as a taxpayer. I can remember having a discussion with my father. He pointed out to me that I was to be one of the first group of Canadians who was to be able to draw eventually on the Canada Pension Plan after having contributed to it every year of my working life.
The pages are smiling. Perhaps they think 1966 makes it a long time ago that I went to work. I think I have a responsibility, not just on behalf of the pages who are
Government Orders
starting and those of my generation that paid in 1966 and onward but to every working Canadian to make sure this plan does remain financially viable.
To finance this plan when it was introduced in 1966 the contribution rate was initially 3.6 per cent of contributory earnings. That was split evenly between the worker and the employer with 1.8 per cent being contributed by each. This rate remained in effect until 1986 which allowed a reserve of some $42 billion to be built up. That was built up because expenditures had been less than the plan's income from contributions and interests. From the start it was recognized that contribution rates would have to be reassessed in the mid-1980s as the plan began to mature. More recently it was recognized that the plan's financing requirements would have to change to reflect changing demographic conditions in Canada, including fertility and mortality rates.
We are all naturally pleased that Canadians are living longer, but the reality of the fact that Canadians are living longer means we have to recognize there are extra requirements on our social programs as people live longer and draw on this plan for a longer period of time.
It was this obvious reality that led the current government to undertake, as one of its first official functions after coming into office in 1984, to launch with the provinces a comprehensive review of the plan's financing. An agreement was reached in December 1985 with the provinces to put the Canada Pension Plan on a sound, long-term financial foundation and keep it there.
It is significant to note that it was not a unilateral federal decision. It was reached in consultation with the provinces. The member for Calgary Southwest mentioned this earlier in the debate this morning when she explained how these consultations were done and some of the steps that were involved in consulting with the provinces before the changes were proposed.
The Canada Pension Plan operates in all provinces except Quebec. I think we all know that. Quebec has a similar plan with similar benefits and identical contribution rates. There are currently some 10 million Canadians contributing to the Canada Pension Plan and 3 million more pay into the Quebec Pension Plan. Tbday there are more than 2.7 million people receiving pay-

Government Orders
merits from the Canada Pension Plan and some 800,000 receiving benefits from the Quebec plan.
As a fiscal Conservative sitting and thinking of this plan, I would rather back up 26 years and start over again. Unfortunately we cannot do that. I was just thinking of what great shape we would be in today if we could establish this plan on the same footing as private pension plans with the same requirements they have to face when they fund pension plans. This was not done and we cannot back up 26 years.
This plan is like public pension plans in virtually every industrial country. It was designed with a pay as you go approach. This means that each working age generation pays for the pensions of the previous generation. The security of the Canada Pension Plan benefit is therefore founded on the continuing commitment of the government and the people of Canada to maintain the plan.
In spite of the fact that I had some reservations about it there are also some advantages to this funding approach. They were able to pay benefits in the early days of the plan's lifetime without requiring extremely high rates of contribution. The problems of managing a large fund in the public domain are avoided.
We could argue at considerable length whether this is an advantage or disadvantage but currently the fund would need $400 billion to meet all of its liabilities, and a fund of that size would be difficult to manage. It is also a moot point to bring it up because we obviously do not have the funds to manage. Because Canada Pension Plan is essentially financed on a pay as you go basis the contributions must closely match the rising expenditures of the plan. Expenditures arise for three main reasons. First, the Canada Pension Plan is still maturing. That means more and more retired Canadians are receiving Canada Pension Plan benefits. Second, lower fertility and mortality rates have resulted in the aging of Canada's population. Third, benefits have been enriched on several occasions without corresponding increases in contribution rates to cover the additional costs such as benefits for the disabled.
Bill C-39 which we are currently debating would increase benefits to dependent children of deceased or disabled Canada Pension Plan contributors by $35 per
month. That would take it up to a total of $148 per month.
We cannot ignore the reality of future costs. Projections of future spending anticipate that Canada Pension Plan expenditures will double over the next 40 years. This reflects the fact that more contributors are retiring and more contributors are living longer and drawing on the account.
It is very difficult to make statistics sound interesting, but it is important to this discussion to illustrate just how the expenditures have grown. When this plan was still in its infancy in 1970, the expenditures represented one-half of one per cent of contributory earnings. That was because there were very few people retiring at that time who had been participating and those who had, had contributed for only a very few years.
By 1975 the expenditures had increased to represent 1.4 per cent of all contributory earnings. In 1980 they had gone up to 2.7 per cent. In 1985 it was up to 4.3 per cent and in 1990 the expenditures in the program had increased to 6.1 per cent of all contributory earnings.
From this point we look at projections. It is projected that by the turn of the century, in nine years' time, the expenditures under the program will represent 7.5 per cent of contributory earnings. By the year 2010 it will be up to 8.6 per cent and up to 13 per cent by the year 2030.
These projections anticipate that Canada Pension Plan expenditures are going to double over the next 40 years and contributions are going to have to rise accordingly if we are going to maintain the fund.
In 1985, after extensive review involving the provinces and the general public, the federal and provincial governments agreed to establish a long-term financing program for the plan. This was a long-term plan that would ensure that contribution rates move smoothly and gradually to the levels required to meet future benefit outlays.
The legislation which implemented the agreement set a 25-year schedule of contribution rates so that employees, employers and self-employed persons would be aware of future contribution rates and plan accordingly. Rates under this schedule were set to rise in annual steps from the 1986 level of 3.6 per cent to 7.6 per cent in the year 2011.

The legislation also required that the federal and provincial governments review the existing schedule every five years to ensure the contribution rates would continue to be set at appropriate levels in the light of new actuarial projections. Five more years must also be added to the schedule. If this is not done by agreement among finance ministers then it will happen automatically under a formula which incorporates the financing principles in the 1986 legislation.
According to these financing principles, the plan's reserve is to be maintained at approximately two years of benefits. This reserve would be used to smooth out the effects on contribution rates of both expected and unexpected changes in economic and demographic conditions.
As a result of the first five-year review required for the 1986 legislation, federal and provincial ministers of finance agreed in January 1991 to adjust the contribution rates in the schedule to reflect new information provided in the most recent actuarial report. This report is called the 11th Statutory Actuarial Report. It identified the following trends that would create a need for higher rates of contribution to the plan in both the short and the long term.
Lower rates of fertility and mortality are resulting in a population with relatively fewer workers and more retired Canadians receiving benefits. Second, a drop-off in the rate of growth of worker productivity is resulting in slower increases than previously projected in wages on which rates are calculated.
If contribution rates were not increased, the reserve would fall to less than one-half a year of benefits by the year 2011, a level inconsistent with the target of two years of benefits established by the 1986 legislation. As a result finance ministers agreed that the combined employer-employee contribution rate should rise in steeper annual steps from the current 4.6 per cent rate. Under the new arrangement the contribution rate rises to 9.1 per cent in 2011 compared to 7.6 per cent in the 1986 schedule. The ministers also agreed to extend the schedule so that contribution rates would rise to 10.1 per cent in the year 2016.
What is the impact on employers and employees across Canada? Under the new rates workers who earn the average wage of $30,500 in 1991 are going to have to pay

an additional $7 in 1992. The difference in contributions under the new rates will increase to $15 by 1993 and reach $42 by 1996. The net impact on worker's take home pay will be smaller since Canada Pension Plan is creditable under the personal income tax. I think it should be understood that employers pay the same amount in the plan as do employees.
Even with these increases the contribution rates compare favourably to those which currently exist under the public pension plans of most industrial countries. The future age structure of Canada's population in terms of the ratio of plan contributors to beneficiaries will be similar to those which already exist in many of the European countries today.
It is of great importance to Canadians particularly at this time that they see that their federal and provincial governments have a commitment to the long-term strength of our national institutions and respect for the viability of our economy. The Canada Pension Plan is one of the most important social security structures in our nation. I know that all members of this House are going to support the confirmation given by Bill C-39. The Canadian people are going to appreciate that confirmation knowing that governments are acting to keep their plan sound and secure now and in the future.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to share some concerns with my colleague from Red Deer with regard to disabilities. I also want to ask him more about the schedule and the contribution rates as they affect the working man and woman and the employer.
There is a reserve fund with regard to CPP of about $40 billion that gives a three-year trust there. Some people in the House today suggested that it is lent back to the provinces at preferred rates. That is not true. Those funds are lent back proportional to the contributions that are paid by the province. If the province of Alberta through the contributions pays x dollars into the fund and there is a surplus, that surplus is invested back in the province of Alberta at a very much lower rate than the market rates. It is taxpayers' money that is being invested back into the province where it came from at a much lower rate. I think this is good use of taxpayers' dollars and one that we should encourage.

The other was with regard to disabilities. My colleague from Red Deer knows quite well about people with disabilities perhaps not understanding the workings of the CPP. He knows that we have developed new manuals on disability provisions. They have gone to about 120 private insurance companies across Canada, plus every workers' compensation office across this country. Posters have been made and distributed. There are also kits for all MPs in this House with regard to CPP, especially the disability and the funding thereof. We have become far more pro-active with regard to helping those people so that they do not suffer too long.
The remarks of my colleague for Red Deer were extremely beneficial. He said that the schedule of rates was going to start to increase as of this January and then increase again in 1997.
For all the people across Canada, I wonder if he could reiterate just what those schedule rates will be. What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? I would like to ask the member for Red Deer what this means to the employer and to the employee. How much more is he or she going to be paying to keep this fund financially stable and viable right across the country?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague and I should have got together so I would have the right papers in front of me. She asked a great many questions. They were very good questions.
I mentioned how difficult it is to make a speech involving statistics that sounds interesting. Like the hon. member said, these charts and graphs are available and there have been extensive consultations across Canada.
I started my remarks by mentioning the story about the weekend and bringing one piece of legislation in front of a particular group and that particular group wanting to know why they had not been consulted in the earlier stages of the legislation.
We have in front of us today legislation that has involved extensive consultations with groups right across Canada. The member for Calgary Southwest mentioned the meetings with the workers' compensation groups and the insurance agencies. There have been employer groups and labour groups consulted. There has been
tremendous consultation because this does impact on Canadians from coast to coast.
Every Canadian wants to know if they have a sound program in place and that their pension funds are safe. They also need to know how to plan.
I will get to the point very quickly. The member asked about the contribution rates. A plan has been established that sets them for a 25-year period. They are set at a rate which is going to continue to be shared between employer and employee. The contribution rate will increase at about .02 per cent per year each year until 1996 and .025 per cent beyond that.
It being two o'clock p.m., the House will now proceed to Statements by Members Pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me first because I wish to mention to the House our First Nations who came last during the Remembrance Day ceremony at the War Memorial here in Ottawa.
According to the Assembly of First Nations Chief, Ovide Mercredi, the wreath he laid on behalf of aboriginal veterans came at the close of the ceremony almost as an afterthought.
The Dominion Command of the Royal Canadian Legion which organized the November 11 program says the wreath it laid is on behalf of all Canadian veterans, native vets included. The federal government concedes that following the official party and the diplomatic corps, perhaps Canada's native people should be given a special spot since, as Ottawa puts it, Canada has always and will always be grateful to its native veterans.
This slight appears to be a classic case of perception being reality particularly at a critical moment in our nation's history. Canada's first citizens should not be treated last.
November 18, 1991

Mr. Speaker, recently an elderly Mississauga woman was being rushed to her local hospital. A short while later she was unloaded at a school parking lot because the ambulance has been told that there was no bed available for her anywhere in the city.
The Government of Ontario has since announced further bed closings and hospital cutbacks, blaming the ever-shrinking federal transfer payment. This is yet another example of how this government's assault on medicare is disabling health facilities across this country.
I call upon the government to acknowledge that its amputation of medicare funding is forcing the chronically ill to bear the human costs of federal economic mismanagement.

Mr. Speaker, the French CBC program Le Point has just done three reports on environmental problems in Abitibi-Temiscamingue.
I hope that these reports, which emphasize the scope of the environmental problem due mainly to mine tailing sites in our region, will finally get some action from the governments, in particular the Government of Quebec which is responsible for several of these sites.
These mine tailing sites cover a surface of more than 40 square kilometres, which is the equivalent of the distance between Montreal and Quebec City. These sites threaten not only our lakes and our subsoil, but also public health.
I therefore ask both levels of government to act jointly to create an environmental research centre in our region in order to find solutions to this serious problem that threatens our environment. This issue has become a priority for all my constituents.

Mr. Speaker, Sunday marked the 30th anniversary of the introduction of medicare in Canada. The passage by the CCF of the Saskatchewan Medicare Insurance Act of 1961 brought to Saskatchewan universal accessible medicare. This was followed by a national program passed in the House of Commons in 1966. In Saskatchewan, the implementation of universal provincial medicare required a protracted struggle and the resolution of a 17 day strike by the doctors of the province that were backed by the Liberal opposition and doctors' organizations in Canada and the United States.
It is time to salute the vision and determination of Saskatchewan innovators like Tommy Douglas and Woodrow Lloyd. It is time that we reaffirm our commitment to a national health care program.
The federal government must cease its cutbacks to medicare and resume its fair share of funding or national medicare will not survive another 30 years.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday on CBC I heard a radio report claiming that the Leader of the Official Opposition blames this government for the constitutional pain Canadians are presently experiencing. He said that a constitution cannot be put together in a week and that the people of the country must be consulted.
It is incredible to me that these comments can be made by the person who is widely considered responsible for our present constitutional problems. The Leader of the Opposition and his party repatriated the BNA Act with entrenched changes that excluded any input from Canadians. He put together a constitutional agreement in the back room of a restaurant during the night while most Canadians slept.
Well, Mr. Speaker, Canadians are not asleep now. If the opposition leader thinks he can fool the Canadian public with his attempts to rewrite or distort history, he has misjudged Canadians. Truth will win out and his

attempts at distortion will only make the public more aware of another truth. The Grits are willing to put partisan politics and their quest for power ahead-
The hon. member's time has expired. The hon. member for Hamilton East.

Mr. Speaker, last week was a week of mourning for Montrealers, Quebecers and Canadians as well. With the demise of Cardinal Leger we lost a truly great man who had devoted his life to the poor. And that, Mr. Speaker, on the second anniversary of the death of our former colleague, Jean-Claude Malepart.
Members of all political parties gathered last Sunday in Montreal to attend a play called "Le Faucon' ' dedicated to Jean-Claude and his family in recognition of all the work they have accomplished.
I am happy to see, Mr. Speaker, that through the work of these men and women who, like Jean-Claude Malepart and certainly like Cardinal Leger, believe in the less fortunate, the Sainte-Marie CIDC is now $64,000 richer.
Jean-Claude has not been forgotten. His memory lives on through his widow, Pierrette, and their two daughters, Sylvie and Nathalie, and we are all very happy that the work of this great Canadian family allows this CIDC to keep operating. We are all losers now that Jean-Claude is gone.

Mr. Speaker, the third National Seniors' Safety Week was held this year from November 12 to November 18. I am proud to announce that the event was sponsored by the Canada Safety Council.
Since it was established in 1968, the Canada Safety Council has associated itself with nation-wide initiatives aimed at reducing injuries, deaths and financial losses caused by accidents as well as general health hazards.
With the support of the private sector, governments, businesses and community associations, the council draws attention to safety issues affecting all Canadians and the seniors in particular.
The theme of the event is "Safeguard the Best Years of Your Life". Thus, the council is making sure that our seniors continue to drive safely.
I applaud the Canada Safety Council for its active communicative role in promoting awareness amongst seniors.

Mr. Speaker, since 1975 Indonesia has illegally occupied the former Portuguese colony of East Timor and in that time at least
100,000	people out of a population of 600,000 have lost their lives to the brutal regime imposed by Indonesian forces.
Now the government of Indonesia has mounted a more pervasive assault on the East Timorese through such methods as aggressive birth control and forced resettlement programs.
The East Timorese must surely wonder how their situation could be so different from that of Kuwait or the countless other human injustices that have been tackled and won with the weight of the international community. In the past, East Timor's small size and remote location have served as a veil, permitting a horrible assault on an impoverished people who aspire to nothing more than a just and peaceful society.
As we contemplate an emerging new world order, I call on the government to make sure that Canada's voice is heard and that the plight of the people of East Timor is not overlooked in the rush of events elsewhere.

YM/YWCA PEACE WEEK PROGRAM

Mr. Speaker, it is encouraging to note the continuing stream of positive and constructive examples which help to reinforce both the image and the reality of Canada as a country of the world. I was recently proud to witness one such sterling example of Canadian outreach to new citizens of various nationalities and cultural origins

through the work of the international committee of the YM/YWCA in my own riding of Fredericton-York- Sunbury.
The Fredericton Y has played a key leadership role in developing the peace week initiative in Canada and, in fact, the peace medallions presented across the country were originally designed and produced in our city. Among its many dimensions, peace week includes the hosting and orientation of refugees and immigrants who have been selected to make their new homes in Canada. This year the local Y has presented the peace medallion to St. Paul's United Church for its impressive role model in sponsoring and welcoming refugee families over the past several years.
Let us hope that the YM/YWCA Peace Week Program will touch the hearts of all Canadians and inspire us to national pride in our identity as peacekeepers in the world.

Mr. Speaker, last week Canadians were saddened to learn of the deaths of two prominent Canadian humanitarians, Paul-Emile Cardinal Leger and Dr. Robert McClure.
These two men came to represent Canada as few others have. Cardinal Leger, an ordained Catholic priest, went on to attain the highest office in his church in Canada by being nominated a Cardinal in 1963. In 1967 he stepped down from his episcopal seat to work as a missionary with lepers and handicapped children in Africa.
Dr. Robert McClure also attained the highest office of his church when in 1968 he became the first lay Moderator of the United Church of Canada. Dr. McClure had a distinguished career as a medical missionary, serving primarily in China, Palestine and India.
Both Cardinal Leger and Dr. McClure exemplified the very best of the spirit of service to humanity and Canada is proud that they called this country their home. The world is immeasurably better for having had these two humanitarians in its midst.

Mr. Speaker, Canada mourns the passing of one of its most illustrious sons, Paul-Emile Cardinal Leger, whose entire adult life was dedicated to serving others.
With his deeply religious thinking and his deeds driven by compassion, he affected the lives of several generations of men and women, on all continents and at all levels of society.
His innate kindness and profound wisdom made thousands of people who had the privilege of meeting him consider him as a father. However, he will remain best known as a member of the family of mankind who was a much loved brother to the poor, the sick and the forgotten.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, the Sidbec plant in Ville Emard had to close down part of its facilities. One hundred and forty more workers lost their jobs, making a total of nearly 400 this year. These lay-offs are the result of government policies that are having a disastrous impact on the steel industry.
Southwest Montreal has already been severely affected by an incredible rate of plant closings; general lay-offs; and a 50 per cent unemployment rate.
Last Monday I met the unions at Sidbec. They are putting pressure on the government to put the industry back on its feet and save these jobs in what used to be the industrial heart of Montreal and our country.
The only way to put southwest Montreal back on its feet is for the government to put a stop to economic policies that are having a devastating effect on workers.
If Jean-Claude Malepart were still alive, he would say: Zero per cent inflation is fine, but what's the use if we have 50 per cent unemployment?

Oral Questions
THE LATE PAUL-EMILE CARDINAL LeGER

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the most famous prince of the Catholic Church, Paul-Emile Cardinal Leger, is no longer with us. His passing is mourned by all faithful Catholics in Canada and throughout the world. We have lost our beloved spiritual grandfather.
I remember Cardinal Leger's eloquence and incredible simplicity. Who else but the Cardinal, at the height of his episcopal career, would have dedicated his life to serving the lepers, the most forgotten people on this planet, thus teaching the whole world a great lesson in humility.
The charities of the Fondation Jules et Paul-Emile Leger will perpetuate his cause. I earnestly hope that his deeds will be an inspiration and an example to all those who continue his noble task.

Mr. Speaker, in my province of Prince Edward Island, truck drivers and other users of Marine Atlantic Ferry to New Brunswick are bracing themselves for another winter of delays. Such delays add to the already high cost of doing business and make vital industries like tourism more vulnerable to disruption.
No one knows for sure, but it is estimated that 30 to 40 per cent of trucks will experience significant delays this winter. The problem of delays is also compounded by the age of the ships. Three out of four are over 20 years old. All the ships cost more to operate and break down more often.
I urge the government to approve the construction of a new ferry for Prince Edward Island regardless of a decision on the fixed link. The five to ten years it would take to build a bridge would only see more delays at the ferry, more costly repairs and more chances for disruption to the Prince Edward Island economy.

Mr. Speaker, a decision of the Treasury Board meeting of July 14, 1988, instructed the Ministers of Pubic Works, Environment and Transport to address the question of which department should be responsible for making expenditures on highways in national parks.
Three years and four months later no decision has been made. Accidents and fatalities are occurring at an alarming rate in Banff National Park.
It is imperative that the President of the Treasury Board set a deadline for the three ministers for resolving the question of custody so that we can proceed with the much needed construction of the twinning of the Trans-Canada Highway through Banff National Park.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. We read in the newspapers that the government intends to announce a 6 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums.
The news has taken employers and employees completely by surprise. The general view is that this is the worst possible time to increase premiums, just as we are trying to get out of this very difficult recession.
My question to the Minister of Finance and Deputy Prime Minister is this: Will he announce today that he does not really intend to follow through with this massive increase and that he will take steps to help Canadian employers and employees during this difficult period?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago we announced the government's decision to increase contributions to the unemployment insurance plan by from 2.8 to 3 per cent, because the unemployment insurance account's deficit will be much higher than was forecast. That is why the premium rate was increased. The purpose of this decision is to keep the unemployment

insurance account solvent and minimize any impact on the government's financial accounts. Canadians should realize that if we let the unemployment insurance deficit increase at will, unemployment insurance recipients will have to pay the price.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am terribly sorry to hear this news from the minister.
I have a question for the Minister of Finance. In the budget of 1989, when his predecessor announced the new policy that it was pulling out of funding for UI, he said: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums". That is a quotation from the budget of 1989.
I would like to know why the Minister of Finance today has broken the promise of his predecessor in the budget of 1989. Will he reverse that decision which is contrary to the announced policy of this government by his predecessor in the budget in the spring of 1989?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada does contribute to the UI fund in terms of providing advances. It has done so in 1991 to the tune of $2.1 billion and it will do so in 1992 by providing an additional $1.3 billion. So the government is acting consistently with the comments of the previous Minister of Finance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance why he does not withdraw this announcement because the intention of the government was clear that in a period of recession that we are in at this moment the last thing that the economy needs is an increase in taxes from employees and employers. What we need at this moment is some money in the industries and the consumers in Canada to buy the goods that are needed to get this country out of this recession that will be two years old very soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. Leader of the Opposition would rather postpone the
Oral Questions
difficult decisions to a further day and place the burden of that responsibility on future generations.
The fact of the matter is that the government has a responsibility to establish a premium rate on the basis of three criterion. The first one is the preservation of the financial integrity of the UI account. Second, we have to take into consideration the impact upon the employees and the employers. That indeed was done in this particular case. Finally, we have to take into consideration the impact of the UI deficit on the over-all fiscal objectives of the government. We weighed all those considerations and we made the decision that the Minister of Employment and Immigration has just announced.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has just announced a 3 per cent increase in the contributions employees and employers make to the unemployment insurance plan.
This is the third increase since the 1988 election and apparently we will have a fourth one in the coming months. Does the minister not realize that Canadians cannot take this new tax? How will we get out of the recession when he always raises the premiums paid by employees and employers? How can workers get through the next winter with yet another tax increase?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the deficit of the unemployment insurance account were not increasing, there would be no need now to increase unemployment insurance premiums. But the situation is such that if we do not act, the deficit of the UI account will grow, putting its integrity in question.
As the Minister of Finance just pointed out, no doubt the hon. member would prefer to postpone the problem to another time, but the fact remains that we must live with reality and the reality is that we have chosen an in-between solution which will ensure over time that this account will again be viable and have a positive balance by 1995.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the same minister. Just before the last election the government announced a reduction in UI premiums. Since then we have had two increases, with another two on the way. This means that Canadian

Oral Questions
workers and small businesses have seen the UI premium increased by over 50 per cent since the fall of 1988.
In the spirit of consultation, did the minister seek the advice of his commission of employers and his commission of workers before announcing just a few minutes ago the new increase in UI premiums? If he did get the advice, what was the nature of the advice of his commissioners?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes indeed the Minister of Finance and myself met with the commissioners. At issue is the financial health of the UI account and the additional burden on employers and employees. The difficulty of course was finding a balance between the two. I believe that we have achieved a reasonable balance.
I believe that Canadians realize there are no quick and easy solutions to the problems we face on this issue. The hon. member and his party may try to lead the people to believe that money will simply fall from the sky, but the unemployed and other Canadians who are quite anxious about their future know that money is not falling from the sky. That is why we have taken this responsible course.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs. It concerns the government's proposal for a number of constitutional conferences and a national conference on the Constitution. The minister appears to have gone a fair way in meeting some of the concerns certainly that my party has had about a more inclusive process, a process that would be a constituent assembly or a process similar to that.
I would ask the minister to confirm that a national conference on the Constitution will be held with participation which balances region, language, gender and diversity of opinion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that it is our intention to hold
a series of five conferences, plus an arrangement with aboriginal people that may depart because of the nature of aboriginal issues in its format from the other conferences. One of those conferences, the last one, would be in effect a summary conference that would help the special joint committee come to conclusions that may allow us to move forward the process of getting agreement on constitutional debate in the country.
We would certainly try to ensure that all of those conferences were representative. Five of them will focus upon particular aspects of the proposals, but we will ensure that they are representative of considered opinion in the country and that they are operated in a way that will allow not only parliamentarians but also other Canadians to move forward steadily toward a consensus on constitutional change.

I wish to ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister must know that the success of the constitutional conference depends entirely on the confidence Canadians have in it. It is not a partisan issue but a question of public trust. For him to obtain this trust, can the minister assure us that the views of all those excluded in the past like the unemployed, the poor and other groups will have as much weight this time as those of the traditional experts on the Constitution? Can he assure us that all viewpoints will be considered in discussions on the Constitution?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is seeking an effective balance among the legitimate perspectives on constitutional issues. Of course experts must be perceived in a traditional sense, but I agree that it is also important to have other groups whose interests are affected by the outcome of constitutional discussions. The exact balance must be determined in the future.
I hope to have an opportunity to discuss this balance with the Leader of the New Democratic Party, with the Leader or a representative of the Liberal Party, and with others who, I believe and trust, share our interest in a fair and balanced result.
November 18, 1991

I will take the minister's point that he will consult with the other parties on the representation at these conferences because it will be very important that all points of view are brought together if we are to reach a consensus.
On March 14 last, following the issuing of a $400,000 grant to the Business Council on National Issues, I asked the Prime Minister if similar financial support would be made to other groups that would also want to do research and prepare their presentations on the Constitution and on the national unity debate.
I want to ask the minister if the government has considered the proposals of these other groups and if such resources will be made available to groups participating in the conference to ensure that all of the delegates arrive at the table on an equal footing.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on constitutional matters and on others we are operating with some resource constraints. We have made some millions of dollars available to aboriginal groups, for example, to ensure that they can undertake extensive consultation of their own membership.
We are prepared to look at some limited funding of some other kinds of conferences. I think it is essential to the effective functioning of the conferences discussed earlier in this Question Period that there be a willingness on the part of the government to ensure that financial resources are not an obstacle to the attendance at those conferences of people who might have to travel some distances to get there.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might simply express my appreciation and that of the government for the leadership between opposition parties that the New Democratic Party has shown this morning in its agreement to take steps that will ensure that the special joint committee can get back into operation so that we can make progress on the constitutional-

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance,
Oral Questions
who will be aware that this government's high dollar policy is wiping out jobs right, left and centre. For every one cent increase in the value of the dollar, $2 billion worth of export business is lost to Canada. The 13 cent hike in the dollar since 1984 has triggered massive lay-offs in mining, forestry, and fishing, all of which are heavily dependent upon export sales.
I ask the minister why he persists in a policy which is wreaking such economic havoc and causing so much pain.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we do not have a high dollar policy. The exchange rate is established in the marketplace.
As far as exports are concerned, I would advise the House that the merchandise trade balance rose by $8.1 billion at an annual rate of $13.5 billion in the month of August. Contrary to what the hon. member suggests, we have a positive merchandise trade balance and our trade with the United States is improving.
There are other fundamentals that have to be dealt with and that is the basic competitiveness and productivity issues that we face as an economy. I know the hon. member does indeed welcome the initiative by my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology to deal with this on a partnership basis.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister that those statistics do not buy groceries for the 178,000 more Canadians that are out of work this year than last year, thanks to the policies of him and this government.
The jobless rate in Newfoundland is up to 18 per cent and bankruptcies there have skyrocketed by something over 71 per cent, not to mention the increase in the number of homeless and the hungry across this country.
I ask the minister how he can be so callous, so insensitive as to stand idly by and let the Bank of Canada hold the dollar at such an outrageous level, creating even more bedlam and misery.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one enjoys the fact that this country has gone through a recession in the process of restructuring and adjustment.

Oral Questions
No one enjoys the fact that there is high unemployment. The fact of the matter is that we must get the fundamentals right.
Our approach to revitalizing the economy is to bring down the pressures of inflation so that we can bring down interest rates on a long-term basis. That will provide the recipe for sustained recovery and price stability. That is our goal. That is our objective. It is quite obvious that while the indicators are somewhat volatile, there is every clear indication that the economy is strengthening.
There were 43,000 new full-time jobs created last month and 108,000 full-time jobs since August. That is certainly not good enough. There were 24,000 brand new jobs created last month. Certainly that is not good enough but it is pointing in the right direction.
Housing starts are up 202,000 on an annualized basis. Business confidence is not as robust and buoyant as we would like to see it but Canada does not stand alone. We have problems all around us. We are dealing with the fundamentals and when we get the fundamentals right, we will have long-term sustainable recovery.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Recent reports suggest that the United States government has decided to delay the conclusion of the U.S.-Canada-Mexico free trade agreement until after the U.S. presidential election in November 1992.
The Canadian government on the other hand has consistently insisted that it is in Canada's interest to have a rapid conclusion of the discussions of these negotiations.
Is it now the position of the Government of Canada that the negotiations will be delayed, that the conclusion will be delayed until 1993? Has that become the position of the Canadian government as well as of the U.S. government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is not my understanding.
My understanding is that the negotiations are continuing. Canada is involved in those negotiations and there has not been any delay, artificial or otherwise, established as far as I am concerned.

Mr. Speaker, the minister should know that the chief U.S. trade negotiator stated recently that she would not bet her salary on the fact of these negotiations being concluded before the U.S. presidential election.
If Canadian policy is being determined by U.S. trade policy, what confidence can the Canadian people have that when the U.S. government demands, as it has been doing, that the cultural industries and the auto pact be on the table, U.S. policy will not dominate the situation as well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a lot of ifs associated with that question and it is rather hypothetical.
I can assure the hon. member that we are not engaged in the North American free trade negotiations from the standpoint of improving and benefiting the United States or Mexico. We are there because we believe that it is appropriate for Canada to be there and to protect Canada's interests.
We are there because we want to expand trade, liberalize trade because trade has been good for Canada in the past and it will be good for Canada in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the question of the 7 per cent increase in UI premiums.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration says that money these days is not flowing from the sky. That is right. Money is in fact being taken from people's pockets.
I want to make the point to the minister of employment that this is the same thing as a $1.3 billion tax increase. I want to ask the Minister of Finance how he can possibly justify a $1.3 billion increase from people's pockets at a time when the economy is limping, people are out of work and this economy is struggling, right across Canada.
November 18, 1991

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is very much aware that there are certain factors that have to be taken into consideration in establishing the premium rate. One is the financial integrity of the unemployment insurance account. If we did nothing, there would be a cumulative deficit of $4.6 billion by the end of 1992. By the end of 1993 it would be $6.2 billion and by the end of 1994 it would be in excess of $7 billion. That would certainly put the UI account on very shaking footing. Therefore, that has to be taken into consideration.
As well, we take into account the difficulties faced by the employee and the employer as well as the over-all fiscal impact upon the government accounts. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, question No. 132 will be answered today.
With the exception of the multi-year operational plan (MYOP), does a department have the right to shift salary resources to other internal priorities without Treasury Board approval?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Under the current rules and procedures, a department may not adjust the amount of salary resources available to it without the approval of the Treasury Board. Even in the MYOP, while departments may propose internal reallocations to increase or decrease salary resources this ultimately will
Routine Proceedings
need to be considered and approved by the Treasury Board.
The PS 2000 initiative calling for the implementation of operating budgets in the 1993-94 fiscal year will fundamentally change the Treasury Board's approach to resource management. Under operating budgets, managers in the Public Service will be given budget flexibility to reallocate dollars between the salary and non-salary portions of the operating budget. This will enable managers to choose the most efficient and effective way of achieving program goals. This represents a change from the traditional approach of central controls to one of making the manager more responsible and accountable for resource management.
In summary, the current rules and procedures are as follows:
-Section 31 of the Financial Administration Act requires each deputy head to divide each appropriation granted by Parliament into allotments in the form prescribed by the Treasury Board. The allotments are approved by Treasury Board and cannot be varied or amended without the approval of the board.
-The basic allotment structure in use for most departments and agencies (excluding Crown corporations) within the Public Service is:
-Salary and wages-all personnel costs are charged to this allotment;
-Salary adjustment reserve allotment-funds set aside to offset all or a portion of the costs associated with salary increases expected in the next fiscal year; and
-Other operating costs-the balance of funds appropriated to a vote.
-In 1985 the Treasury Board assigned to the Secretary of the Treasury Board the duty of approving on its behalf certain allotment changes of an administrative nature including the authority to review and approve the reallocation of funds to or from salaries and wages.
The question as enumerated by the parliamentary secretary has been answered.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard (Roberval) that Bill C-39, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee B.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate on second reading of this bill and look forward very much to this bill going to committee where it can be amended in the manner that is necessary to make it the kind of legislation that we need to have with regard to most particularly the Canada Pension Plan.
As we are all aware, the Canada Pension Plan has been in effect in this country and with its partner, the Quebec Pension Plan in the province of Quebec, since 1966. The purpose of this is to provide a measure of protection to Canadian workers and their families against loss of earnings due to death, disability or retirement.
November 18, 1991

It covers virtually all employed and self-employed persons between the ages of 18 and 65, and it is optional to the age of 70, who earn more than the year's basic exemption. It operates everywhere in the country, as I have said, including in the province of Quebec where the parallel Quebec Pension Plan is in force.
It is financed through contributions from employees, employers and self-employed persons and from the interest earned on those contributions.
Everyone who is employed has a contributory period which either began in 1966 or at the age of 18 and ends when the contributor takes his or her retirement pension or reaches the age of 70. A person who spends time out of the paid labour force caring for a child under seven for whom a family allowance benefit is payable can drop those years from the contributory period if it is to their advantage.
In other words, this is a good plan. It is a plan that Canadian workers and their families depend upon and it is a plan that is part and parcel of the social fabric of this country. But this plan, like many other financial institutions in our country, is under a form of assault due to inflation and other problems facing us as we come to the end of the 20th century.
Indeed, the most recent actuarial reports show that if contribution rates to the fund are not increased, the Canada Pension Plan risks insolvency. That is only sensible when you consider it, Mr. Speaker, and it certainly applies to a number of the people in this House, those of us who were bom in the famed post-war baby boom, creating the largest demographic bulge in this country. As we march onward to the years of retirement that increased number of people out of the paid work force who are receiving benefits will obviously increase to an insupportable level if the fund is not increased.
By the government's own reckoning, short term increases in expenditure are due to higher than expected take-up of early retirement, an idea than has been pushed a great deal because of unemployment problems in this country today, and a lower than expected productivity in the Canadian economy. In the long term, higher expenditures are due to lower assumptions for future fertility and mortality rates and lower assumptions for productivity increases.
