The schedule for the increase in contribution rates will be $7 in 1992 for each person with an average wage of $30,500. This contribution increases to $42 by 1996 allowing for a combined employer-employee contribution rate of 4.6 per cent in 1991 to 9.1 per cent in 2011, as opposed to 7.6 per cent by 2011 if the current contributions schedules are maintained.
What are the good points of this bill? One good point is that the bill will ensure the continued good health of the Canada Pension Plan which is absolutely to the benefit of all Canadians. It will provide increased benefits for the 170,000 children of deceased plan participants and benefits will rise as of January 1992 to $148 per month from $113 per month.
A third reason to support this bill is the increased benefits for women. One of the things that is very close to my heart is the whole question of credit splitting in the Canada Pension Plan.
In 1978, the Canada Pension Plan was amended so that divorcing spouses could have pension credits earned during their marriage divided equally between them. Previously, women who stayed at home to raise their children received no pension entitlement. Either spouse could apply for the split within three years of the divorce, however, only 2 per cent of spouses did so. The major reason for this was that this particular benefit was not well known. I well recall some time in the early 1980s bringing this point to public attention in Halifax through a radio program and getting a lot of complaints from a number of my colleagues. The problem was that if you did not specify the splitting of pension credits in a marriage contract or a separation agreement, or in the minutes of settlement of a divorce case, then the wife claiming a split of the husband's benefits was out of luck because the contract precluded her claiming them.
The second thing was that most women would be unaware of this unless told so specifically by their lawyers. The tragic point was that very few lawyers practising in Canada were aware of this. If husbands were aware of it, they obviously were not going to tell their divorcing wives at the time in question.
In 1983, the Canada Pension Plan Appeal Board ruled that the standard clause in divorce settlements, that the parties would have no further claims, that all claims were exhausted by the particular contract or minute of settlement, precluded equalizing pension credits later. In other words it became more and more difficult for

Government Orders
women to seek this redress and to take this benefit, a small one in many cases, but it made a difference.
The difference that it made could be a significant difference particularly to wives and families in low income categories. In 1986, the Canada Pension Plan was amended again. At that time, for subsequent divorces, credit splitting rights were declared to be unrenouncable unless provincial family laws explicitly provided for it. In other words, unless there was a provincial statute saying that you could renounce this benefit, you could not renounce it. Even by signing a contract you could not give up this specific right. This received a fair amount of publicity and consequently a number of applications for credit splitting took place over the next four years throughout Canada. However, in the fall of 1990, the Ontario case that had gone before the Canada Pension Plan Appeal Board was appealed to the higher court in which it was ruled that "no court order may produce a result contrary to those of statutory arrangements". Again the credit splitting question was placed back into limbo.
The 1987 amendments to the Canada Pension Plan were designed to make the splitting of spouses' CPP credits automatic upon the notification of divorce. However, currently one or both parties must notify the department of the divorce and supply the necessary information so that the credit may be split. There are a great number of reasons why this does not happen: ignorance of the provision, apathy, a lack of awareness and the fact that a number of lawyers are unaware of the specific situation. The level of request is low.
It is absolutely necessary that the government find a way to integrate a provision in this bill so that the welfare of the non-contributing spouse is guaranteed. In other words, the appeal case in 1990 said that "no court order may produce a result contrary to those statutory arrangements". If the statutory arrangements specifically said that credit splitting will be automatic I suspect that the problem will be solved.
A study by National Health and Welfare shows that 94 out of every 100 women marry and that one in every three marriages ends in divorce. In 1988, 56 per cent of single mothers lived below the poverty line, many trapped in a vicious cycle of poverty which condemns not
only them but their children to live in dire circumstances. We are not suggesting that the credit splitting of Canada Pension Plans will solve this problem, but it will help. To the average mother living at or below the poverty line, having a very difficult time in collecting maintenance payments, child support payments, the automatic credit splitting of Canada Pension can make a difference.
We realize that this may seem small in the over-all scheme of financial matters, but I think there is a moral responsibility on every one of us here in terms of women who do not receive proper support from their former husbands, in terms of women who are in almost every case subject to some form of financial disadvantage and in terms of women who still make 60 cents for every dollar that men make.
I have said this so many times that it is almost like a record. I could just push a button and the record plays, but I am going to say it again to the hon. member from Algoma East. The figure of 60 cents for every dollar that men make includes women employed at salaries such as the women who sit in this House, female doctors, lawyers, managers, engineers, upper level public servants and so on. When you remove those women from the statistics the average woman in Canada who is employed makes 50 cents for every dollar that a man makes. The real tragedy of those statistics is that they have not changed in over 40 years. That was the statistic in the post-war era of the late forties and it is the statistic today. That becomes very personal to me because it means that in the year I was bom that was the statistic, and 43 years later there is no change. I think we should be ashamed of that as a country.
This particular bill is not going to solve all of that, but it at least creates some small redress which is necessary on the part of this government. The problem is that various governments, Liberal and Conservative, have tried to fix it and somehow each set of amendments to the bill has managed to fall down a rabbit hole and not solve the problem for women who need this problem solved.
There are a number of other good points about this bill. One is the question about a disabled contributor's child benefit. Up to now, only natural or legally adopted children could be paid a disabled contributor's child benefit if they became dependants of the contributor after the disability commenced.

Disabled contributors' child benefits would now also be paid for children who are adopted in fact or who come under the custody and control of the contributor after the start of the disability.
This is a very important addition as well. I do not want to get into the area of my hon. colleague from Hamilton Mountain who is very much on top of the situation, particularly with respect to the disabled. However, I do want to make some points with regard to the whole question of custody, care and control of children. Particularly in this day and age the breakdown of the family frequently puts a grandparent or an aunt-almost always a woman-in a situation in which a court will grant her the custody of a grandchild or a niece. It might be someone else who in the words of the legislation in the province of Nova Scotia "has an interest in the custody, care and control of the child". In other words, many children end up with a custodial care giver through the courts who is neither the parent by blood nor by adoption.
In the past these people who come forward in the vast majority of cases out of a deep sense of caring for the child and out of a deep sense of a moral obligation to look after the child are often left with an inability to take care of that child because the relevant legislation affecting parents and children has excluded them.
I suppose to a degree this is within the purview of the Law Reform Commission. It is within the purview of this House as well not just to look at this legislation we are amending now but to make an attempt to do some sort of wholesale review of legislation as it affects women and children generally to ensure small benefits which do not cost the government a huge amount of money but which can make a difference between a bare minimum form of existence and an existence that perhaps goes slightly above that to an existence that is the true birthright of all people who live in this country.
There is so much poverty and so much misery in this country because we are told we cannot find the proper dollars and channel them in the proper way so that the proper programs are in place to assist people. When people lose benefits because of mistakes in legislation that are tantamount to misprints then all of us bear a responsibility.
This is why I say that I look forward very much to going to the legislative committee that will deal with this bill
Government Orders
and talking about amendments that can clean it up further, tighten it up better, and can make sure that benefits for Canadians under the Canada Pension Plan are done in the manner in which they should be done. We must ensure that we do not allow certain people in certain circumstances to fall between two stools because the House of Commons is too large and we are too busy to notice the small mistakes that can engender misery for large numbers of people.
It is the kind of thing where each one of us on all sides of the House must make sure that the t's are crossed and the i's are dotted, particularly in this recessionary time when we are faced on every side with cutbacks. A piece of legislation like this can make a vast difference in my own Atlantic region. We are very concerned there with the cutbacks in transfer payments, with the death blows dealt to the unemployment insurance plan, with the skyrocketing bankruptcies and all of the attendant misery of a recession that has the four Atlantic provinces in a death grip.
Just this past week while I was at home in my riding I drove around and I saw the number of small businesses that have closed in small shopping areas around my city of Halifax and the outlying areas. I saw them closed. I saw barred windows and boarded up establishments. That tells me more clearly than any statistic anyone gives how people are suffering in Atlantic Canada. At the very least we must do what we can.
This bill in and of itself is a reasonable bill. It needs some fine tuning. It needs some cleaning up and it needs some amending. I know that my hon. colleague from Winnipeg North will be looking very closely at this, as will my hon. colleague from Hamilton Mountain.
I look forward to working with them and indeed with the government members. I suspect that this is one of the areas where we can show that we can work together on all sides of the House to make sure that we are putting in place a bill that is of maximum and optimum benefit to 11 Canadians.
I know the minister would agree that the people of Atlantic Canada have suffered a great deal and expect to see some respite from their government to make life a little better.

It may well be that this bill properly amended and brought back to the House at report stage will have at least a little good news. It is a very dark tunnel and this may be just one small candle at the end of the very dark tunnel.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-39.
As we all know in this House the primary role of this bill is to keep the Canada Pension Plan solvent through increases in contributions by employers and employees. We know under the current condition that if we did not amend this bill by the year 2001 our pension fund would basically only have a six-month period of funding for the plan claimants.
The departmental officials have made the claim that this is not really a mismanagement of the fund but it was basically an inability to calculate accurately the birth and death rates from a calculation of 20 years ago. I can understand that.
There is also the diminishing worker productivity and early retirement. We on this side of the House are going to support this bill because there is enough economic stress and depression in the country right now without us tampering or putting any cloud of doubt around our Canada Pension Plan and our disabled pension plan as well as the other funds such as family allowances, et cetera.
When we analyse the current economic climate that we are in we have still to face up to the reality that this is another tax on employees and on employers. Even though the numbers are small, for example in this particular bill, we are talking $7 per employee per month. In other words it is a $42 contribution by the employer over a six-month period.
It seems like a small amount of money, but it is a fact that there is a tax on our new bankruptcy bill coming in. Here is another added tax on our Canada Pension Plan. Think of all the tax increases that have happened with this government. I think there have been well over 40 now if we include legislation that is in first, second or third reading.
The people of Canada are frustrated with the current tax climate in this country. I had a bit of time on the weekend to go over this bill. As I was reflecting on it I
thought that rather than continue the debate on the specifics of the bill I would address the fact that maybe what we should be doing is talking a little about what we can do to try and create some more wealth and try to reverse the capital flows that are leaving this country right now. The flight of capital from this country right now because of the current tax designs that exist has reached a crisis proportion.
We know that in the province of Ontario alone in the last year foreign investment which usually goes into direct investment was down by close to 50 per cent. That is a tremendously high number. When we think of the number of jobs we are losing in this country it is no wonder we hear of the decrease in foreign capital. We need foreign capital in this country. I keep repeating myself in this House and sometimes I wonder if the government ever pays attention to anything said in this House. It always says: "Give us ideas in order to advance the debate". Very rarely do I ever see it take these ideas.
I have been campaigning in this House of Commons for the last two years to change the tax system. I believe that if we were to take a radical approach to changing the fundamental personal and corporate tax design in this country we would not be sitting here today debating this bill in the way we are. We are asking for a further indirect tax increase from employers and employees, not to mention the government's contribution.
The way to create wealth in this country is not by adding to the tax litany. The way to increase wealth is to lower the basic tax structure. When people make personal or corporate profit they do not tend to want to leave it in Canada. Because of the tax designs that we have they want to take this money and look for other places to put it. Most people who make large sums of money in this country today either want to put it in the islands or they want to put it in Switzerland or they want even to move it to the United States. We have over a million Canadians living in the state of California. One of the reasons these people are going there is that there is a tax incentive.
Why do people put money in the Bahamas, in Nice and in the islands? They put money there because there is a better tax rate. It is the same in Switzerland. They put money there because of a preferred tax rate.
Because of the lack of confidence in this country today and because the spirit of this country is depressed, we are seeing more than ever a flight of capital. It is not just shrinking foreign capital but also a lot of our own

domestic capital is looking to go either to the United States or the islands or even Europe.
What we have to do is reverse that flow of foreign capital. The only way we are going to reverse that flow of foreign capital is by making sure that we have an incentive for people to come and invest in this country.
The embassies and the consul generals in this city monitor this House of Commons. Week after week after week they see a tax in this bill and another tax in that bill. They see a litany of taxes. It does not matter that they are just small amounts. These small amounts added up along with the paper burden do not attract people to participate in the economic growth of this country.
I have been saying in this House of Commons for the last two years now that what we should have is a single tax rate. We should have a rate where we are charging people not more than 20 to 22 per cent both on the personal and on the corporate side.
What will that do? Let us just take some of the people who are popular Canadians. Let us just take a Canadian artist like John Candy. He has made a tremendous contribution in this country. We are reminded of this by last weekend and obviously again next weekend. He has invested heavily in my home town team, the Toronto Argonauts. If there was a preferred rate this is the type of person who would find a lot more incentive to participate in the Canadian economic life than currently exists.
There are a lot of John Candys in this country. They may not all be actors but there are a lot of people in business, sport and a lot of other sectors of the economy where that capital should be based in Canada. The way you do it is with the tax system.
Why can we not make a country like Canada into a Switzerland in terms of attracting reserves? Surely to goodness we can do what they do on islands like the Bahamas where they attract large pools of capital. I do not mean we can attract in terms of lifestyle but in terms of foreign investment.
When large pools of capital come to a country and they put it in financial institutions, it puts downward pressure

on interest rates. That is what allows our entrepreneurs to get capital which they in turn use to go out and create jobs.
When people are working they pay taxes and that ultimately leads to less unemployment insurance and less welfare payments. This would ultimately lead to a situation where we would not have to be worried about our Canada Pension Plan being jeopardized. It is absolutely ludicrous in my opinion that we are in a country as rich as Canada in terms of resources and entrepreneurial spirit, and we are not galvanizing it. We are not turning it on. We are not utilizing it. We are not using those resources to attract capital which ultimately will create larger revenues for the country.
It is so simple to me. Consider those who make a couple of hundred thousand dollars in a year. It could be some of our superstars in industry or in culture or in sport who sometimes make as much as a million dollars a year. When they are given a tax act the way ours is structured today, which is in some instances close to 60 per cent, it is no wonder they want to park enough money here in Canada to live and then tend to move offshore.
Can we imagine if we reversed that and that capital stayed here? Can we imagine if we were sitting in this House today and instead of having more than two million people unemployed they were working and paying taxes?
Can you imagine what we could do if that kind of condition existed? It requires the government to take a leap of faith. It seems to me that if we are going to mobilize people in a positive way, we are first going to have to show them that the legislation we are putting forward in this House is sending out signals of fairness.
All of the legislation we have put through this House in the last 60 or 90 days has basically been sending signals of unfairness. Week after week all we do is sit in this House and talk about another tax increase: "Oh, well, it is not that much. It is only $7 a month here and on the Bankruptcy Act it is only 5 cents per person per week". It is from GST to bankruptcy tax. Now we are trying to cloud the Canada Pension Plan. I think the way to motivate a work force is to treat it fairly. This government, whenever it has found itself short, when it is trying to keep its fiscal framework in order, always goes for a

tax increase or the selling of a Crown corporation to get it off the books.
When this government talks about productivity it forgets that the key to productivity in this country is a motivated work force. This government controls the only instrument that can turn a work force in this country on, and that instrument is the tax act.
We sit in this House today and talk about the Canada Pension Plan which is something that seniors in our country have never really worried about before. They have never really considered that our Canada Pension Plan was in any jeopardy.
I realize that we want to maintain a fiscal responsibility on this act. I said it earlier today and I saluted the member for Calgary Southwest that it is a good move. We want to get our fiscal framework in order. In the process of doing that we have to look at the entire package. One of the things I believe would maybe create a lot more wealth in this country, which would allow us to fund this pension plan in a much more progressive way and maybe without going to these taxes for employees and employers, is by radically reforming the tax act. At the core of that reform has to be a simplicity of the act so that people in this country can judge fairness.
I would submit if that approach were implemented the productivity levels in this country would be such that it would attract new foreign capital to this country, which is ultimately a key to job creation. God knows we need job creation in this country in the worst way right now. A radical reform of the tax act would probably encourage a lot of those people who are tempted right now to move their resources offshore to keep their resources here and invest in this country.
That ultimately is what we are supposed to be doing in this House. We are supposed to be devising a way to get this country out of its chronic depression. There is a chronic depression out there today and we should be using our creative juices to try and figure out ways to pick the morale up.
Today we are talking about the Canada Pension Plan. By adding a further tax on employers and employees at a time when we are trying to pick ourselves up and trying to avoid going back into a second recession is a two-edged sword.
Yes, it is fiscal responsibility and we must keep the Canada Pension Plan in shape, but I think in the process of addressing this issue we should also look at the total plan. We should see what we have to do to attract capital and mobilize the will of this country again so that we can get those two million people back to work and make sure that the treasury of this country has all the resources it needs.
The Canada Pension Plan, one of the greatest in the world, should never be thought to be in jeopardy by any of our seniors in this country or by the people who are working hard and thinking about the fact that in 15 or 20 years from now when they are seniors they will want to make sure that plan and that fund are solvent.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-39 and the amendments that are being offered by the federal government in co-operation and as a result of negotiations with its provincial counterparts.
The Canada Pension Plan can only be amended by agreement between the federal and provincial governments which makes amendments to the act extremely difficult at best and sometimes impossible at worst.
I want to say at the outset that my party supports the two amendments that I am particularly interested in today. The first one is the increase in monthly benefits to the children of disabled or deceased contributors to an amount of some $35.
Having said that, I want to remind the House that around 1986 or 1987 a major review of the Canada Pension Plan took place and an agreement was arrived at between the provincial governments and the federal government for a whole number of amendments to the CPP, including a substantial and very much needed increase in CPP disability benefits to the then current recipients.
With the co-operation of the opposition parties at that time we again rushed through these amendments as we are being asked to today because there is a deadline for getting those improved benefits through to recipients of the CPP disability pension plan.
We did that only to discover that provincial governments immediately deducted an equal amount to the increases in the CPP disability benefit from programs that provincial governments were paying those same people under provincial benefit programs. Insurance companies also paid the disability benefit to the same
November 18, 1991

individual as did employers under different pension plans.
At that time there was a great outcry both from the government side and from the opposition. They said: "What was the sense in increasing benefits to those recipients who badly needed them only to have a second, third or fourth party sometimes deduct an equal amount from benefits that they pay so that the individual was no better off financially?"
I see the federal government has not learned anything in the last four or five years because there is nothing in these amendments that would prevent the same thing happening again. If that happens I think we will be doing a great service to the children of these recipients whom we are now trying to help.
I would hope that the committee emphasizes that part again when this is referred to a legislative committee, hopefully within the next day or two. That is my first concern, that it has not been addressed in the negotiations with provincial governments to prevent that kind of thing from taking place again.
The other thing that I am a bit disappointed about, even though there has been some movement to alleviate the situation somewhat, is where an individual has become disabled and is under the care of doctors, therapists and whoever else. There is also hope that such individuals would recover and be able to return to a useful occupation. What happens very often, because they hope they can return to work and because the medical profession is always hopeful that they could be rehabilitated, is that it may take them two or three years to apply for a disability benefit under the Canada Pension Plan.
What the Canada Pension Plan says is that unless one makes that application within 15 months of sustaining that disability one will not be eligible for a benefit under the plan.
This could be someone who has contributed to the plan since 1966 when the Canada Pension Plan first came into effect. Suddenly, because of changing circumstances, those individuals would be ruled ineligible if they did not apply for that benefit within 15 months of that disability first taking place.

The small change that has been made in the amendments before us is that if the applicant failed to make such an application as a result of mental incapacity, the government and the administrators of the plan would be willing to take another look at it. That is fine. I welcome that because it is something that was not there before, but many Canadians suffering from a mental incapacity have simply failed to apply for a benefit because they are continually hoping that they will recover from the incapacity.
I think in all fairness the government has to take a second look at that. It is certainly not fair to the individuals and it certainly provides a disincentive in many cases for an individual to become rehabilitated. In other words, it is in the individual's best interest to apply immediately for a benefit under the Canada Pension Plan for a disability pension and to heck with everything else. To me that is counterproductive to trying to get people back into the work force.
Surely it is fair to say that an individual should have the opportunity-and the individuals I know would welcome it-to enter rehabilitation programs. Having done that they should not be penalized for not making an application for the benefit within the time constraints that are laid out under the legislation.
I think it is being pound wise and penny foolish, to coin an old phrase, to continue with that approach. I do not think it makes any sense in these days of enlightenment toward concerns that people in the disabled community in Canada have.
Another problem I have is on the other side of the coin, when someone is disabled to the point that they cannot continue to work any longer. We have a situation under the Canada Pension Plan to avoid all the legalities involved. To put it in a nutshell, one has to be practically comatose in order to apply for a benefit and receive it.
What the act talks about is that in order for an individual to be eligible for a disability benefit under CPP, the person has to be "(a) incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation".
I take a look at members on the government side and members on the opposition side. Every one of us has had individuals in our constituencies who have had a tremendous problem in establishing a claim because they could maybe walk down the street, sit on an elevator. I had one such chap, even though there are no such jobs anymore,

Government Orders
driving an elevator up and down. They used to have them in the Eaton Centre in Toronto but they do not have that anymore, someone sitting on a little stool punching buttons for the customers. That does not exist anymore.
I finally got this one fellow a benefit. After many, many years he got the benefit. Then his doctor decided that it would be good for him mentally to enter a program that taught English as a second language. It was good for him mentally, it was certainly good for the guy physically, and he agreed to do that, unbeknown to me.
He entered the program, notified CPP, and he was immediately cut off benefits. Here was a man who was trying to help himself hopefully to get back into the work force and play the traditional role that he felt would help him provide a means of support for his family, and he got cut off. It took me three months to get him back on. Even then, the guy had to leave the program he was in. There was no way he could receive that benefit while remaining in that program. I told the guy to get out of the program and we would see if we could get him back on CPP. It is stupid, to say the least, to treat people that way.
Even though an individual is incapable of working, if he is willing to at least try to enter a rehabilitation program, then why are we preventing them from doing so? We provide the disincentive that says: if you go into that program, your benefits are going to be cut off. That is what happens, and I think it is high time, and the government promised this four or five years ago, that it changed that kind of silly approach to these things.
Surely it would make sense if we changed the definition of disability under CPP from both severe and prolonged to something akin to significant or extended disability respectively. It would make an awful lot more sense and would be fairer to the individual. I think it would be less of a drain on the Canada Pension Plan, quite frankly, if that more enlightened approach to the problems that people face who become disabled.
There is one other item I want to touch on before I sit down. That is the question of where a couple unhappily find themselves in a situation where they must separate or even have a divorce.
There have been cases that were existent in 1986 and 1987 when we last looked at the Canada Pension Plan. We tried to deal with it at that time and had a great deal of difficulty in doing so for a variety of reasons. There was a case reported recently, within the last three or four weeks, of a woman who had been married to this man for some 30 or 35 years, and the marriage broke down.
It turned out that the male either continued, or ended up, in a common law marriage with a younger female for a period of about five or ten years. Then he died. When he died, the first wife, the first woman, was denied any benefit under the Canada Pension Plan. She was denied any benefit under the Canada Pension Plan. No, I am sorry, she had received the benefit under the Canada Pension Plan. Then it was discovered because of this common-law relationship that she probably was not entitled to the amount of benefit she had been receiving. Canada Pension Plan officials were demanding that she pay it back.
I think I am correct in the facts. That woman, an elderly person, without any visible means of financial support for herself, in all likelihood will lose the only possession she has, which is the house she and her former husband had paid for in order to provide herself with an income in her later years.
We tried to address that kind of problem in 1986-87.1 think it is time we took a hard look at saying that on marriage breakdown Canada Pension credits should be split and they should be split automatically. At the present time it is not. What happens, and the argument goes, is because these are under property laws which fall under provincial jurisdiction, that property which includes pension credits has to be split under provincial jurisdiction.
I think that is kind of sad. Here is an elderly woman who has given her life to a marriage and a breakdown occurs for whatever reason and she is left with with the old age pension. No Canada Pension Plan benefits, even though she may not have been in the work force, as a part of a benefit her husband received as a result of the work she performed in the home. To say that she is not entitled to a part of that pension benefit seems to me to be ridiculous. It is certainly something that this committee should take another look at or at least get a commitment from the minister when he appears before the committee to make a real commitment to look into

this with the provincial governments because it would also require their agreement.
There is a last point I want to make. As you know, under the Canada Pension Plan, there is a child bearing dropout period. In other words, a woman can leave the work force for a period, I think, up to seven years to look after a child and she will not be penalized in the calculation of her Canada Pension Plan contribution period of benefits at the time she is ready to retire.
It is an area that had not arisen before, but has since arisen. The theory is that the seven year old child will be attending school in the formative years and the mother, usually the one who looks after the children in our type of society, could be penalized because she has not made contributions. We looked after that. The seven year dropout provision was fine insofar as it went.
I am interested in taking a look at the act from the point of view of recognizing that there are many care givers, women, mainly mothers, who stay at home to look after disabled children, kids who may not go to school within that seven year period, kids who may never go to school at all because a number of school boards, not having the tax base that there may be in a city like Toronto or Vancouver or St. John's, cannot provide the means to educate a disabled child as can be done in some major centres.
If we cannot provide the means to give such children an education by providing municipalities that do not have the tax base to provide that education, then surely we should not be penalizing the mother who in the main looks after that child and stays at home to do so.
That is another area where I think we should try and get a commitment from the minister when he appears before the committee to take that up with his provincial counterparts to make sure that kind of care giving is not being penalized. It is not only unfair to the woman who in the main is the care provider, it is certainly unfair to the child.
I see I am being signalled that I have a few minutes left. That is about all I wanted to say. It may be a number of years before the Canada Pension Plan revisits this place again. This may be the last opportunity before the next election. I would simply urge members of that committee to seriously discuss not only the questions I
Government Orders
have raised, but many from other members of the House in order to make a real commitment in trying to address those concerns.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much interested in the comments of the hon. member because the question of Canada disability pensions is something that I as a member of Parliament work with just about every week. I meet with constituents who have questions or are in the process of making an appeal. I agree with much of what the hon. member says.
I would like to point out to the House that there is a lot of co-operation and insight that is necessary when an application is made. It certainly helps to have the co-operation and understanding of the local member of Parliament who has had this problem brought to his or her attention and certainly the departmental officials. I always try to bring in the medical profession as well. In the example that the hon member uses where a person's work life has come to an end, we need the co-operation of the medical profession to make that call. Neither the hon member nor I are members of the medical profession. I see one member across from me who is. Sometimes it is a difficult call. When I talk to doctors I try to encourage them to try and come to that conclusion on behalf of an individual. It is so important because a person has to come within the ambit of the law.
One of the examples the hon. member gave was an individual who took on a job teaching English as a second language. Just to complete the picture, I have had examples on the other side where the department has in fact shown some flexibility. One example was an individual in Niagara Falls who had a heart problem who is working today as a traffic guard. I had the same concern as the hon. member that this would finish him with the Canada disability pension. It was only a couple of hours a day, but his doctor had recommended it as part of his therapy. In that particular instance, when the departmental officials had a look at it, they went along and they recognized and agreed that it could be a part of that individual's rehabilitation while at the same time getting a disability pension.

November 18, 1991
Government Orders
I would like to have one question answered by the hon. member. Perhaps it is just a point of a clarification. I think I heard him give an an example of an individual who's disability has begun and it is 15 months, I believe, before they apply. I hope the impression is not left that that individual will be precluded or his statute barred from making the application. It would seem to me that he or she might only get 12 months retroactive benefits, but that person could still apply if he came from having worked within five of the last ten years or two of the last three. The last example would not be perfect because the individual in this case has been out for 15 months. I do not think I want the impression to be left that somebody could not make the application. I certainly encourage individuals to make the application, if they have been in the work force for five of the last ten years. I just caught the member's example of the 15 months where I could see they might lose some of the retroactive benefits, but they would not be precluded from applying. Perhaps the hon. member could explain to me or elaborate on his comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member has asked me that question because it requires some clarification. He is absolutely right in his understanding. I may have left the other impression.
There is one thing I want to clarify where I think I have left some confusion. The individual I spoke about did not go to teaching English as a second language, he went to learn it. He went and took a course to learn English as a second language. He was not working and his doctor felt that it would be good for him mentally to do that, and so he did. As soon as he did, even though he was not working he got cut off. That is the kind of strict interpretation that the language in the act seems to require.
I understand that there are individuals, officers and workers within the Canada Pension Plan system and bureaucracy who exercise some leeway on cases, but it should not be like that. That is the problem with this kind of legislation. Surely to goodness people should have an equal right to access a benefit that they have paid for and which is being administered by a government agency such as the Canada Pension Plan. It should not be up to an individual going to Niagara Falls, for example, and meeting a kindly administrator within the Canada Pension Plan who says: "Mr. Smith, you are absolutely right; you are being treated unfairly. This is nonsense. You are eligible". The same individual could
go into an office in Toronto or Vancouver or St. John's or wherever and meet a grumpy person who says: "I don't care how disabled you are, right. As far as I am concerned I feel lousy this morning". I am not suggesting that is what happens, but the individual is not going to get the benefit even though an individual under the same circumstances in another part of the country receives the benefit because he or she has a more sympathetic administrator within the CPP.
I would like to have that language loosened up so that an individual who does go into a retraining program of whatever nature is not going to have this disincentive and be disqualified simply for doing so.

Mr. Speaker, the current legislation does not allow for retroactive payment to any applicant who is under age 70 at the time of application if the applicant fails to make that application.
I have seen many constituents that have fallen into this trap. I feel that since those Canadians who have worked have contributed to this plan years previous to their retirement it has therefore become their inherent right to claim what they have contributed to in the past.
Why is there a provision that precludes them from applying or getting the benefits if they did not apply in time? I pose that question and I wonder whether the hon. member could comment on the unfairness of a provision in the current act that precludes payment if one happens to apply late and will not be able to recover that even if one had contributed to it. It is one's basic right as a contributor to the plan.

Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned, where an individual makes an application for disability benefits under the CPP and that disability is supported by a person from the medical profession of whatever type that person's application should be considered in that light.
I have run into cases of disability applications. The most common one is a case of someone diving into a lake in the summer without due care and striking his or her head on a rock or boulder or something and breaking his or her neck and becoming either a quadriplegic or a paraplegic. That can happen at any age and that individual very often is not in a position because of this accident to make an application on time, as the department says. If that individual is disabled, surely society has an obligation to to help and give whatever assistance possible to allow him or her to continue to live in the
November 18, 1991

mainstream of Canadian society. That is what this whole thing is about.
It comes down to what kind of society we want to live in and what kind of society we want others to live in. Surely to goodness when we get a piece of legislation that is so strict and the language so tight that it allows practically no leeway there is something wrong with it, especially when it is dealing with individuals who more often than not are being not denied but certainly restricted to any entry back into the work force. Surely we have an obligation not only to those individuals but to ourselves as well.

Mr. Speaker I am very pleased to speak today on Bill C-39, which was tabled just two weeks ago, I believe.

For my own constituents in Mount Royal riding, to address this bill and its implicit amendments to the Canada Pension Plan is somewhat different from what they live with under the Quebec Pension Plan, although for people living anywhere in Canada this plan is a cornerstone of the social safety net that we have built so carefully in this country since 1966, I believe it is.
In my riding where close to 20 per cent of the constituents are 60 years old and over, it is quite an amazing reality. This plan and the program and its implicit impact on Quebec as a guide or direction will be very important in the future.
Many of the changes do not apply to Quebec except for over the next five-year period for which the Quebec Pension Plan has been amended to increase contribution rates at a similar rate for 1992 to 1996, but it does not as yet have a 25-year schedule as does the Canada Pension Plan in the decisions that were taken jointly at the federal and provincial levels.
Government Orders
The benefits, and I want to make this abundantly clear, are not the same in Quebec under the Quebec Pension Plan as they are under the Canada Pension Plan and so I would like to keep my remarks fairly general.
As members of Parliament we are not only interested in how it relates directly to our constituencies but also in how it relates and how the policies brought forward by the government relate to all Canadians from coast to coast to coast. In that regard I think this bill does many important things, particularly with respect to children and to some of the touch-up and remedial measures that are brought in.
There are some questions that have been raised by my colleague who is leading our party in the debate, our member from Winnipeg North. He has raised some very pertinent questions as have other members-and I hope that they will be addressed with a great deal of seriousness-with regard to the well-being of the children who are addressed quite particularly in this bill and the benefits as a result of either a disabled family member or a loss through death. They will be able to have a better income to help support them as they move through their childhood and adolescence to age 18 and, if they are at university, from 18 to 25.
Mainly, as I pointed out, Bill C-39 seeks to preserve the health of the Canada Pension Plan and its ability to make payments through an increased contribution rate. They are looking at a 25-year plan and particularly an adjustment to this five-year period. We have an example of how two levels of government can work together to take a look at changes that are needed.
With respect to the specific amendments, the bill increases the Canada Pension Plan benefit levels for
170,000	dependent children of deceased or disabled plan participants. I think as we are looking more and more at the rights of the child, the needs of the child, as we are looking to sign an international agreement with respect to the child, and as we note the level of poverty, it is important to address all our concerns so that the children can become a well educated work force and become satisfied members of our society and contributing members of society. This is a welcome move. The

November 18, 1991
Government Orders
amount, the $35 we are talking about, may not sound like a great deal of money. If we multiply that times $170,000, I think that it is a significant amount and is at least one step forward in addressing the acute question of child poverty, the one that is preoccupying all of us.
In the light of poverty it is not only poverty in a financial sense that is implied when we talk about poverty, but it is poverty that relates to inappropriate nutrition and inappropriate clothing in the rather harsh and unkind atmosphere of Canada.
It relates to the kind of housing that these children are brought up in. It relates to the size of the family and the structure of the family, whether it is a single parent family headed by a mother or another type of family. We know that close,to 80 per cent of those families live below the poverty line and that it has very serious implications for the well-being of the child.
Any move that we can make to alleviate the stress on children particularly at a time of loss of a family member or if there is a disability of a family member becomes a very key public policy which we welcome on this side of the House.
When I think about the Canada Pension Plan I think about what it is meant to do. It is fundamentally meant to protect us as we age in society and in a sense ensure that although we no longer are in the position to make a contribution to the working world in the sense of work for pay, we still are able to contribute to society in many other ways. Those ways are within the voluntary sphere, within the sphere of enabling role models to exist within society in demonstrating that older people have a place of importance.
To do that you really need to have a healthy society that has financial means to feed, clothe and house its members. In this pension plan the problem that we are dealing with in our own lives and those of our friends is how to have ample income at the end of our working years, be that at age 65, 70 or before or for many reasons such as early retirement, et cetera.
What more noble goal could a country have than one which helps maintain an income stream for Canadians living in any of these situations?
If we think about it, how many of us have friends and neighbours who have retired and who depend on the
Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security and the supplementary benefits that come along so that we can have an adequate living style in our country? We all know that there are more and more Canadians benefiting from these kinds of programs.
We are addressing in this bill the rights of the retirees, the state of health of those retirees, the disabled and the children of deceased plan participants. I guess these important areas and evolving areas have seen changes in the pension plan since it was first conceived back in 1966. I might add it was by a Liberal government.
Quebec provides benefits for its population under the pension plan which was established in 1966, at the same time as the Canada Pension Plan. It exercised its constitutional prerogative to establish a comparable provincial pension plan in lieu of the Canadian Pension Plan.
It would be fair to say that the two programs in many respects are similar in their framework design and eligibility criteria, though the benefits can differ quite significantly.
At the moment Quebec has agreed to amend its own contribution rates to match the increases made in the CPPs for the next five years as set out in this bill. That points out the similarities in this program.
I am told however that Quebec is expected to introduce amendments to revise its own pension plan law, possibly by the end of this year. For the longer period beyond five years, Quebec will still have to pursue its own review of projected benefits and contributions to establish its own requirements for the next 20 years.
I think it could have a different kind of outcome for those under the Quebec Pension Plan than for those found under the Canada Pension Plan. I am not saying that that is better or worse. It might be different.
Despite the differences that exist, I nonetheless believe there is something we can learn from Quebec and we might want to examine that in committee. If we look at what Quebec has done, it has found a mechanism to use the funds in a very creative and helpful way for industry. It has enabled this massive amount of money to be put to constructive and good use in the interest and well being of the citizens of Quebec and the industry in Quebec through the Caisse de depot et placement.
November 18, 1991

I wonder whether there is not an idea there that is worth exploring, an idea which would allow us perhaps to give some consideration, and it may not appear in this bill but it could be examined under this bill, to establishing a dedicated fund for a portion of the contributions that come into the Canada Pension Plan to be invested in a creative way, somewhat similar to what Quebec does in the Quebec model, while the balance could continue to be on call at the low rate of interest for the provinces.
We are in this bill trying to preserve the health of the Canada Pension Plan and its ability to make payments through increased contribution rates. The schedule of increase of the contribution rates will be $7 in 1992 for each person earning the average wage of $30,500. This contribution will increase to $42 by 1996, allowing for a combined employer-employee contribution rate of 4.6 per cent in 1991 and that will increase to 9.1 per cent in 2011 compared to 7.6 per cent by 2011 if the current contribution schedule had been maintained.
Mr. Speaker, I point out to you that Canadians right now sense that they are being taxed to death in many different ways. For the government to bring in what it perceives to be a necessary change at this particular time, I do not think is going to be very happily received by the contributors. It may be necessary but there has to be a different mechanism at this point in time.
The lower and middle income families are hard pressed by the number of people who have their hands in their pockets, from the federal level, from the provincial level, from the municipal level, from the sales and excise taxes. All kinds of people have their hands in their pocket. The government has just increased the unemployment insurance payments both for the employer and the employee and now we are looking at the same kind of increases for the pension plan.
I would hope that in committee there will be a close examination of whether or not one needs to improve it or to insure it to this degree or whether there is not something here the general revenues ought to incur.
I am not a professional in this area. I am not an expert in this area. I believe and hope that both the parliamentary secretary and the members of that committee will take this whole question of the sense of the Canadian
Government Orders
population, that they would like to have a tax revolt, seriously into consideration as they look at this bill.
My colleague from Winnipeg has spoken eloquently to the precise changes in the bill. On behalf of my own constituents in Mount Royal riding, let me address again some of those major principles.
We are considered by the world a leader in how we treat our citizens with caring and compassion. One has only to look at the social safety net that is in place, hopefully not too tampered with and hopefully not too diminished. That would include medicare, family allowance, Old Age Security, pension plan and all the other social network systems that are in place for the well elderly and the not so well elderly as well as for our children.
These kinds of programs could become bureaucratic nightmares for those who try to have access to those plans. You have heard a number of members in this House, Mr. Speaker, talk particularly about the definition of disability, what are the criteria, how do you get access, the time delay in getting access and how it creates additional stress. I hope that kind of bureaucratic problem will be effectively dealt with as the members of the committee address the issues.
I see the parliamentary secretary shaking her head yes. I am very pleased to note that. Certainly we do not need any increased stress on people who are already in a situation of stress.
With those few comments, I would like to wish the committee well in its undertakings. I hope that the small amount of money will relieve those children who are desperately in need. I am sure it is not enough.
However, there are circumstances beyond which we cannot go and it is a step by step process. I hope that the review procedure will indicate that we are not in such such fiscal disarray as I seem to understand from the parliamentary secretary's initial remarks that the fund is in need of additional financing and that this could have been perhaps re-evaluated earlier in 1986 when the first revisions were brought in where it allowed early retirement.
I understand that the then health minister, the present energy minister, indicated that it was not going to have a serious impact. It has or else there were some miscalculations. It has been said that the fund needs something like $90 billion. Is that the amount of money that the plan seems to be short? If that is the case, I hope it will

November 18, 1991
Government Orders
be examined. Ensure yourselves that those are really the financial needs. I would really hope that you will reduce the burden on the contributors as much as is possible while ensuring that the fund is stable and at the same time look at what kind of service is offered to those people and what kind of access they have.
I would like to quote something the National Council of Welfare has said. "We believe it is fundamentally wrong that a public pension program set up to cover the entire paid labour force is incapable of producing benefits large enough to keep most of its beneficiaries out of poverty". It is from that perspective that I hope the government will carefully address the issues that have been brought forth as it brings in a bill of this nature and that we will not have a smoke and mirrors piece of legislation, that it is not just a pretty package, but it will have substance and give succour to those who are in need.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from Mount Royal for her splendid debate on the issue, as usual, as on many other issues.
I particularly want to focus my comment on what she said about the dedicated fund. I think she has touched one crucial point of this debate and that is, has this government in fact been a good financial manager over the last many years? Why do I say that?
As I think was said by the parliamentary secretary to the minister of health in opening debate on this bill, we would like to secure the financial soundness of this plan for our seniors. When I opened my debate, I said nobody would argue against the need to secure the financial soundness of this plan for the seniors of our country.
Again, I would just like to note, because my colleague from Mount Royal did indicate the need for a dedicated fund, the need for sound financial management of our plan. A Winnipeg Free Press editorial of January 13, 1991, did indicate the point as well in terms of how the finance minister of this government had managed to squander so quickly the premium increase he imposed four years ago.
Not one of the provincial ministers questioned the federal minister on this point. The provincial ministers were happy to agree, as has been announced by this government in opening debate on this bill, and who
would not be happy if they dip into the fund at reduced interest rates. Therefore, I think we have to be very careful about the implication of this.
My colleague from Mount Royal indicated the timing of this increase.
Is it the time to do it today? I was glancing at the press release by the government dated October 24, 1991. It says that "in addition to adjusting contribution rates for the next 20 years to reflect new forecasts of expenditures, the bill also extends the schedule by five more years to ensure that there is always a 25-year schedule of rates". Let me proceed to page 2 and the appropriate quotation. It says that "as a result of the first five-year review of the CPP contribution rates by federal and provincial finance ministers, rates will be increased in two stages to ensure that the new rate will be in effect for January 1992".
The first stage of this increase is being implemented by regulation provided under the existing CPP legislation. The second stage of the increase, and I will conclude at this point, an additional increment beginning in 1997 will be implemented once the new legislation, the proposed amendment, has received the required provincial approval.
One wonders why the haste. Why today when in fact this implementation will be in the beginning of 1997.

Just one word. I guess it is a very happy kind of circumstance when you can get money for much less and not have accountability in terms of having to borrow on the open market. They are borrowing out of Canadian taxpayers' pockets. That is exactly what the member pointed out. They could have waited until a little bit later. I hope you are going to examine that when you get into committee. Thank you veiy much for raising that point.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this bill because the Canada Pension Plan and Quebec Pension Plan, along with a number of other measures that have been introduced in Canada over a number of decades, contribute to a quality of life and a security in this country that I think we as Canadians believe are impor-

tant in allowing people to live full, productive, fruitful lives from the time they are bom until the time they die.
Therefore, it is an honour to be able to speak on this program and on this bill, and as my colleague before me has done, to raise some issues that I hope the members of the committee examining this proposed legislation will look at very carefully.
Without going too much into the positive benefits of the legislation, let me raise some of the issues that I hope will receive some attention in committee.
When we are increasing fees like this, we need to recognize the full impact of the fee increases affect those on modest and lower incomes. There is a limit on the income at which people can contribute to the CPP and benefit from it. The impact of any increase in fees falls disproportionately on those earning very modest incomes. In this case the limit on income under which one can make contributions is approximately $30,000.
There are a number of changes in legislation and contributory plans that fall into the same category which have seen an increased financial impact on very modest income earners over the last number of years. Unemployment insurance fees, for instance, fall most heavily-again, because there is an income limit on the program under which you can contribute-on those earning the most modest incomes.
Such things as student loan fees are a tax on a benefit that one receives only because one happens to be from a very low income household. It is fairly important for the committee to look at the cumulative impact on modest income families of a number of policy changes, not just this latest increase in the fees.
It is also important to point out that the CPP was brought in in recognition that over a period of time there would be an increasingly elderly population, and a larger proportion of our population that was retired, not earning. Therefore it was important to do everything possible through the tax system, with RRSPs and such things as CPP, to encourage people to set aside enough for their retirement years so that there would not be a massive demand for public support because people simply did not have enough income to live on.
We have seen the intent of that whole approach of encouraging people to do as much as possible to provide for their own retirement, whether through government
Government Orders
or private programs, being undermined by such things as the clawback of Old Age Security which is going to hit increasingly more modest income seniors' homes as time goes on. I hope the committee will put that into the context in which they are looking at this bill as well and the impact of it.
As well, we know that the situation of small businesses in our country today is not good. We have seen the dramatic rise in the number of bankruptcies and the declining number of jobs and, therefore, the declining number of people contributing through income tax and through programs such as this to the public good in Canada. Businesses go out of business, those jobs being lost forever and therefore the economic base on which we can support such programs into the future are significantly eroded.
Again I think the committee has to look at the impact of this along with increases in unemployment insurances fees and a number of other new expenses such as the cost of administering the GST which falls far more heavily on small businesses than it does on large ones. It should also make sure that in protecting the security of our CPP, we are not creating greater damage out there than the benefits we are achieving, whether it is to modest income earners or to small businesses or to the economy in general.
In that light, I want to pick up on a point that was barely mentioned by my colleague who preceded me and it is the necessity to look at the management of the fund. If this is intended to be a self-financing pension fund then I believe it should be managed as any other good fund. It should not be a plan that uses the contributions received from Canadian workers and employers in a way that subsidizes other activities. In other words, those who contribute, whether as income earners or as employers to the Canada Pension Plan, have a right to be assured that their contributions are gaining the same revenues that any well-managed pension plan would gain in the private market and to know that the revenue on the money in the fund is in fact being used to pay benefits and not being used for other purposes.
I hope the committee will have a very careful look at that because it goes to the heart of what makes the rate increase necessary. How the fund is managed is one aspect of that and how is revenue attributed to it is also aspect of that.

Government Orders
Another aspect of it though is what elements of public policy have led to the need for this increase in funds. While it is matched by a small increase in benefits for instance to surviving children of beneficiaries, the majority of the need for the increase appears to come from the fact that there are and will continue to be fewer contributors while there are and will continue to be more beneficiaries.
Frankly that is something that is happening throughout Canadian society. Canadians are living longer, they are healthier longer and they are more active longer. It is a great tribute to one of the best health care systems in the world of which we should all be proud. Unfortunately it does present us with the problem of how we are going to make sure that people do not live those extra years in poverty but live them in a way that allows them to enjoy them.
However, we also have to look at the other side. Why are contributions not able to meet the obligations? Clearly if you have a higher rate of unemployment, if you have a policy of high unemployment, if you have, as we do now, close to 1.5 million Canadians not working, not earning and therefore both they and their employer not contributing to the Canada Pension Plan, it affects this pension plan and creates directly the need for greater contributions by both employees and employers.
I think we need to look at those other public policies, such as the unemployment policy, that leads to this kind of situation.
We also have to look at the larger number of older workers who are losing their jobs and are not ever again making it back into the labour force. Certainly I and many other members of this House have had some very sad experiences of speaking to constituents who at the ages of 50, 54, 55 are unemployed for the first time in their lives and know that they are never going to be in the labour force again. That is an extremely difficult situation.
As critic for the Public Service I see it in the area of employment that I have to most often deal with and that is the downsizing and lay-offs and contracting out within the Public Service which has reduced the surplus of income to the Public Service Pension Plan over payouts. There is a surplus despite what the National Citizens Coalition might want people to believe that has dropped
from about $400 million a year down to $50 million a year. It very clearly is something we need to be concerned about, when public policies such as lay-offs, early retirement, contracting out of work that was formerly performed by wage earners, is starting to undermine the largest pension plan in this country.
There are a couple of other things that I hope the committee will have a look at. I note that what is described as technical provisions of the bill for instance is greater information sharing among a number of social programs: family allowance, OAS, CPP. I certainly hope that the committee will seek the advice of the Privacy Commissioner in terms of the Privacy Act and any concerns that he may have about that, but I also notice that information is going to be made more freely available to others outside government, so I think that is also a concern.
For instance, I notice that information will be able to be released with regard to criminal proceedings. I want to draw to the attention of the committee that there is another area they might want to consider and that is the way in which the federal government does or does not make information available out of these programs to usually women who are not receiving child support payments that they should be receiving. If we are freeing up the release of information and the access to information about beneficiaries of government programs then that is a very serious area that we need to look at.
I can only compliment the government on the improvement in the children's benefits. We have all been made very aware through the National Symposium on Children just a few weeks ago of the terribly difficult situation of children growing up in poverty in our country. Even though this particular provision will touch
170,000	children, and that is a small proportion of those millions of children who are deprived of opportunities, deprived of education and deprived of the same future as the majority of Canadian children by the simple fact of poverty. This is a small but hopefully significant improvement in the lives of some children.
Finally I want to address the status of women and pensions because I think it is something that the current changes before us do not adequately address. In my view it is high time that we looked at the status of people who work but do not necessarily earn wages in our society. The group consists primarily of women who assume child bearing, child rearing responsibilities for a considerable

period of what otherwise would be an income earning period in their lives.
I hope that the committee will question why changes are not being made so that women who stay at home have greater access to a pension. It is still true that two-thirds of the elderly poor in Canada are women and it is largely because they simply do not have the same ability or access to create pension plans for themselves.
Pension splitting has been mentioned by a number of speakers, so I will not go into details on that, but that is certainly something I hope the committee will address.
One other matter I want to mention is that the committee have a look at the administration of CPP. Whatever the legislation says about the benefits, if one cannot access those benefits in a fair and speedy manner, one does not have those benefits. There are certainly problems in the staffing that is provided with respect to CPP and other benefit programs that severely impact on individuals and create great hardship, for example, if a spouse dies and one has to wait two or three months to start receiving a survivor's benefit. My colleague has already read the statistics on the large proportion of recipients of CPP benefits who have incomes below the poverty line in Canada. When one is already living at below the poverty line, one cannot afford to wait two or three months for a reduced pension. One has to have it right away. That is simply a matter of providing efficient and sufficiently staffed offices to process those applications.
Similarly, if a couple on retirement applies for pension splitting and it takes six months as it has in some cases I have dealt with, it takes six months to process that. That sends out a message that the other spouse, usually the wife, really is not entitled to a pension, it is something which is being done as a matter of generosity to her. In fact it means that an entitlement that a couple has to split their income and to maximize the tax benefits from that has been denied to them for six months.
I hope the committee will consider an amendment to the legislation that would make pension splitting retroactive to the date of application, the government is incapable of providing sufficient staffing to process those things quickly.
As I said, I welcome a look at this bill. I welcome the opportunity to address it. I reaffirm some of the points
Government Orders
that have been raised earlier by others, for instance, the definition of disability and particularly the need to be more generous in accepting definitions of emotional disability or mental disability in processing applications.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the indulgence of the House and I look forward to following the committee's progress on this bill. I hope we will take this opportunity to look at other issues around CPP, the impact of such legislation and the increases in fees at this time in our economy and who it is affecting most.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to my colleague who made some extremely enlightened remarks. I would like to point to two issues that she raised and ask if she has any further information. On the first issue, with respect to having done work on the divorce bill as it went through this House, there was great discussion about the problems around the collection of alimony and how to find the missing spouse.
There was to have been a follow-up by the Minister of Justice. There was the example of I believe Manitoba and the use of the Health and Welfare system so that one could locate the missing spouse and ensure that he or she would meet his commitments with respect to child support payments.
When you look at the exchange of information between programs that is going to be allowable between the CPP, the Canada Pension Plan, the Old Age Security and family allowances information, they tell you that the reason they are doing this is so that pensioners would not experience the frustration of changing their address for their Old Age Security cheque and then have their CPP benefit go astray.
Second, pensioners who submitted a marriage certificate for spousal allowance would not have to send it in again to qualify for the CPP survivor benefit. Third, mothers who receive family allowances for young children would have automatic benefit of a CPP child rearing drop-out provision without having to make a special declaration at a later date.

November 18, 1991
Government Orders
Would it not be fine if they would add another reason? It would be to enable the reduction of the amount of children who live under the poverty line-well over one million children-in this country, most of whom are as a result of broken homes and most of them because the child support system is in arrears and they cannot find the parents.
Certainly they would be able to find the parents under this system, so I would hope there would be an enlarging of that particular aspect. I thank my colleague for bringing that particular aspect to our attention.
She also talked about fair return on your money as a contributor like a taxpayer on your investment dollar. It would seem to me that we are taking money from three pensioners. We are putting it into a fund to be paid to them at a given point in time.
At the same time, that money is lent out to the provinces at a much lower rate. I believe it is around 4 per cent. No one on the government side is standing up to speak to this issue. If they were standing up to speak to the issue, I would ask them the question but as they are not doing so, I will ask my colleague: Do you know of any of the provincial governments that have started a payback to the federal government of the money borrowed since 1966?

Mr. Speaker, if I may start with the first question: No, I am not familiar with the current status of either how the contributions are used or how the rate of return on them is calculated, but I think it is extremely important that the committee assess whether this increase is truly necessary and whether it is necessary at this time.
The committee has got to look at what the rate of return has been on the money people have been contributing for 20 years to this plan, including the contribution of employers. It has got to look at how those compare with other similar sized, well managed funds. I could suggest one or two that members of the committee might want to look at that have managed to pay indexing for instance for the last 10 years without increasing premiums.
I think that is a very important issue for the committee to probe very deeply. It is fundamental to this bill as to whether we need to increase premiums or not.
On the first issue, my colleague raised support and custody child support payments and how to access those. We have a vety serious problem in this country of children going without food, clothing and shelter because one parent, usually the father, has abandoned the family. He can avoid any child support payments by a simple matter of moving from here to Hull, or from northern Ontario to Winnipeg.
The federal government is not doing enough in my view to allow provincial agencies to use federal records to find out where that person is. It comes at two different levels. One, when there is a court order for support, should that person get back an income tax return, or should it really be going to their family?
Second, when there is no income support order, what is the obligation of the federal government, which after all contributes the bulk of the social welfare payments that then have to pick up the obligations that are not being met by one parent? What is the obligation of the federal government to assist in locating that person who is paying income tax, has a social insurance number and in many ways comes in contact with the federal government? Is there an obligation to assist in finding that person so that an order can be made to appear in court and to settle the issue of what support is necessary for the family and should that information be made available? I think this is a good opportunity for the committee to look at how we can ensure that our children are properly supported by parents who can afford to support them, instead of being supported out of the welfare system which dooms them to a life of poverty.

I would like to make a brief comment relevant to what has just been discussed.
