In an item by The London Free Press of June 30, 1990, a statement by Mr. Don Gass of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, indicated that in 1996 the CPP fund was short more than $230 billion. He indicated that by the end of 1988, the shortfall was in the neighbourhood of $300 billion. Obviously, this is very alarming news. I am glad that my colleague for Ottawa West did indicate how crucial it is for the legislative committee to examine and probe the government on its failure of performance.
November 18, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak about Bill C-39 and about one especially important element of the bill dealing with children.
This government in its Speech from the Throne last May clearly stated its commitment to children. It indicated to the House that one of its objectives would be to see Canadian children better educated, better protected and better nurtured.
Today it does give me pleasure to speak about the proposal to increase Canada Pension Plan benefits for children as well as other proposed changes to the plan which are of particular benefit to children.
When speaking about children and the effect of Bill C-39, I want to make the point that this is yet another expression of the concern of this government for the state of children in Canada. There is some urgency in the consideration of this bill because the proposed increases in the benefits to children contained in this bill are scheduled to go into effect in January 1992. If this is to happen, not only must we in this House give this bill second reading and get it to committee and get it back lor third reading, but it must go to the Senate and then it must go, as I understand it, to every province for an Order in Council ratification before the improved benefits will be payable to families in Canada in January 1992 as is planned.
The major proposal would provide dependent children of deceased or disabled Canada Pension Plan contributors with a significant monthly increase of $35 per child. This represents a 30 per cent increase over the current benefit of $113 per month. This benefit would flow to an estimated 170,000 children in Canada, children of disabled or deceased Canada Pension Plan contributors, if we get this work done, effective January 1, 1992.
The affected children include dependent children under age 18 and those age 18 to 25 who are in full time attendance in school. It is noteworthy that the increase received the unanimous support of the federal and provincial finance ministers at their meeting in January 1991 in concept. As I said earlier, it must be ratified before the end of December 1991 in order for the payments to become effective January of the coming year.
Government Orders
The children's benefit increase was initially put forward in the federal government's 1987 consultation paper on Canada Pension Plan survivor benefit reform. The consultation paper contained a proposal for the over-all reform of the CPP survivor benefit structure in an effort to make survivor benefits more appropriate to the needs of Canadians. While federal and provincial finance ministers agree on the concept of a new survivor benefit structure, a consensus on the design of the benefit structure has not yet been solidified. However, in the interim the finance ministers decided to proceed immediately with the increase for children. Hon. members will also be pleased to note that this increase will not add significantly to the short or the long-term costs of the Canada Pension Plan being less than 1 per cent of the over-all plan expenditures.
The 1987 federal consultation paper was referred to a parliamentary committee which subsequently held public consultations. During this process the children's benefit increase received the support of major interest groups such as the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Canadian Labour Congress and the National Association of Women and the Law. The benefit improvements are in line also with the parliamentary committee's recommendations.
This increase responds to both social change and the economic vulnerability of children. Social changes since the 1960s have had a dramatic impact on the family, and in particular on children. These changes include an increase in marital separations and divorce. There has been an increase in single parent families and family situations where the dependant child of a deceased contributor may not live in the same household even as the surviving spouse.
In view of these developments, Mr. Speaker, it is desirable that the Canada Pension Plan do its part to target more assistance to children who are often the truly real dependants.
The proposed increase will also recognize the sometimes difficult circumstances faced by Canada Pension Plan survivors, as well as by severely disabled contributors having dependent children. We know that children in such situations often have lower incomes than children in Canada as a whole. Therefore, the increase will provide a measure of additional support to a particularly

November 18, 1991
Government Orders
vulnerable group. As such, this increase is an important investment in children, our most cherished resource.
The legislative Bill C-39 also includes a number of minor amendments to the Canada Pension Plan. I would like to briefly discuss two amendments which directly affect children. The Canada Pension Plan provides a disabled contributor's child benefit to the dependant children of a disabled contributor and provides orphans benefits on the death of a contributor. In situations where benefits are payable to dependant children of a disabled contributor, and the contributor should die, it is proposed that the children's benefits would now automatically convert to orphan's benefits without the need for an additional application. The existing need for an application can result in an interruption in payment for children at a particularly difficult time. The proposal would ensure uninterrupted payment and seems a very practical innovation indeed.
The legislative proposals would also provide Canada Pension Plan children's benefits to a child who comes under the care and custody of a Canada Pension Plan contributor after the contributor becomes disabled. Under the existing legislation, only a natural child bom after the month of disability and a child legally adopted after that month can receive that benefit. This proposed change would ensure the equal treatment of children under the program. While these are minor amendments, they will ensure that the plan remains sensitive to the needs of children.
This sensitivity is in line with this government's broader efforts to target more assistance to those in need. Since the beginning of its mandate this government has introduced a variety of income-related initiatives which respond to the needs of lower income families with children. For example, the 1987 amendments to the Canada Pension Plan under then Bill C-116 provided for the payment of two children's benefits where the earnings of both parents were lost through death or disability; previously, only one such benefit was payable. The bill also removed the marital status criteria from children's benefits at that time. This ensured that the provisions were in line with the equality provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Major changes have also been made to federal income supplementation programs and federal income tax provisions. The refundable child tax credit has been substantially enhanced
during this government's mandate. The maximum benefit increased from $384 per child in 1985 to $585 in 1991.
A new $200 per child supplement to this tax credit was introduced in 1988 for children six years of age and under. To ensure that these benefits are more responsive to the needs of lower income Canadian families a November prepayment of both of these benefits was introduced. The refundable goods and services tax credit replaced a federal sales tax credit and provides enhanced benefits as a result of the GST program.
The child tax exemption, which was of greater value to higher income families, was replaced in 1988 by a new dependant child credit to better target assistance. This credit provides increased benefits for third and subsequent children in a family. Also in 1988 the child care expense deduction for children six years and under and those with special needs was doubled from $2,000 to $4,000 per child and the family ceiling was removed.
This government is also proud to have played a major international role on behalf of Canadian children and on behalf of children from around the world. In September 1990 the Prime Minister co-chaired the World Summit for Children. Following that summit the children's bureau was created within the Department of National Health and Welfare. Its responsibilities cover a broad range of issues affecting all Canadian children. The children's bureau is currently preparing an action plan for children.
I would like to remind hon. members of our responsibilities to those children who are among the most vulnerable groups in our society. The proposed changes in this bill are a further investment in our children. Parliament's strong support for these proposed changes on behalf of the children of disabled or deceased Canada Pension Plan contributors will convey to them as well as to all Canadians the concern and the commitment that I believe we all share.
In order that these increased benefits for children become applicable in Januaiy 1992 I urge the members of this House to support BUI C-39 at second reading. They should get it into committee as quickly as possible to get it back to this House for third reading and passage to the Senate and the subsequent process of ratification by Orders in CouncU from all of the provinces. This wUl implement these very important increases on behalf of

children in Canada under the Canada Pension Plan program.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member for Fredericton- York-Sunbury for his presentation. He opened with the statement that this bill is yet another expression of this government's commitment to children because there is the proposed increase in benefits for dependants of deceased or disabled contributors to the plan.
As I indicated in my debate on the bill earlier this morning, no one would argue against giving benefits to children. I have one question. Almost a year ago the Prime Minister participated in the World Summit for Children. Today the member indicated that the children's bureau which was created perhaps around that time is still only preparing a plan of action. It is more than a year later because the summit was about September of last year.
Yet here we are presented with a bill on a tight schedule which must be passed because we will deprive our children of benefits. Is this a sincere effort?
My thoughts on this are shared by one excellent writer, Mr. Leonard Shifrin, The Toronto Star, February 4,1991. He labelled the type of benefits in this plan as a candy coating. True, they are important benefits.
One wonders about the sincerity of this government when we are rushed into passing a bill and when this is related to a statement made when increases to contributions were announced by this government some four years ago that there would be no additional cost to other programs. Now it is asking again for increases. The editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 30, 1991 rightly asked the question: "Why should anyone suppose that the government is counting accurately now?"
I would like the member to respond to this challenge from the editorial. Why would Canadians believe that the figures today are correct and that it has been made on a sound basis? If this government is truly for the welfare of our children, particularly the poor, why has it cut transfer payments for education? Why has this government to date not introduced the child care legisla-
Govemment Orders
tion that it promised during the election campaign of 1988?

Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to agree with the general principle expressed by the hon. member that we should always be acting more quickly in initiatives. This is particularly true for children and certainly on behalf of families with children who are in low income situations, who are in distressed circumstances. I am sure the Prime Minister and all members of this government share his impatience for an action plan on behalf of children to emanate from the children's bureau. This is one which I understand has already been drafted and discussed with many provinces and which requires confirmation across this country. It is an expression of just how difficult the political process can be sometimes. On issues where we have complete consensus and agreement we sometimes cannot move as quickly as we would like. I share your view that we should accelerate our efforts through the children's bureau and follow up on the international summit on children as expeditiously and as effectively as we can.
With respect to the member's comments about the changing rates in the Canada Pension Plan, it is my understanding-and I am not an authority on the Canada Pension Plan-that it was intended and designed to be an actuarially responsible plan from the beginning. It was also to be reviewed in five-year increments and would be accompanied by actuarial studies. I understand that the eleventh actuarial study was the precedent for the proposed change in rates.
The plan has matured and the benefits have been paid. I believe Canadians enjoy very significant benefits from the Canada Pension Plan. However, the financial solvency of the plan is always at risk. It was intended from the start that there would never be less than a two-year capability of benefit reserves in the plan.
We are told now that if the present rates are left unchanged that by the year 2011 the reserve will shrink to less than six months. That is unacceptable. There is no other alternative than to change the rates. Any insurance kind of program or pension plan kind of program that is actuarially sound has to do this. That is what we are seeing here.
I think the hon. member knows that. It distresses me a little to see a sort of political tone put to the questioning of what he knows to be an actuarially designed Canada Pension Plan that is not in any way dependent upon government revenues, either federal or provincial, in a

November 18, 1991
Government Orders
direct and significant way. It was always contemplated that these premiums would change with the needs as the plan became mature. I think to imply otherwise on any political basis is simply not reasonable and not correct.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise and speak on this issue of pensions for seniors.
I hope that when this bill gets to committee it is examined in detail. I hope the committee really takes a look at the plight of seniors in this country.
Our parents and grandparents worked hard to build Canada. They have contributed much and they deserve to be able to live with dignity and an insured income in their retirement so that they do not have to worry about their financial security in their old age.
Much of the discussion this afternoon has had the tone to it that basically if elderly people in this country are not well off, at least they are getting by. The tone of this bill is one of simply housekeeping amendments to deal with some of the actuarial problems in the fund and to give a minor increase in terms of benefits to dependent children and to maybe tinker with the definitions of disabilities.
I think it is important that we in this House and in committee really take a look at the situation of the elderly in Canada. There is 50.8 per cent of unattached individuals over 65 and 24 per cent of all seniors who live below the poverty line in Canada. That is 50 per cent of unattached seniors and 24 per cent of all seniors who live in poverty.
Older women are twice as likely to be poor than men. Elderly women in this country in large measure live in poverty. The incomes of most Canadians drop dramatically when they reach retirement. Even with the Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement the benefits do not meet their requirements.
The Canada Pension Plan was designed only to replace 25 per cent of pre-retirement income. I do not know who in this House believes that they can live on 25 per cent of their pre-retirement income. Only 37 per cent of
employed women and 54 per cent of employed men belong to a private pension plan in this country.
It is unforgivable that in this day and age in a western industrialized society only 37 per cent of employed women and 54 per cent of employed men belong to a private pension plan.
Take a look at what has happened in the last few years in terms of pensions. Workers have seen the values of their pensions cut dramatically by inflation. At the same time investments and pension funds have gone up because of high interest rates. Over and over again private companies have looted their pension funds for their own use. They say that the increase in return because of high interest rates is no longer needed. They do this rather than passing those pension increases on to their previous employees.
Workers do not have the ability to transfer from one pension program to another pension program in this country. They often lose their employer's benefits when they go from one employment to another employment in the private field.
I think we should take a look at the record of this government over the last few years as it relates to seniors and whether seniors are better off now than they were a few years ago.
First of all it brought in the clawback to the old age pension. It is simply saying that seniors do not need any money over $50,000 a year. That is not indexed so it is going to decrease buying power. It is simply saying to seniors: "That is the maximum income you should ever have, $50,000 a year".
There has been an attack on seniors in terms of their ability to look after themselves. The patent legislation on drugs has dramatically increased the cost of prescription drugs to seniors in this country.
Nonsense.

"Nonsense", you say. Just read the reports that indicate the difference between prescription drugs and generic drugs and the cost of them in this country. PharmaCare programs across this country are faced with the reality that prescription drug costs are going up. Go into any old age pensioner group and ask whether their drug costs have not gone up dramatically in the last few years.

They have dropped.
November 18, 1991

They have dropped if they are generic drugs but not if they have been protected under the Patent Act.
The whole free trade deal has opened up this country to an Americanization of our health care system. That is threatening it, particularly when it is coupled with the cutbacks by this government in the transfer payments that will not support health care. Seniors are frightened and justifiably so that health care in this country is under attack mainly because the federal government has reneged on its commitment to a joint partnership in health care and joint funding of health care.
This federal government has washed its hands of housing. It has simply said it is going to turn that responsibility over to the provinces. It has kept a high dollar policy that has hurt our economy.
Where were you in Question Period? There is no high dollar policy.

There is no high dollar polity, they say. When a government consistently does something to keep the Canadian dollar high we on this side finally come to the conclusion, reluctantly, that it must have a policy. If it does not have a policy then it does not understand the consequences of its decision.
Are you trying to tell me that the government does not understand what it is doing? Its policies and procedures are keeping the Canadian dollar high. Are you trying to tell me that is purely accidental? Come on. Even the Conservatives in their ineptitude in financial management cannot wash their hands and say: "We do not have a policy". Maybe they do not, maybe the Conservatives do not have any economic policy.
Then there is the GST and how it has hurt seniors across this country.
Tell us about the rebate.

Seniors repeatedly say the rebate has not covered the increased costs of goods and services they have had to pay. They say this openly and clearly. They are going to ensure the government understands that during the next election when they vote it out.
It is not just in the last few years that seniors have not been adequately served in terms of pensions in this country. The Liberals were in power for much of the last
Government Orders
25 years and they failed to develop adequate pension plans to ensure that all seniors could live in income security and dignity. They did not bring in a homemaker's pension for women when they had the opportunity to do so. They did not bring in programs designed to ensure that all seniors lived above the poverty line.
In the early 1980s, with their great six and five program, they cut the indexing of Old Age Security. They taught the Conservatives how to cut back and the Conservatives learned well from the Liberals in the early 1980s.
What did Bob Rae do?

The Liberals learned and taught the Conservatives how to cut back universally on health care transfer payments and deindex Old Age Security. They then brought in the whole business of the RRSPs. The RRSPs are to make sure that the wealthy do not have to rely on the Canada Pension Plan and that they do not have to rely on such things as private pension plans. It is most beneficial to the wealthy in this country. The Tbries come along and they increase the ceiling for the RRSPs up to the contribution of $86,000. Between the two of them, $11.4 billion this year will be lost in tax revenue for people contributing to the RRSPs. The fact is that tax money is the same as if it were taxed and given back in grants.
The whole issue of how we develop a co-ordinated pension program for seniors from all walks of life, not just for the wealthy through RRSPs, not just through employers and employees to the Canada Pension Plan, is something that this House and this government and this country must tackle. In spite of all of the rhetoric here today, we have not done a good job for our seniors. We have not guaranteed that they have an adequate income so that they can look forward to their retirement with a certain degree of dignity and security of income.
I think there are a number of things that we in the New Democratic Party have continued to set out as things that must be done to ensure that our social security programs are adequate for those over 65. We certainly must restore the co-operative funding under the Canada Health Act. We must restore the partnership in which the federal government shares equally with the province in the funding of health care in this country.

Government Orders
We must reverse programs like the clawbacks to Old Age Security. We must look at at least doubling the Canada Pension Plan so that working Canadians will have access to an adequate indexed pension plan.
An increase in the deficit.
We must make sure that pension plans are available for homemakers.
Do not forget the promise of no tuition fees.

And homemakers have the right to have their work valued and to have their opportunities preserved to ensure that their old age is a time when they do not have to have financial worries.
We must ensure that there is fairness in our taxation, that we do not have large tax loopholes for the wealthy like through RRSPs in which a person who is earning $86,000 and contributes $1,000 a month gets a tax refund of just under $500 a month compared to the person who is earning only $20,000 and contributes $1,000 and gets only a tax refund of $265. What kind of a taxation system is it that for equal contributions to an RRSP fund the wealthy get twice as much back as the low or middle income earner? Is that a fair taxation system? I think we have to take a look at that as well.
The committee should start looking at all of these kinds of issues around pensions.
This bill has some benefits to it. It certainly goes some way in dealing with some of the issues. I like everyone support the increase in dependent children's benefits. The benefit is to be increased $35, from $113 to $154.54.
I hope that the committee looks at whether the government has negotiated with the provinces to ensure that any increase in the federal Canada Pension Plan benefit is not simply taken away from benefits being paid to the same children under provincial income security programs. This is often what happens. Unless the child is totally independent or has sufficient funds to support himself, he is on some form of provincial benefit.
When the federal government or the Canada Pension Plan increases that benefit then there is a decrease in the provincial benefit.
I think it is good that there is a re-examination of the definition of "disabled". I trust that the committee will take a very long look not only at the definitions but at the procedures for establishing disability.
One of the things that is most frustrating to all MPs is to try to work with people in the riding who are applying for these kinds of pensions and feel that they are being held up from receiving a pension because of a very rigid definition. They do not understand. They do not feel that there is justice in it. They have contributed to the Canada Pension Plan for years. They do not understand the difference between prolonged or significant disabilities, extended or other kinds of definitions of terminology. They simply know that they are unable to work in gainful employment and that the likelihood of them working in gainful employment is not there. They do not understand why they have to get so many medical reports and go through so much process. What they see is simply bureaucratic red tape that is intended to disqualify them.
I think the committee needs to take a look at how we set in not only legal definitions but procedures that have some human face to them and take into consideration the nuances that a person feels when they are disabled.
I have had people saying that their disability pensions are being threatened because they have taken a job as a volunteer in an agency. They are putting in a few hours a week helping at a centre. In order for that centre to give them some recognition, it does two things. It refers to them as being employed rather than a volunteer and it may give them an honorarium to offset their costs of bus fare, clothing or something else. All of sudden someone comes along and says: "But you are working; you are employed by a non-profit agency". Here is an opportunity for a person to improve the quality of life and it is being threatened.
I see the Speaker is indicating that I have one minute left. I guess I do not have time to talk about the issue of the actuarial soundness of the fund because that is another major issue this committee must look at.
The provinces have been receiving money from the fund at a cut rate. That does have some benefits to
November 18, 1991

provinces, to Canadian taxpayers, but it is at the expense of our seniors. I hope that the committee takes the opportunity to examine whether the benefits to the provinces outweigh the disadvantages to seniors.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I thought, since it is approaching six o'clock, I would rise and bring to your attention and that of the Thble the existence on the Order Paper of an order framed as a motion for concurrence which will, at 6 p.m. this date become an order of this House, an order requiring the government to revoke a statutory instrument, that being the Agricultural Exhibitions Loans Order.

Mr. Speaker, during the five or six minutes I have left, I would like to respond first of all to comments by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Surrey North, who, among other things, criticized the Liberal Party because of certain aspects of our former policies.

The previous speaker seemed to take umbrage at the fact that this party when it was in government brought in the CPP but that it was not quite up to the specifications that he thinks are adequate. He forgot to mention the fact that the plan exists because of efforts of a Liberal government in the 1960s, as does the national medicare plan, and proceeded instead to focus his comments on a tax.
I try not to be overly partisan in some of the things that I say here but this one really caught me by surprise, particularly coming from the NDP. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in our province the NDP is now known as the party that never delivers on promises. It is the party that promised free tuition fees and then abandoned that. The promise of public auto insurance was abandoned. Promise after promise has been abandoned by the party that stands up and pontificates on what a good pension plan it
Government Orders
would bring in if it ever had the good fortune to be elected as a national government, a thought that sends shivers up my spine.
The member from Surrey North talked about RRSPs being a major cause of unfairness. The party of organized labour came in here to complain about the deductibility of contributions to pension plans, the party of Bob White and the United Auto Workers, whose members have one of the fattest pension plans in Canada, the party of organized labour across Canada, each of whose units goes about trying to negotiate the fattest pension plans possible and whose members all get deductions for every dollar they contribute to their private pension plans, wants to foreclose the possibility of self-employed individuals making their own little nest egg through RRSP contributions. That is the kind of party the NDP is. If somebody can get a good job with security of tenure and a nice pension plan, well they can just roll in it. But if somebody has to go out and create jobs for other people and take risks, well, they better be prepared to live on the CPP when they retire because that is all they are good for. I cannot believe it.
On the CPP itself, I have a couple of concerns that I want to raise on behalf of my constituents. First of all, I do not know how many people in my generation have commented to me that they do not ever expect to collect the Canada Pension Plan. This is a very commonly held notion among people of my generation, that somehow or other this fund is just not going to be worth that much to us when we reach retirement age and that indeed is the reason for the enormous support for Registered Retirement Savings Plans among people who are my contemporaries.
The thought is that we have to provide for ourselves because for some reason this plan is just not going to make it to the end of our days in the form that it now exists. For that reason, I would like to say that I am entirely in support of the principle of re-examining at an early stage the adequacy of funding from an actuarial point of view of the Canada Pension Plan.
It is fundamental to the survival of the social network in our country that each Canadian believes that the system is there not just to support somebody else but that it will support each of us. Every Canadian who is contributing must believe that if he or she becomes

disabled, unemployed or is sick that our social benefits will be there for them to rely upon.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you have indicated, all members of the House of all parties have joined together tonight to debate a subject euphemistically known as the situation in Yugoslavia.
Over the past six months members of this House and the people of Canada have watched with horror as the country of Yugoslavia has tom itself apart. All of us have spoken to constituents whose hearts are tom and broken when they see what was their former homeland being mined in the devastation of war. Many of them have spoken in telephone conversations with relatives and friends in Yugoslavia whose voices are tightened by fear and apprehension of what is going to happen to them.
Tonight we want to express our concern, our worries, our apprehensions for the people of Yugoslavia and our repugnance for what is going on in that country. The very foundations of this Balkan country, which when created seemed to afford an acceptable political solution for the peoples of the region, are now being shaken. All these peoples have reached the conclusion that Yugoslavia as we know it can no longer continue to exist. A new arrangement between Yugoslav republics must be found. The present situation in Yugoslavia is a tragedy without precedent in recent European history. As you know, thousands of lives have been sacrificed and hundreds of thousands of innocent people have been forced to flee from their homes because of the fighting.
It is also the most significant challenge to European security and stability since the democratic upheavals recently experienced in all the countries of eastern Europe. I will try to explain the situation as the Canadian government sees it. To begin with, the current situation in the Yugoslav republics is highly complex and there is
November 18, 1991

no one explanation for the conflict between Serbs and Croats. This conflict is not purely ethnic or purely ideological or religious or economic in nature. These factors are all involved, but what we are seeing is the bitter fruit of deep rooted visceral recriminations and fears that date back for decades. It is also and above all a sign of the flagrant lack of trust between these ethnic groups. In the Yugoslav conflict, accusations of genocide are tossed back and forth with disconcerting facility.
It is true that the elections held during 1990 in all the Yugoslav republics brought results in certain republics that stood in stark contrast to those of others. Thus Serbs and Montenegrins elected socialist parties of clearly communist origins. By contrast, the Slovenes, Croats, Macedonians, and the nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina rejected communism. All these governments, elected in many cases on highly nationalistic platforms, immediately began to transform the relationships that had governed them until that time. It was then that fundamental and so far irreconcilable differences began to appear between the Yugoslav republics.
The Slovenes feel that their situation is relatively simple. They account for 90 per cent of the population of Slovenia and the vast majority voted by referendum to form an independent republic. In Croatia, where 75 per cent of the people are Croatians, a referendum also showed that the majority desired independence. However, the Serbs in Croatia who make up 12 per cent of the republic's population are one of the Gordian knots in the present crisis. Many of them have taken up arms to express their strong opposition to the Croatian plans for independence and even to claim their own independence from Croatia. Ethnic Serbian regional governments have even formed within Croatia. Their goal is to maintain these territories in a renewed Yugoslavia, where all who wish to may continue as a part of the country, despite the forceful redefinition of boundaries that this would entail.
This is what Serbia and its allied Montenegro are also advocating. The republic of Macedonia, in the country's far south, shares the Croatian desire for independence from the Serbs. Meanwhile, in a recent referendum, the Macedonians voted in favour of a sort of association where a certain number of the ties, mainly economic in nature, would be retained with the other republics.
Finally, there is Bosnia-Herzegovina, a microcosm of Yugoslavia, containing an amalgam of peoples including Muslims numbering 44 per cent, Serbs numbering 31 per cent and Croats 17 per cent. Complicating all this is the additional claim to a form of autonomy being made by the Serbs of Bosnia, and the Albanians and Muslins of Serbia.
A mere glance at the map of Yugoslavia shows that to divide up the country according to aspirations of these groups would be virtually impossible. Thus we see that we have before us a situation infinitely more complex than some of the protagonists would have us believe in their efforts to gain support. We have a very delicate interplay of peoples all in varying degrees claiming the right to self-determination. We also have before us ethnic groups which, right or wrong, fear greatly for their physical and cultural survival.
How can the rights and the safety of the minorities be guaranteed and the legitimate aspirations of the majority peoples be respected at the same time? In our system we would accomplish this by dialogue and comprise. In Yugoslavia the opposite is true. We find deep distrust on all sides, for example between Croatian and federal armed forces, which makes it tremendously difficult for either side to take the first step. The well-known story of the 12 or 13 cease-fire agreements bears sad witness to this.
The international community and especially the European countries are faced with a tremendous challenge. On the one hand are the legitimate aspirations of various national groups which wish to rebuild relations with their neighbours on new foundations and to participate in the construction of a new Europe. On the other hand is the gratuitous use of violence by the Yugoslav federal army, which is out of the control of the government and which has its own political agenda, and by numerous armed groups in Croatia, Serbia and elsewhere which are using force as a political argument. All this is taking place in Europe, which we felt was finally safe from the threat of military confrontation when the cold war ended.
The international community is not looking on passively as the savage war in Yugoslavia rages. In spite of

what is being said by the protagonists who see the only acceptable solution as their own, the European community, supported by the 38 countries of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, has made available to the parties a series of peace making and negotiating tools.
From the very outset of the crisis the European community, in particular the Netherlands presidency, has taken concrete steps to create conditions for a cease-fire. A diplomatic offensive unprecedented in Europe has been mounted by the Netherlands Minister Van den Broek and his colleagues in an effort to stop the fighting. They have developed compromise solutions which have had some positive results. The violence has quelled in Slovenia and the federal forces have withdrawn from the republic. They have also managed to assemble the Yugoslav parties around the same table to discuss a comprehensive solution to the crisis.
None of this would have been possible without the support of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. This forum, which aside from Yugoslavia itself includes all the European countries, Canada and the United States, has stood surety for the efforts of the European Community. It was the CSCE that gave the European Community the mandate to send a mission of 200 observers first to Slovenia, then to Croatia, and now to other areas at risk.
As soon as the mission was announced,Canada expressed its interest in participating. With Poland, Czechoslovakia and Sweden, Canada gave a broader stature to this mission co-ordinated by the European presidency. Often under threat and in dangerous straits our observers have borne witness to the repeated violations of the various cease-fire agreements by both sides. They have also provided their assistance to avert violence in localized confrontations. Finally they have contributed to a number of operations to provide humanitarian assistance to those who are suffering in the conflict.
We should all take pride that Canadians have been able once again to play a peacemaking role in foreign conflicts. I know that my colleagues in the House would applaud that effort on the part of the Canadian peacekeepers. But our country is not limited to acting through multilateral organizations alone. Even though we are far
away our government has seen the civil war in Yugoslavia as an issue of great importance to its foreign policy.
Our colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, has taken a personal interest in this matter. She has made use of her numerous meetings with her European counterparts to exchange views on the situation and to see what specific contribution Canada could make. She has attended a series of international conferences with the Prime Minister. The most recent of these was the NATO summit meeting in Rome. It reaffirmed the need to achieve a peaceful solution to the crisis in Yugoslavia.
On November 8, 1991 Canada joined the European Community in imposing economic sanctions on Yugoslavia. This action has been followed by similar measures by the United States, Japan, Australia and other countries.
The Government of Canada decided to impose sanctions on all Yugoslav republics to show unequivocally our wish to see all parties cease hostilities and participate fully in the negotiation process. Canada supports the principle of negotiation contained in the proposal tabled by the European Community at the peace conference in Yugoslavia. We believe that sanctions, as difficult as they may be, constitute the best means at our disposal at this time to end this senseless war.
We cannot say it often and firmly enough. Canada is opposed to modifying boundaries by force and to imposing a fait accompli. If these are the Yugoslav army's objectives in Croatia it had better think again. Canada shares its position with all the countries of the European Community, NATO, CSCE and the United Nations Security Council. We also strongly oppose the attempts of the Yugoslav army and ultra-nationalist militia to seek to modify the ethnic make-up of certain regions by force, thus causing the exodus of tens of thousands of people.
Several forced evacuations of civilian populations, particularly women and children, have already occurred in various regions of Croatia. The Yugoslav army's determination to control Dubrovnik can only be understood in this light.
Some of our colleagues in this House have suggested that Canada grant diplomatic recognition to the unilateral declarations of independence of Croatia and Slovenia. They may do that again tonight. In so doing they have echoed the demands of the members of Canada's Croatian community who see this recognition as a way of countering Serbian claims against Croatia. This responds to the express wish of a majority of Croats. They
November 18, 1991

maintain that diplomatic recognition would end this violence. A number of us have received a fax today from the Croatian Information Centre again requesting this.
Canada's position on this is clear. We must always support the move of other members of the international community to have a co-ordinated peace offensive. By recognizing the independence of Slovenia and Croatia now we would ring the deathknell of the negotiation process.
That is why Canada, the European Community, Japan and others have imposed sanctions to allow the negotiations to continue. If these negotiations are a total failure, violence and force would be the only means left to settle this crisis.
I am sure that no one in this House or anywhere else in Canada wants this to happen. We feel that it is necessary to ensure that genuine negotiations are held to determine the future of all the constituent parts of Yugoslavia and to ensure that this takes place with full respect for the rights of all concerned. That is exactly what we are prepared to do by imposing sanctions. This will convince all parties to end the violr ;e and to return to the negotiating table.
Canada has also been active in the United Nations where the Prime Minister initiated the debate on Yugoslavia. Canada played a key role in informing the Security Council about the crisis in Yugoslavia. This led to resolution 713 and a greater role for the Secretary-General. This has proven especially important in the last few days. The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have stated repeatedly that Canada was prepared to contribute to an international peacekeeping force in Yugoslavia. If the conditions can be established for sending such a force, Canada is prepared to play an even greater role in the peaceful resolution of this conflict.
Canada did not wait for the United Nations to debate the issue before imposing an embargo on the sale of arms to Yugoslavia. Since the start of the crisis the Secretary of State for External Affairs has refused to issue licences to export arms or other military goods to Yugoslavia.
I do not wish to overlook the sustained efforts made by our employees in our posts abroad. They are in Belgrade and Zagreb and since the beginning of this crisis they have ensured the security of Canadians living in or visiting Yugoslavia. Two letters have been written to all Canadians in Croatia who are registered with our embassy recommending that they leave the combat area. Recent contacts with these people nevertheless indicated that most of them had chosen to remain in Croatia. Croat and Slovenian citizens who intend to stay in Canada and who would have difficulty getting to Belgrade can obtain visas for Canada from other Canadian diplomatic missions in the region.
As I said at the beginning of my speech, the crisis in Yugoslavia constitutes a challenge to the security of Europe. It also constitutes a challenge to the international community as a whole in its efforts to assist small groups of nations unable to agree among themselves on the form of their future relations.
Canada is in the forefront of those nations wishing to assist Serbs, Croats, Slovenians and other Yugoslavs in overcoming this crisis. Our country will do all it can in co-operation with our friends and allies to help these peoples to restored peace and harmony.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say also to the member of Parliament for Mississauga West that we hope during the course of debate we will have the opportunity to hear about his concerns. We know he does have a substantial number of Croatian Canadians in his riding and we certainly will welcome his involvement in the debate.
In that spirit let me begin by saying that many Canadians have waited a long time for this Parliament to address this issue. As each day goes by we have seen more suffering, tragedy, destruction, death and more conflict. The level of deep apprehension, concern and anguish, sometimes directly for those who have loved

ones or family in that besieged part of the world, has reached a pitch of not knowing what to do. There is frustration in not finding in this forum an opportunity to have it expressed.
I would just say in parenthesis that it may demonstrate, as we look at the role of Parliament, that we must find a much better way of making this institution flexible enough and responsible enough that it can deal with these recurring international crises with a great deal more sensitivity and certainly a great deal more speed.
I do not want to give a speech tonight on parliamentary procedure, but rather I want to talk about what is happening in Yugoslavia and what should be done to end the killing as soon as possible.
I must say that I waited with some anticipation for the comments of the parliamentary secretary to see what initiatives the government may be announcing tonight to provide further involvement, further engagement, further intervention, and unfortunately and sadly there was nothing more to say.
The reason I remind the House of this is that it was just about a year ago today that this Parliament was seized with the issue of what was happening in the gulf area. I could tell then there was no hesitation. There was no too little too late. There were no modest, prudent, cautionary words.
The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs were standing on the barricades ready to do anything possible. The entire western world was being mobilized. The largest army of the last 40 years was being readied to be launched. Thousands of ships were in the gulf ready to impose a sanctions program. It was all done because we were going to have, to quote the United States President, a new world order where aggression, conflict and the use of arms would not be the arbiter of human affairs and we would find a way to resolve these problems before they resulted in senseless killing of civilians.
We have retreated a long way from the brave new world or the new world order of a year ago to where we are today on Yugoslavia. One of the real tragedies, aside from the loss of life and the destruction of property and the breakdown of civil order in what is left of Yugoslavia, is the disillusionment of the world that increasingly sees double standards being applied as to whom and where
and when and how the international community will respond.
If the parliamentary secretary really thinks in his heart that what has happened up to now on behalf of the European Community or the United Nations is enough, then I would ask him to go back and read the speeches of his Prime Minister and others who talked about the need finally for the world to say that we will not let force become the big stick that beats people back, that the international community will find a different way, and that sovereignty of nations imposes duties as well as rights. The primary duty of any nation is to protect the lives of its citizens and when it begins to abuse that right and not fulfil that duty then the international community has a right to intervene.
I would say that one of the better speeches of the Prime Minister was the one he gave at Stanford University a couple of months ago in which that same principle was put forward, except now when we look at the practice, now when we look at what is happening, where is it? It may be that Yugoslavia is not sitting on a pool of oil. It may be that Yugoslavia does not fit in to the strategic design of the great powers. It may be for all kinds of other reasons when we get down to the fundamentals, the issue is still there.
Tonight in towns and villages in Croatia there is fighting going on and people are being killed and the international community has gone fishing. There has been action. There have been calls for conferences and eight, nine, ten, twelve cease-fires-broken immediately-but what has been missing has been resolve, political will, a real full scale, full court press by the President of the United States, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Prime Minister of Canada and other European nations to show they really mean business.
The parliamentary secretary referred to the United Nations action of an arms embargo. I would refer him to the article written by Olivia Ward, the correspondent from the United Nations, saying that arms were flown to Yugoslavia several weeks after the embargo had been imposed, including from many of the countries which were sitting on the Security Council. She goes on to say in the article that to make the embargo really work the council would have to set up a sanctions committee as we did in Iraq to deal with violations and to expose those who are still sending arms into that area. The author concludes that so far the council's five permanent

members have shown little interest in such far-reaching measures.
I would add a further paragraph saying: And neither has Canada shown much interest in ensuring that those sanctions were being fully imposed. I have not seen the secretary of state or the Prime Minister or our ambassador to the UN saying: "Hey, Security Council, your laws are being fought and your resolution has got holes in it. Do something about it because you are aiding to the killing". There is not a word.
Does the parliamentary secretary think that is a bold, new initiative to deal with the problem of conflict?

The fact of the matter is that on this crucial issue where we know that we once again talked about sanctions, finally the European Community admitted that it was failure, that it could not do it and referred it to the United Nations. I say to hon. members: Where has it been? Have you seen another resolution from the United Nations asking for an oil embargo that might really have enough impact to bring the parties to the
table and which would really send a tough message that we want negotiations? Silence.
On several occasions when we have asked in this House the representatives of the government-and I want the member for Mississauga to take the plug out of his mouth and out of his ears and listen-the Secretary of State for External Affairs refused to answer. This government did not go on record as supporting an oil embargo against those nations.
Is that a defence of the new international order? Is that a defence of the rule of law? Is that a defence against the unacceptable use of force to influence world affairs? I am surprised at the silence.

speechtext: We know where you were.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
I will welcome you. I will sit here with great anticipation to hear the member for Mississauga get to his feet and come forward with proposals for an oil embargo and come against the fact that his government will not do the kinds of things it should be doing. We will wait to see him make his statement as to what he thinks should be done because we know the things that his government is not doing at the present time.
The hard reality is that it is not just a question of the human suffering because there is a fundamental stake for all Canadians, even if they do not turn on their TV sets, even if they are not wrenched by the kind of catastrophe going on. They must recognize that there is a fundamental issue of world security at stake because this is the test case in eastern Europe where there are all kinds of instabilities, where there are all kinds of groups sort of looking to find a greater sense of freedom, a great sense of self-determination, and where they are looking to see what kind of security framework will be put in place to allow those discussions and those ambitions to take place under peaceful conditions.

I recall quite vividly being at the CSCE conference in Moscow in September when the delegations from eastern Europe, Czechoslovakians, Hungarians, Russians, Poles and others came forward with proposals about how the CSCE itself could strengthen its mechanisms for involvement in cases like Yugoslavia.
That international organization that was being held up by the former secretary of state last year as being the bright new hope for world order was finally having to come to grips with a real tough issue.
The newly developing democracies of eastern Europe themselves were coming forward with proposals to toughen up those mechanisms. As a result, guess who was dragging their feet? Guess who was saying no? We expected some of the big powers to say no. They were giving all kinds of excuses about why it was impossible. But why Canada? Why did we back away? Why did we retreat?
I want to quote a comment by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs who spoke about this. I will not bother you with the entire paragraph but she said: "The Moscow meeting was not the right time or context to take such decisions. We will deal with it in October, from October 22 to 24". That was a month ago. Where is the Canadian voice of the CSCE talking about the need for tougher mechanisms and the need for a new security structure for all the kinds of incredible challenges and tests that will emerge in that part of the world?
Once again there is silence. Once again it meant finding refuge on the sidelines. Here were the newly developing democracies reaching out for leadership, for the kind of direction that an experienced country and middle power of great diplomatic reputation like Canada can give, and what was the answer of our secretary of state? It was neither the time nor the place, "I was busy", or whatever it may be. It is sad. It is very sad. What a missed opportunity.
Canadians today are searching for what it means to be a Canadian and to have our own sense of identity. One thing that has given real raison d'etre for this country since the inception of the United Nations is the idea that when it comes to international affairs we could provide a middle way. We we were not afraid to take real leadership. We could reach out and be innovative in trying to enhance and strengthen the world order through the rule of law and through new international institutions until now.
When we are called, we will not respond. We are silent. As a result the chaos continues. There is a need to begin putting into place a new security arrangement that will be absolutely essential if we are not going to have a combustion in eastern Europe as it goes through the throes of freeing itself from a former imperialist system and now finds itself in a new era. We should be very clear. There is nothing sacred about the status quo.
We must let evolution take place through democratic elections. We must let self-determination take place through peaceful means, through protection of minorities. That will require a very effective, international, multilateral framework, and this is the time to start building that. This is the time to show that we really mean business. It is time for a new ethic of intervention, one that will move us beyond where we are now.
The failure in not doing so will have repercussions for years and years to come. We would like to hear very clearly the voices in this Parliament tonight speak out to give some new resolve to the government, to give some new will and determination, to start putting on pressure at the United Nations for a meeting to begin with for the imposition of oil sanctions.
Second, the voices should start saying that the international community has to get tough. If some of those great powers do not want to go on then let them say so. Let it at least be visible as to who is standing in the way of some resolution of this conflict. Let us make the arms embargo a meaningful one. Let us start arguing for closing the loopholes and putting a sanctions committee in place. Let us take the initiative. Let us show some leadership. Let us go to the CSCE the same way and ask for an emergency meeting, which is clearly our right under the by-laws. Let us get the foreign ministers together, sitting down and saying: "It has gone far enough. It is too much". If the CSCE is going to have any meaning in the future, if it is going to have any relevance to the problems of Europe, it must act now. It means looking at new mechanisms. Let us not follow the advice of our secretary of state when she says: "Another time, another place". The problem is right now.

As Canadians we must also grasp hold of the responsibility to deal with the deep humanitarian suffering that is going on in that area. There have been $1.5 million in valuable contributions to the Red Cross, but does that really ease the suffering of the 60,000 or 70,000 people who are trapped tonight in Dubrovnik without water, without electricity, without sewer treatment, without food because they are blockaded? Do you think that is going to help them?
Going back to the fundamental principle that was in the United Nations covenants, is probably in the covenant on genocide, and is certainly in the CSCE covenants, it is certainly part and parcel of the new ethic of intervention, we cannot allow a government to deliberately starve and maltreat its citizens. If that means that the blockade in Dubrovnik must come to an end and there must be ships of the international community there to do it, then so be it.
It is interesting how things get lost. Two weeks ago there was talk at the NATO summit meeting in Rome that maybe NATO, which does have a standby force, which has the mechanisms, which has the military committee, which has more generals than you can count, which has incredible planning going on, was going to be asked to deal with the problem of the blockade of Dubrovnik.
The shield comes up, the wall and the curtain descend and no more is heard about that proposal because there is a fundamental lack of political will. All the sweet words and brave descriptions we heard tonight from the parliamentary secretary do not cover the fundamental fact that chaos is erupting inside Yugoslavia and if it is not stopped and solved by peaceful means then it will lead to chaos in other places at other times.
We have a responsibility as a privileged, protected nation, one that has the respect of many other nations of the world to be more than simply an echo, to be simply more than a "me too", to be simply more than saying we will do only what is necessary, not what really will count.
I say to members of this House tonight that there is only one way that will happen. Every one in this House tonight has to get on his or her feet and speak with a commitment and a dedication, to say this is a time of testing, this is a time for this Parliament to be heard, this
is a time for Parliament to lead the government and show Canadians and the world that we will not stand by and watch the world being engulfed in this kind of chaos, that we will do everything within our power and our influence to show that we can solve these problems by peaceful means.
