speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be dividing my time with my colleague from Victoria. I know there are many other members of this House who want to speak in this debate but will not have the opportunity to do so. I particularly want to single out colleagues such as the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan and other members who have spoken out publicly and with eloquence and have expressed their deep concern, their sense of anger and reflected a sense of betrayal that too many of their constituents have felt at the silence and the lack of response of their government at a time that they were looking to their government for leadership.
This is an opportunity for this Parliament to tell our government, to tell our minister, that the silence must end. Canada must at last play a role of leadership, not only within the United Nations but as well, as the previous member pointed out, within the CSCE which has established mechanisms to respond to a crisis, to a human tragedy, a political tragedy, a tragedy of a country that has ceased to exist.
Surely as a Parliament that must be the basis of our understanding, that Yugoslavia no longer exists as a nation. We must recognize that the people of the republics of Yugoslavia, whether it be in Slovenia and Croatia which voted overwhelmingly, 94 per cent, for independence in a referendum, whether it be the people of Macedonia who voted in a referendum in September for independence, whether it be the elected representatives in Bosnia and Herzegovina who in the middle of October proclaimed the sovereignty of that republic, that Yugoslavia is no more.

November 18, 1991
Surely the most fundamental obligation we have as elected representatives is to speak the truth and from that truth to draw the conclusions that surely must follow. What are those conclusions and what should Canada be doing at this time that we are being tested as a nation? What has this new world order meant for the people of Dubrovnik, what has it meant for the people of Vukovar, what has it meant for those who are hungry in Zagreb, what has it meant for the children who are among the 350,000 refugees fleeing from the madness of this war, what has it meant for the eight year old boy in Vukovar who talks about the people in the refugee centre who cannot understand how today people are trying to resolve this conflict through violence?
What in fact should the response be? If we accept the fundamental principle set out in the CSCE documents of self-determination, surely we should recognize that the people of Slovenia, the people of Croatia have spoken loudly and eloquently for independence, for freedom and for democracy.
At the same time the European community has recognized, and indeed the leaders of Croatia in particular have recognized, the importance of respect for the rights of minorities. In fact, President Thdjman of the Government of Croatia has expressed himself very clearly as being prepared to grant to all people who reside in Croatia every internationally respected right for minorities, to do so under international monitoring and to recognize also that it may be that there is an important need for arrangements under international supervision with human rights guarantees, to respect the rights of minorities. We know that the historical fears do run deep, that the 600,000 Serbs in Croatia, looking back on history have those fears.
At the same time, we must not be mired in the death and tragedy of the past. We know that the Albanian majority in Kosovo has been brutally repressed for too long. Our obligation as parliamentarians is to recognize that we must in the absence of leadership from this government provide leadership on behalf of the people that we have the honour to represent.
What does that mean? It means for example that there must be a role for the United Nations, for peacekeeping forces from the United Nations, but not, as has been
suggested by the President of Serbia, in a de facto greater Serbia. Troops that are set up within the territory of Serbia would in fact achieve the objective that has been set out by Serbia, to carve out chunks of territory. The United Nations must not be a part of that scheme.
The international community and Canada must state very clearly to the Yugoslavian army in no uncertain terms that they will not yield one inch of territory to violence, brutality and bloodshed. The Yugoslavian army must be called upon to withdraw beyond the boundaries of Croatia, to stop the violence, the death, the injury, the destruction, the creation of hundreds of thousands of refugees. We have heard the desperate appeal from the mayor of Dubrovnik, Pero Poljanic, who says: "We are desperate, dear friends, we need you. At times we think we are crying in the desert." This historical jewel is being utterly devastated by shelling.
We must understand and we must accept that it is not a question of when Croatia will be independent; it is a question of how much blood will be shed before that independence has been recognized. I say on behalf of my colleagues that too much blood has been shed and Canada has been silent for too long.
Some say that Serbs and Croatians cannot live in peace. The reality is that until this conflict they have done precisely that. Families have intermarried. There has been that relationship of trust. Yes, it has been devastated, it has been tom, but that can happen.
Ultimately Canada must lead in the call for an unconditional withdrawal of troops, to urge that there be United Nations peacekeepers, not within the territory of Croatia, but in fact on the border between Croatia and Serbia. We must lead in the call for an end to the brutality that led to the woman from Croatia who came to my office and brought in a piece of shrapnel from her front yard. She was able to escape from that scene of terror. I hope that Canada will be very generous in granting visitor's visas to those who are trying to escape from that terror as well.
We must impose tough economic sanctions. We should have done it a long time ago. My colleague from Victoria on October 8 spoke on behalf of this party, urging those sanctions, urging an oil embargo. What have we done? Finally, a month later, economic sanctions. But what about the oil embargo? No action there at all.
November 18, 1991

Finally, humanitarian assistance is desperately needed at this time of crisis. This is being called for by the Croatian community, but also by the Serbian community which, on the eve of Remembrance Day in church services in Vancouver prayed for peace but also prayed to raise money to buy and send the necessary medicine, food and clothing. I want to pay tribute in particular to the Croatian community in my own area of Vancouver which has, in fact, sent that humanitarian relief. But it is up to our government to show true leadership and provide additional humanitarian relief.
Finally I want to pay tribute to the young people who have shown their concern for their relatives and families, for their loved ones, who have petitioned this Parliament, who have joined in echoing the words of the President of Croatia who said "We will not succumb to military force or economic blackmail. Our liberty is our life".
Mr. Speaker, let that call be heard in this Parliament and throughout this land today.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway for yielding part of his time. As our critic for external affairs, he certainly could have added even more to the debate than he has. But in order that as many members from our party as possible can participate in this discussion, we have decided to split our time.
This is a solemn debate. It is not a debate for partisan division. It is a debate in which all members of this House must come together to speak with one voice. The tragedy in Croatia must immediately come to an end and the Government of Canada must speak for all Canadians in saying that this tragedy must come to an end now. But in order for us to do so effectively, we must not shrink from placing responsibility for the tragedy where it belongs. As the Prime Minister said in this House on October 8: "The army, operating under the name of Yugoslavia, has run amok. It is absolutely out of control".
In a report by the Secretary-General of the United Nations to the Security Council, the Secretary-General concluded, on the basis of his investigations, and I quote
from page 12 on a report from Cyrus Vance to the Secretary-General:
Despite the occasional participation of the full eight-member socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and presidency at the Hague Conference, the de facto authority of the central government in Yugoslavia has been seriously impaired since the development of the 3rd of October, as well as by the situation on the ground. A critical result is that the JNA no longer has political direction from a civilian authority that enjoys the support of all the republics and all the communities of the federation.
Mr. Speaker, when you called this debate, you said it was about the situation in Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia no longer effectively exists, and certainly, in the words of the Secretary-General, "no longer has political direction of the army that is out of control in Croatia". That is the place where this Parliament's understanding and this Parliament's statement must begin.
The people of the world are horrified at what is happening. But we are also horrified at the apparent inability of the international community to act.
As other members have already said, it stands in stark contrast, in bitter contrast, to the actions of a year ago when faced with the situation in the gulf.
I come, as all members have, from a week in our ridings. I come from a meeting on Friday night in Victoria where people of the Croatian community came together. They, along with all people in this country, simply cannot understand how it is that this tragedy is allowed to happen and the world community cannot act to stop it. We have had resolutions and speeches, we have had half-hearted sanctions and we have had failure-and all members of this House must speak to the point-of the international community to act.
Over a month ago, the Secretary General of NATO came to visit Ottawa. In the course of conversations he said, and he put it personally: "I have the divisions necessary to go into Yugoslavia and stop the fighting". He said that NATO would not do so because it might get caught in a quagmire.
If that is the reason for the international community not to be acting, it is an international crime. We do not advocate that NATO go in. Just as NATO should not have gone into the gulf, NATO should not be operating outside its borders, as it is in fact for that reason politically obsolete. But the Security Council of the United Nations can call on the member states, as it did in the gulf, to provide the necessary peacekeeping forces to

November 18, 1991
go in and stop the devastation in Croatia. This House must make that statement now.
It is a matter of international law that the rights of the people of Croatia cannot be violated by force as they are now being viola ed by force, that the priceless international heritage of that community cannot be taken away. The time has come for the international community to move, through the Security Council, to intervene under the flag of the United Nations to stop the fighting in Yugoslavia.
The word tonight from Yugoslavia is that there is at least some calm in Dubrovnik. If that lasts, that may be something to be built upon. However, that is not going to be enough because last June the people of Croatia voted 94 per cent for independence. It ought to be the policy of this House that the voice of that 94 per cent of the people of Croatia must be given an opportunity to be heard. If the people of Croatia want independence, as other countries have achieved independence, as our colleagues to the south in the United States of America once had a revolution for independence, as we now celebrate the spring of hope throughout all of eastern Europe, as other countries are achieving their independence, so too must the people of Croatia have the right to independence.
The first step is peace and the second step is that the international community must afford the people of Croatia the opportunity to determine whether they wish to have an independent country.
All of us prefer to have some level of cohesion in that area but it must be clear that the people have the right to determine their future in a new Europe. We in the international community must be ready to give them that right.
Finally, let me say that there is the issue of humanitarian aid that must be dealt with and dealt with more effectively than it has been to date from all accounts. The government first put up $250,000 on behalf of Canada. Then it contributed more to bring the aid, as I understand it, to about $1 million. However, there are reports that aid is not getting through. It is said to be routed through the International Red Cross and there are substantial reports that it is not getting through. That aid should be routed through Slovenia to be sure that it gets in to the people of Croatia who need it.
Let me conclude my remarks by offering to the House the experience to which I referred earlier. The Croatian community in Victoria was speaking with a clear voice, and I think we have all had various experiences of this in the last week. About 200 people from the Croatian community, including those from the Hungarian community, came to speak in solidarity with the people of Croatia.
The sense of frustration and hopelessness as the reports continued to pour out of Croatia was palpable. However, we must now take the glimmer of hope that there may be today and try to work with it and build on it and show leadership in Canada, to see that this tragedy is brought quickly to an end and that those in Croatia who want a free, independent Croatia have the opportunity to have it.
When the meeting was over, Mrs. Maria Micic gave me a letter from her sister who has spent much of the last period of time below ground, suffering bombardment. She asked me to deliver this letter to the Prime Minister, which I will do on his return from Paris. It is a letter which is poignant and feeling. It speaks of the experience that has been inflicted on so many in this century, the hundreds of thousands of people who have been the victims of civil war and of war between nations.
We are once again called upon, as a Parliament, to speak out for peace. I would ask all of my colleagues to join in that plea tonight.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to you today about the terrible situation in Yugoslavia. After listening carefully to comments made in the House so far this evening, I had trouble understanding what kind of message the opposition was trying to send us. I know the Canadian government is trying to help the people of Yugoslavia, and I realize perhaps something else should be done as well. However, if I recall correctly, during a similar discussion we had a few months ago on the war in the gulf, the same opposition parties voted against the same UN resolution.
I will just say that I find it difficult to understand them, and that is putting it mildly. Perhaps I could explain what Canada is doing at this very moment. What we want
November 18, 1991

above all is to stop the killing and persuade both sides to embark on a peaceful settlement of this conflict.
As you know, Canada has acquired considerable experience in peacekeeping, and I would like to analyse the situation in Yugoslavia from that perspective. The situation is somewhat complex. It is not just a war between two armies, which would lend itself easily to a classic peacekeeping operation.
There are a number of factors that complicate matters: ethnic differences, a federation that has fallen apart, the security status of minorities, nationalism, ancestral rivalries and conflicts, mistrust of one's neighbours, the impact of these tragic events on the population, and in fact all the tragic consequences of the breakdown of the social order and civil war.
I also find the situation in Yugoslavia disturbing because it was in this country that the first sparks flew that started the conflagration of World War I. Yugoslavia is certainly not an island, and as a result, current instability may spread to neighbouring states. However, there is a definite difference compared with the situation in 1914, so much so that I feel there is hope the past will not repeat itself.
No major power has a personal interest in the region. The country's immediate neighbours are anxious to take advantage of the end of the cold war to progress politically and economically. There is no mechanism in the region aimed at preventing, restricting and regulating conflicts, such as the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, also known as the CSCE, or the United Nations. To end this conflict, our only hope is to find ways to stop the warring parties and start negotiations.
Canada has acquired a broad experience of peacekeeping operations. The peacekeeping concept was first proposed by a Canadian, Lester B. Pearson, at the time of the Suez crisis, to help the belligerents agree on a cease-fire. For this concept, Pearson was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, Canada has taken part in all UN peacekeeping missions. Today, more than 1,000 Canadian soldiers are deployed in peacekeeping operations in the gulf, Cyprus, the Sahara and the Middle East. We are also involved in the latest peacekeeping mission in Cambodia, where two members of Canadian
military personnel have already started setting up operations designed to support the peace process in that country.
Since we have a long history of involvement in these missions, the greatest tribute to Canadians who served the cause of peace came when the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded in 1988 to peacekeeping forces throughout the world. A magnificent monument commemorating that event and dedicated to Canadian soldiers who took part in those operations is now being erected on Sussex Drive.
However, it is not enough for Canada to look back on the achievements of the past. A nation that has acquired such a vast experience of peacekeeping has a duty to share that experience with countries where new conflicts break out, in this case Yugoslavia. I take great comfort from the initiatives taken by Canada in this respect.
It was Canada that first requested a special meeting of the Security Council and the sending of a peacekeeping mission. The Prime Minister himself discussed the matter. We have learned from experience that sometimes belligerents must be helped to agree on a cease-fire and we realized that intervention by peacekeeping forces might be useful at this time.
Canada has played an active role in persuading a major organization like the CSCE to intervene in the Yugoslavian crisis. Some countries were surprised at our position, considering that we are not a European state. Maintaining Europe's security is our concern. Canadians fought in two world wars to protect the cause of peace in Europe.
Our troops have been part of NATO for 30 years, always for that same reason. How could we remain silent within the CSCE when the war in Yugoslavia threatens the very peace for which we fought for so many years?
Canada did far more than condemn violence and ask for a peacekeeping mission to be sent. Our desire for peace goes further than mere words. Canada joined the European nations that formed the cease-fire monitoring mission in Yugoslavia.
The mission was organized to see whether it was possible to avoid the conflict, and if not, to see whether the conflict could be controlled, and if that were not the case, to see whether we could at least protect innocent civilians from the more violent effects of combat. Under the enlightened and energetic leadership of the Nether-

November 18, 1991
lands, the observers went well beyond their mandate to try and establish and maintain a cease-fire.
Zagreb, Vukovar, Dubrovnik, Split-many of us barely knew of the existence of these cities before we heard about them in the media. They are the names of cities where the observers went and where they are continuing their peace efforts.
I wonder whether Canadians or even hon. members fully realize the extent of Canada's participation in this monitoring mission. We assigned 11 people to this difficult task. I am told they are peacekeeping experts, and it seems they are making an exceptional contribution to the mission.
All of us here salute their courage and selfless attitude. Let us join their families in giving thanks that they have been spared so far and in praying that they will return safe and sound. These Canadians show that we want to bring peace back to Yugoslavia. They give substance to what we say in the halls of Europe and the world.
I said earlier that the Yugoslav conflict is far more than a classic confrontation between two armies, and I highlighted some of the more complex aspects of the situation. What we have here is civil war.
Peacekeeping operations have also become more complex, more refined and better able to deal with the underlying causes of a conflict instead of with its military manifestations, pure and simple. They have evolved to the point that today they include missions responsible for monitoring respect for human rights, ensuring the safe return of refugees to their countries, organizing national referendums, supervising elections and responding to humanitarian needs.
Canada has both military personnel and civilians who are experienced in such missions. We have people working in the human rights monitoring unit in Salvador. We gave our assistance when elections were held in Haiti, and Canadians are once again involved in restoring democracy to this troubled country. We are now involved in a mission responsible for organizing a referendum in the Western Sahara, in the national reconciliation campaign in Angola and, since quite recently, in the general UN mission responsible for restructuring political institutions in Cambodia.
Canada has also played a leading role in the development of peacekeeping concepts. A 34-nation committee of the United Nations is studying all aspects of this activity. I find it revealing that, since the end of the cold war and the resulting revitalization of peace keeping, this committee has chosen a Canadian as vice-chairman, who also chairs its working group.
Innovative ideas together with a vast experience of new peacekeeping possibilities may give us a way to resolve the Yugoslav situation.
Needless to say, Canada has already contributed to the efforts to bring this conflict under control. We have advised the CSCE and the UN. We are participating in the observer mission in Yugoslavia. We support the European peace conference. We have condemned acts of violence. We have applied sanctions and provided aid to innocent victims. But the fighting still goes on. However, it seems that the parties in conflict and the European Community are now considering putting in place a peacekeeping force to end the fighting and allow talks to be held.
I understand that the UN Secretary General has sent his special representative, Cyrus Vance, and his Assistant Secretary for Peacekeeping to Yugoslavia to see what can be done in this regard. We should be pleased with this development.
As I already noted, Canada is highly regarded in the CSCE, the European Economic Community and the United Nations. We have maintained an impartial policy toward the parties in conflict. I therefore think that we are well placed to continue to take part in peace efforts, to which we attach great importance.
In their deliberations, international organizations and the parties concerned will look at various roles that peacekeepers could play in Yugoslavia. For example, they could guarantee the security of minorities. They could supervise the cease-fire and the disengagement of forces. They could also participate in humanitarian aid efforts and introduce confidence-building measures.
Furthermore, the trans-Yugoslav highway and railway will certainly have to be reopened and the economy will have to be revived. Relief will have to be provided in combat zones and refugees will have to be returned to
November 18, 1991

their homes. Finally, respect for everyone's human rights will have to be ensured.
A peacekeeping mission in itself cannot solve the Yugoslav crisis. It must be accompanied by a general desire for peace. Moreover, the enthusiasm aroused by its presence must not predetermine the final settlement. Thus a temporary cease-fire line must not become a new de facto border.
To conclude, I will say that Canada has played an important, appropriate, impartial role so far in this crisis. Some signs indicate that with some encouragement, the parties may now agree to lay down their arms. We should maintain our assistance to get them to stop fighting and to start negotiating.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address this emergency debate on the issue of Yugoslavia, but I believe by agreement I am going to share my 20 minute allotted time with my colleagues from Scarborough-Rouge River and Hamilton West, with your permission.
We are here this evening to address a very serious crisis in our world, that which exists today and has existed for too long in Yugoslavia, a situation which is deplorable for the consequences it has wrought upon so many innocent victims in Yugoslavia: 3,000 dead and 350,000 displaced persons in a modem society is totally unacceptable. It is particularly unacceptable when we remember so well the reaction of the international community to the crisis that occurred within the last year in the Middle East when Iraq invaded Kuwait.
It appeared that because our own self-interest was so much at stake we could do nothing more than react. Today we have all these innocent people within Yugoslavia who are suffering so much personally and it appears that those who have power to change things in the world are not prepared to take the necessary steps or do not have the political will to bring about a peaceful resolution to the problem that exists.
Sovereignty sensitivities in this area have translated into inaction. This is unacceptable. Young people, students, men and women who have learned over years, mind you under a stern dictatorship, to live together
despite their ethnic and cultural differences today are suffering.
One of my early memories as a student was being in Yugoslavia and being entertained by other students in Yugoslavia. It was one of the richest cultural and ethnic experiences I have had to date.
It was an experience to have Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians and all the cultures of Yugoslavia coming together. We all shared our song and our dance routines and our tales of our cultural past together. It was a rich experience. I saw people in that country all living together peaceably at that time. It is certainly distressing to see what is happening today.
I believe there are remedies which the international community could have taken long before now and which have been suggested and to which we must address ourselves. For example, it has been suggested for some months that an oil embargo against Yugoslavia would have some impact in causing the conflict there to dry up literally for lack of energy resources. We have an arms embargo in place. Despite this the international community has not done what it could have done to make sure that the arms embargo was effective.
As we talk about embargoes against the country of Yugoslavia, which is unnecessarily at war and conflict at the present time, we have to be aware that we must turn our attention to the humanitarian needs of so many people who have been displaced. We must assure by whatever means is necessary, through provision of supplies by ship and by air, that the people who are the innocent victims in this turmoil have their needs met.
The Serbs and Croats themselves have asked for international assistance. There have been attempts we know by the European Community to try to bring about peace in this region. Unfortunately although perhaps there is some tenuous possibility this evening, so many cease-fires have not brought the result that we want.
It is true that when the people of Yugoslavia see other nations and republics around them looking to a new life freedom and when they look back to their cultural past and heritage, they do look for a new relationship. I believe that the international community could support the European suggestion of there being a Yugoslavia composed of six republics co-existing in a loose confed-

November 18, 1991
eration. Before any of this process can take place we must have peace in that area.
It is incumbent upon us to do something to right the situation. If we continue to treat the crisis in Yugoslavia with distant vacuous words of regret and feigned worry, the condemnation of history' will rightly rest on our shoulders.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I remind myself that it is a privilege for me to stand in this place on behalf of the constituents of Hamilton West. It is my duty to rise in this debate, an emergency debate requested of the government by the Official Opposition no less than three times in the last 30 days. It is an emergency debate on the tragic events in Yugoslavia which have resulted in the dreadful unnecessary loss of life.
I say unnecessary because this is another idiotic war which might well have been prevented if the United Nations, the only institution that can organize the world community, had heard from our government. Where were the voices opposite? Lest we forget, it was this government that led the charge against Saddam Hussein and wasted no time in declaring that it would send a flotilla of ships to the Persian Gulf. In the aftermath of that war this government was also one of the first to carry the flag of that new world order. Things will be different now, the government declared. No more shall the spectre of war be allowed to raise its head before the international community. The international community is now a tool for peace, for security. Should any nation forget this, the international community will surely say "not again".
Where were the Security Council resolutions on this particular crisis? We remember several from the Persian Gulf conflict but why not this time? The Official Opposition declared at the time that because this government tied itself so closely with the United States, Canada could no longer act as an intermediary between nations. Canada's voice should have been heard long ago on this matter, but we are stuck with a government which is nothing more than a surrogate voice for the United States.
While Yugoslavians are dying and while Canadians of Yugoslav origin and descent were feeling pain here at home, where was our government? Where were the
United Nations resolutions condemning the violence and calling on the Yugoslavian army to cease its attacks and withdraw from Croatia?
I have said it before and I will say it again, you cannot negotiate-and I will tell the hon. member for Mississauga South again-at the point of a gun.
We in the opposition call on the Canadian government to take a stronger role in mobilizing the international community into acting decisively to help bring the Yugoslavian conflict to an end. It is a conflict which has already cost thousands of lives.
As we speak this evening there are over 50,000 people blockaded without food, without water, without electricity, without medical supplies in towns such as Vukovar and Dubrovnik. We hear or read the names of these towns in the news but they seem so remote. We cannot forget that the international community, particularly Canada, has not proposed any meaningful measures to end this civil war.
Toward that end the Liberal Party calls for increased humanitarian aid by way of air or sea where possible to relieve suffering civilians. We also call on other members of the United Nations to help bring an end to the conflict.
The Liberal Party called for such action as far back as last June. If our government had led the charge back then perhaps some of the bloodshed would have been forestalled. It is one thing for the government to posture on opposition demands to change legislation but an entirely different matter not to listen to those voices which are crying out for peace.
Here is what they are saying in my riding of Hamilton West. Boris says: "We just want to live as human beings again". My neighbour Peter says: "The houses are burning; the children are crying. Help us put an end to these barbaric actions".
I am not here tonight to stand up for moral superiority of Croatians over Serbians or Serbians over Croatians. I am here not to lecture Canadians on why one side should win over the other side. I believe it is my duty to stand up for justice and the justice that must be seen to put an end to this war. The justice I see is in putting an end to the destruction of towns, villages and families and brothers against sisters. The justice I see is that my country will stand up and lend its voice to rally other nations behind that drive for peace.
November 18, 1991

Are we so morally superior that we can race to the Persian Gulf but not to Vukovar? Are we so superior that we can allow this war to be fought until it is over? That may be a long time. It may be just a short period of time, but not for the Yugoslavians, not for the people who must put their crumbled lives back together again.
My message is brief. Their request is uncomplicated: use whatever influence at your disposal to mobilize the international community to act to bring an end to this horrific conflict. This House, this party, the government and the NDP have to work together. We have to show constructive action and constructive leadership on this issue.
The high moral road will be taken when this government stands up for whatever is left of this new world order and says it will help show the path to peace. That will be justice.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address this very important issue here this evening for sue minutes or for however long it shall be.
This is a very sad and frustrating experience for many of us on both sides of the House who have watched the evolution of this terrible affair in Yugoslavia taking place principally now in Croatia. We have seen all of the innocents involved. We have seen the old people and the young people. We have seen the death and the mutilation and the destruction and we wonder why it goes on in the face of the will of so many around the world to see it ended.
Some will ask: What can we do here in Parliament? We all acknowledge there is not a magic solution to be accomplished here, but Parliament enables us to articulate for Canadians our wishes, our views and our positions as a people and as a nation. It is through Parliament that we can urge and convince our government to act the way we want it to act. That is why we are here tonight.
We want our government to act aggressively for peace and not just to go through the motions. This government did not cause the problem in Croatia and this Parliament did not. It is one having roots going back quite far in history. It looks to me on this side of this House that sometimes the government does not know exactly what it wants to do. It does not seem to be seeking out and
aggressively pursuing creative new ways of addressing peace in the situation in Yugoslavia. I do know for sure that that kind of a problem did not stop Mike Pearson 50 years ago. He sought out the new solutions.
What is missing here is effective international leadership in attempting to resolve the failure of our international community to bring about some amelioration of the problem in Croatia. What we have here is a failure that stands in stark contrast to the effective action the international community took in the Kuwait situation approximately one year ago.
I know the international community has tried. There have been European community observers in the field. There have been peace proposals. There have been cease-fires. There has been a lot of talking about a peace force, about an oil embargo, about economic sanctions, but this all seems to be worth very little in the face of what is now happening in Croatia.
Last week we saw the terrible sight, and I know there is much worse going on, of the Yugoslavian army using the historic city of Dubrovnik for target practice. We have simply got to do more.
Some say this is just a civil war, that we should not be intervening. In my view, this is no longer simply a civil war. It is clear I think from most international observers that the country of Yugoslavia has failed to control its army. The army is doing what it wants, where it wants and is operating without the political control of the people of Yugoslavia. We have seen in Slovenia, which has taken approximately the same type of democratic steps that Croatia has, that it has achieved the measure of independence, or at least has come a long way to achieving the independence which it seeks and it is not experiencing the type of war that is now going on in Croatia. This is not civil war, this is anarchy.
The use of the army to smash resistance in Croatia, in my view, is shortsighted and I believe that history will show us that we cannot use an army to achieve a goal in the face of and in contrast with a viable, democratic initiative. The guns simply cannot hold out forever.
I want to close noting that this tragedy cries out for international intervention because the innocent in Croatia need it, because we want to do it, as a country we want to participate and because both of the sides in

November 18, 1991
Croatia have actually requested it. What is holding us up? It is ineffective international action.
I want to leave three questions with the House that have been put to me by individuals from the Croatian community in Canada. Apparently Canada sent five observers to Croatia. But did they ever go to Zagreb? Did they ever leave Belgrade? I am told they did not. What are they doing there for Canadians in monitoring events in Croatia?
Second, I understand that the Prime Minister refused to meet a Croatian delegation on or about September 22. I do not know why he would have refused. Maybe he had reasons but it does not look like he really cared.
Third, why did Canada choose not to speak to its own resolution put to the Security Council at the United Nations? It was put to the Security Council through France. Surely if France permitted Canada to put the motion through its seat at the Security Council it would have permitted Canada to speak to it. I am told that Canada did not speak to it.
I leave these questions for the government. Obviously it believes it has answers. I leave the floor to other members of the House to continue debate on this tonight.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one week ago today only several hundred yards from this Chamber, Rabbi Reuven Bulka, Honorary Chaplain of the Royal Canadian Legion, speaking at the Remembrance Day ceremonies commented: "The opposite of war is not peace. Peace is only a state of not being at war. The opposite of war is harmony".
Yugoslavia was in a state of uneasy peace for many years but harmony has eluded it and never developed in this region. In the past few months the world has witnessed in horror the deterioration of this fragile situation into a state of all-out war.
Let me express first of all that Canada's heart goes out to those who are personally suffering themselves in this situation. In addition, the challenge is twofold for the world community. First, the terrible bloodshed and death and the malevolent destruction of entire cities and villages must stop. Second, following the cessation of hostilities which must inevitably occur, the conditions for
mutual trust that are essential for a state of lasting harmony in this region must be established.
These are not easy tasks. The roots of this conflict reach deep into history and the base human desire for revenge and retribution has increased rather than diminished over time. It is tragic that when an unprecedented era of freedom and justice beckons all the people of Europe, Yugoslavia has descended into a cycle of intolerance, inflexibility, death and destruction.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asks the government to take immediate and decisive action to end the slaughter. We could not agree more with the feelings expressed and the objectives stated. There is no point in having a debate on that issue. We think exactly the same thing.
However, the hon. member also said that so far Canada and the European Community have done too little too late. I must disagree with the hon. member on that point.

I am sure that the member knows and remembers that one of the benefits of being in government is having the opportunity to change things for the better. But he also knows that one of the frustrations of being in government is recognizing a problem and being unable to solve it alone. Such is the case in this desperate crisis in Yugoslavia. I would like to have a formula that would convince the parties to drop their weapons and negotiate a fair and lasting settlement. But the politics and the emotions of this region defy any such straightforward solution.
Consider for a moment the complex ethnic interrelationships in this region. Serbs make up 66 per cent of the people of Serbia but in one part of its territory, the province of Kosovo, 90 per cent are Albanian. In Croatia 75 per cent of the people are Croatian but fully 12 per cent are Serbian. The ethnic mix is even more complex in Bosnia-Herzegovina where 44 per cent of the people are Slavic Muslims, 31 per cent are Serbs and 17 per cent are Croats.
Establishing peace and stability in a region of such entrenched ethnic tension is not easy. But I want to assure the House and the people of Canada that we have not backed away. From the outset Canada has been outspoken and clear. We seek for all the peoples of Yugoslavia a peaceful, comprehensive and negotiated settlement that protects minority rights, ensures no

unilateral or forcible changes of borders, and provides for appropriate financial and legal arrangements among the constituent parts.

Through official international channels, we have communicated our views to the government and peoples of Yugoslavia.
From the beginning of the crisis, Canada has played an active role in the efforts made by the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe for a peaceful resolution of the conflict.
We wholeheartedly support the CSCE's statement that the rivalries in Yugoslavia must be resolved through peaceful negotiations, as the CSCE's Helsinki principles provide, as well as the statement relating to any forced change in the boundaries within Yugoslavia being unacceptable.

However, the CSCE was unable to act effectively in the spring because a number of countries, among them at that time the U.S.S.R., were loath to see it move on a conflict within the borders of a member state. The member state of Yugoslavia was a member and is a member of the CSCE. It was also uncertain. So the torch was passed to the European Community to try and settle this conflict.

We made sure that this initiative was taken in the context of the CSCE's broader responsibilities and, like Czechoslovakia, Poland and Sweden, we put Canadians on the observer teams sent to Yugoslavia by the European Community.
But the most important effort was undertaken at The Hague peace conference, chaired by Lord Carrington. We have supported these efforts as the major activity, and we continue to support Lord Carrington. Indeed, in accordance with the United Nations charter, we must first try to solve conflicts at the regional level before going to the Security Council.

The question is: How long can these efforts be made and made again while the obscene killing goes on before some more resolute action is required? Once again there is not a simple or superficial answer.

The Prime Minister and I have uniformly condemned the violence and intolerance in that country that have led to all-out war.
Secondly, we were among the first to show the international community the potential consequences of that tragedy.

Canada was the first country to request a meeting of the United Nations Security Council on the Yugoslav situation. The reason that Canada did not speak to that motion is that the rules of the Security Council did not permit us to despite repeated requests. Our view is that the Yugoslav crisis poses not only a human tragedy of enormous proportions but also a direct threat to international peace and security in the area. The collapse of an effective governing authority exacerbates the potential for civil strife and further endangers the peace and security of neighbouring countries. This call for action on the part of the Security Council has been resisted by some of its members who believe that the tragedy of that country remains an internal matter and that Security Council action would constitute interference in its internal affairs. Unfortunately, despite our own pleading, despite our own lobbying, despite our own work with each and every member of the Security Council, including the permanent five and the rotating members, that view has been held by one permanent member that has a veto: China.
We agree that this is outmoded thinking and it is deeply damaging in the circumstances. We do have some basis to hope that China will soften its stand, but in the meantime there is little that we can do except to try and continue to make the case as we do daily.
The situation also poses a direct challenge to the principles enshrined in the charter of Paris and the aspirations of all participating countries in the Confer-

ence on Security and Co-operation in Europe for the peaceful settlement of disputes. We have called for the establishment of a peacekeeping mission and have indicated that we are ready to contribute resources to such a mission.
Last week both the Serbian dominated Yugoslav presidency and Croatia at last called for the UN to send peacekeepers. They are not however in agreement over some vital issues of where the warring forces will be separated.
The UN Secretary-General's special envoy Cyrus Vance and the undersecretary general responsible for peacekeeping are now in Yugoslavia to see what can be done. Our monitors remain there in co-ordination with the European Community which is the one that is directing the monitoring process and which makes the decisions on where members of the monitoring mission go. Such a peacekeeping effort could have several roles, some of which have been alluded to earlier:
First, the supervision of a cease-fire in the disengagement of rival forces.
Second, basic protection for the security of minority groups in the republics.
Third, assistance in the distribution of humanitarian aid and the return of displaced persons to their homes.
Fourth, the supervision of relief for blockaded army camps and a general monitoring of the activities of the Yugoslav army.
Fifth, the reconfirmation of existing borders within Yugoslavia.
Sixth, assistance in the reopening of crucial road and rail networks.
Seventh and finally, the establishment of confidence building measures at the grass roots level between the rival factions.
These are steps that Canada has urged in every forum. It is a large order but it does follow the concept of moving from peace to harmony.
Canada stands ready and willing to contribute to such a comprehensive peacekeeping mission and we have been from the beginning. But even to contemplate peace the leaders of the parties to this conflict in Yugoslavia must be brought to the bargaining table for genuine discussions. This necessity presents a difficult dilemma for
countries outside the conflict. How can they force the issue without further hurting the people who are already affected?
As in other areas of conflict, Canada has sought to use economic and political levers for peace in an evenhanded way while at the same time provide humanitarian assistance to the victims of the violence.
When the crisis began I instructed my department to refuse systematically to issue any permits for the export of arms or other military goods to Yugoslavia. Canada has not only supported UN resolution 713 but has moved in advance of it.
The Prime Minister and I have written to the leaders of the parties involved in the crisis, urging them to end the violence and pursue a negotiated settlement. I have met with the foreign ministers of Yugoslavia and Croatia and will take every similar opportunity to do so in the future.
Our government continues to receive calls for recognition of those republics which have unilaterally declared independence. I know this is a sensitive point. We shall continue to resist such pressure. First, we believe along with members of the European Community and after much soul searching and discussion that recognition of republics that wish to leave Yugoslavia should only be given within the framework of a general agreement. This was discussed with members of the European Community, the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe and NATO, and I have discussed this personally with Cyrus Vance and with Peter Carrington.
Recognition of Croatia and Slovenia at this time would signal the end of the negotiation process and would leave force and violence to settle the issue.
It would also jeopardize the fate of other republics and minorities that have called for other kinds of arrangements for Yugoslavia.
We steadfastly believe that the first requirement for any political solution is peace within the region. Canadians are participating in the international cease-fire monitoring mission, as I pointed out, that was mandated by the CSCE and led by the European Community. Canada will continue to do what it can in the Conference on Security and Co-Operation in Europe to serve the cause of peace.
Also, Canada has fully supported peace efforts by the European Community. The EC has played a leading role

in this crisis because it has more influence than anyone else on the Yugoslav republics, several of which are seeking membership or have at least expressed the hope of membership in the community. So the community, it is believed, has some leverage.
Earlier this month we joined the European Community in announcing a package of sanctions designed to apply pressure to the various factions in Yugoslavia. Specifically, we suspended Canada's general preferential tariff treatment to Yugoslavia. We put Yugoslavia on the area control list, which means that any export to Yugoslavia now require an export permit.

We announced that all requests concerning Yugoslavia made under the terms of the program for export market development and under the Renaissance program for Eastern Europe would be rejected, and we suspended trade development and support initiatives for Yugoslavia.
We welcomed the suggestions made by the European Community for other measures to strengthen the arms embargo, and which favour an oil embargo.
We also reacted with our hearts. At the NATO summit in Rome, I was the first one to urge the other foreign ministers to combine sanctions with specific measures to make humanitarian aid more effective.

We have moved early to provide assistance to victims. Our first step was to provide the international committee of the Red Cross with a contribution of $250,000 in support of its programs in all regions affected by the crisis.
On November 8, we went well beyond this. The Prime Minister announced from Rome that Canada would make an additional $1 million available for humanitarian relief. Funds will be provided for the Canadian Red Cross to purchase emergency relief and medical supplies for the International Committee of the Red Cross to use in Yugoslavia, and the Canadian forces will provide air transport to move those supplies into place.
I will be announcing the details of this effort within the next few days. In the meantime, NATO countries are giving active support to the efforts of the UN and the Red Cross. While the tragedy in Yugoslavia unfolds,
many thousands of miles away there are thousands of Canadian families who are directly affected. For the many Canadians of Croatian, Slovenian and Serbian descent, the events are not simply video images on television screens. They are family, friends and special places and personal memories.
I know, without being out of order, that many of them are here to hear us today and many of them will be watching at home. Each day the pictures of war score direct hits on their hearts and their peace of mind as well as those of all other Canadians.
Since the beginning of this crisis, the safety of Canadians has also been on our minds. We have advised by letter all registered Canadians in Croatia to leave the zones of conflict. All Canadian missions are in a position to provide Canadian visas to Yugoslav nationals and locally engaged staff in our Consulate General in Zagreb continue to operate the mission and offer assistance to Canadian citizens in Croatia.
But we must also comfort and support the Canadians here at home who have families and friends in the area. They live peacefully in our neighbourhoods among us with people of all races and creeds, from every comer of the world. They work side by side with people whose families arrived here three or four hundred years ago. They value peace, freedom, order and equality of opportunity for members of their families and the people of their communities as well as those in their homelands. They tolerate diversity, differences of opinion or political affiliation because they live in our country in a generous society and a tolerant one. They value that harmony that is the cornerstone of our society.
We ask them to help us. They are involved emotionally and otherwise. We ask them to help us in calling for leaders in all parts of Yugoslavia and its component states to stop shooting and to come together at the table.
We can impose strict sanctions. We can condemn violence and plead for peace, we can meet around the clock in our various fora and we can pass all of our resolutions, but the people of Yugoslavia must themselves find that harmony that is crucial to their future. That is neither an avowal of failure nor an unwillingness to do everything in our power to support peace efforts and to provide relief. It is a note of caution for Cana-

November 18, 1991
dians who think that there are quick and simple answers even as we are searching for those new answers.
We pledge to make every effort to assist the people of Yugoslavia. When those opportunities are there we will seize them and we will search them out. We will also seek an immediate peace. One more death, one more injury, one more devastated building is one too many. But we do pray for that harmony, we search for it. We join with our allies and we join with our fellow Canadians in seeking it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recognize the interest of members of this House and of the people who have connections in this region concerning recognition.
It is the opinion of all of us who are engaged in trying to make the decisions about what we do both bilaterally and internationally in these matters that it is not going to achieve the number one objective, which is to stop the violence. Recognition simply changes the nature of the combatants and it becomes a foreign war as opposed to a civil war. It does not stop the violence.
That is why I made a point of raising it with those particular gentlemen because they are engaged as emissaries to the region and they are in touch with all the parties concerned and all the leadership of the various states that are involved as well as with others in international meetings. I have discussed it at the United Nations
November 18, 1991

because we are all doing our soul searching on how we should act under the circumstances.
What does Canada do under the circumstances? We are doing everything I believe that we can within the organizations we belong to and bilaterally through our connections with the leadership of the countries involved. Recognition now of Croatia or of any of the others-Slovenia is another state which is in a similar position in terms of recognition-takes away some of the leverage to work toward peace and toward bringing people to the table.
That is certainly the international consensus. It is a question that we revisit time after time and that we will continue to ask ourselves because there may well come a moment when that is the answer. The considered view at the moment is that that time is not yet.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I take part in this emergency debate tonight.
During my term as a member of Parliament, I have had the honour of joining other members in this House in answering debates on the self-determination of nations and human rights.
Tonight, we are specifically debating the independence of Croatia and the war crimes being committed against Croatians. On two occasions I have visited Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Canadian observer during the elections.
It was during the 1989 Croatian election and one year later at the Bosnia-Herzegovina election that I found that democracy worked. I have fond memories of the moment when the election results were announced that the democratic forces of the Croatian Democratic Union won the election.
Those elections were certainly an expression of the will of the people. Yet, the Canadian government is still unwilling to recognize Croatia's independence. I have to ask myself why. Why is this happening? I believe because the will of the government is not there because of an agreement reached at the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in Berlin on June 20, and the Group of Seven Leaders declaration at the London summit of July 16 where they agreed to maintain Yugoslavia in its status quo.
I quote the hon. member from St. Paul's, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the department's press release of June 27. "As Prime Minister Mulroney has said, Canada considers the unity of Yugoslavia to be very important to the stability of central Europe. That is why Canada subscribed to the June 20 statement of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, the ministers who supported the unity and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia."
I would like to quote Andrew Cohen, a journalist who wrote in The Financial Post. He called the unravelling of Yugoslavia "almost a mirror image of Canada and therefore Canadian politicians think Quebecers might identify too much with the nationalists of the republics." The republics of Croatia and Slovenia fall within the sphere of influence of the old world order, that is to maintain the integrity of Yugoslavia, a world order that in 1956 abandoned Hungary when it was invaded by the Soviet armed forces, a legacy that ignored the democratic processes in Czechoslovakia in 1968, a world order that created Yugoslavia in 1918, a Yugoslavia that was created artificially by joining different nations in the subdivision of the Austro-Hungarian and the Ottoman empires.
So we have the first world order as a direct result of World War I, when at the Versailles Conference the victors artificially created Yugoslavia, recognized the independence of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, rewarded the communists in Moscow by helping them build the Soviet empire, subjugating Ukraine, Byelorussia and other nationalities in the Soviet Union and assisted Stalin by ignoring his killings of millions of people. As an example, the artificially induced famine in Ukraine in 1932 where seven million people perished, they ignored the existence of Gulags and all of this in the name of the new world order.
There was a decision made as well to punish Germany and Italy through economic measures after the First World War. That, of course, devastated those economies and gave rise to Hitler and Mussolini.
That then brings us to World War II with all its tragedies. Over 40 million people died, most of them in eastern Europe. At the end of World War II, at the Yalta Conference, President Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill

again divided the world into spheres of influence. The Soviets took over Yugoslavia, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Romania. There was no consideration in those negotiations for the right to self-determination for those countries. The United States of America and Great Britain, being colonial powers themselves, had no problem with either the concept or the execution of delegating those nations to become colonies of the Soviet Union. This led to the creation of two nuclear superpowers and the cold war, the building of thousands of nuclear warheads and rockets by both powers in their respective countries.
The world started talking of a mutually assured destruction in an atomic war. Then in 1986 something very tragic happened in the Soviet Union: the meltdown of an atomic reactor in Chernobyl. Suddenly the people of the Soviet Union came out of self-denial and Mr. Gorbachev was obliged to act on glasnost and perestroika. So we can say Chemobly was a catalyst in the movement for independence of most of the former Soviet republics like Ukraine, Byelorussia, Kazakstan, and the same thing happened in Yugoslavia.
Because of those events, the equilibrium between the two superpowers was slipping toward the United States, and at that very time we had the crisis in the Middle East. The United States was able to take advantage of that situation because the Soviet Union was slowly disintegrating. This gave President Bush the occasion to talk about a new world order.
The consequence of the first world order in 1918 was World War II, or at least the seeds for World War II, and the consequences of the second world order in 1945 were the cold war and the proliferation of nuclear arms. Now we are facing a third world order, and it is a very dangerous stage because of course it could be the seeds for another war. As the United Nations tries to implement the new world order after the war against Iraq, the United States, with its dominance of the United Nations through financial control of the United Nations, becomes the supercop of the world.
In this context, President Bush wants the status quo in Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union. I would like to refer to his speech in Kiev in Ukraine on August 1 where President Bush warned of the excesses of suicidal nationalism. I would like to quote from an article in The New York Times of August 2:
Still Mr. Bush spent much of his day here (Kiev) praising Mr. Gorbachev and his vision of the Soviet Union.
But the Soviet Union does not exist any more. Mr. Bush goes on to endorse Gorbachev:
Americans will not support those who seek independence in order
to replace a far-off tyranny with the local despotism, he said. They
will not aid those who promote a suicidal nationalism based upon
ethnic hatred.
They are fearful of nations like Croatia, Slovenia, Ukraine, Byelorussia, but whether they like it or not, justice and human rights are going to prevail. In this era of communications, it is impossible to fool the people any longer. But we must remember that it is a very dangerous turning point in our history.
What about the west's ideals for supporting duly elected democratic governments, their leaders and the right of nations to self-determination? I say to those western democracies, do not give us rhetoric, stand by principles. What about international law? Remember in 1954 the Hague convention for the protection of cultural property in the event of armed conflict.
Yugoslavia became a signatory to that agreement in 1955. That means that present attacks on churches and monuments are not only an affront to the world's conscience but to world law.
What about the city of Dubrovnik, the gateway to the Slavic world that is being bombarded and the people starved? That city was founded in the seventh century after Christ. It has an historic respect for human rights. The city republic afforded asylum to refugees of all nations. One of them was King Edward of England. That nation state was one of the first to recognize the independence of the United States of America and it is an irony of history that today the communist dominated navy is bombarding that historic city, destroying her monuments and history while America stands by in silence. It is a tragedy for Croatia and all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia.
We say to world leaders: Is this your new world order? We have double standards. We acted one way with Kuwait and are acting differently in the case of Croatia.
Let us talk about Yugoslavia's chemical weapons. We know that Yugoslavia outbid Brazil in winning the contract to supply Iraq with a chemical arsenal and missiles. Therefore, I would like to conclude by saying that our government has the obligation to give a signal to
November 18, 1991

the world by recognizing the duly elected and freely elected government of Croatia. I think this will lead to peace and negotiations. Otherwise, the war will continue and people are going to suffer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the world witnessed the residents of Vuko-var coming out from their underground shelters as their homes burned on the surface.
What is happening in Vukovar and other towns devastated by the conflict in Croatia is a degree of human suffering unseen in Europe since the Second World War.
The United Nations children's fund visited Dubrovnik only to find children left wounded and homeless by a political crisis that they cannot even begin to comprehend.
The destruction that is occurring today is a result of the age old belief that political aims are worth human lives, even thousands of lives, especially if most of the dying is done by the enemy. Fear, hatred, economics, land and political power are as much a part of this war as any other.
Much of the debate thus far has focused on the political struggle, the right of a population to choose its government democratically and its future against the ability of an army to usurp political control with military force and predictable rationalizations.
In every war the aggressor motivates its followers by manufacturing motives of revenge, anger and fear, provoking the kinds of vicious attacks and cruelty that have so characterized the current conflict. In April 19901 was one of the members of Parliament from this House to travel to Croatia to monitor its first democratic election in half a century. We all saw a people filled with hope for democracy, personal freedom and economic prosperity. Many of the same people I met in Osijek, for instance, 18 months ago are dead, maimed or homeless. This is a war in which brothers are killing brothers, conscripts are being ordered to bombard their home towns, and hundreds of thousands have seen their homes and lives shattered by politicians who are indifferent to the horrors of war.
This is a war that has already scarred the Croatian landscape and spoiled its pristine coastline. The destruction of towns and villages, the disruption of trade and tourism, together with panicked military spending will leave Croatia desperate for outside financial assistance. The rest of Yugoslavia will no doubt suffer the economic and diplomatic consequences of world-wide condemnation, as well as the full burden of a crippling foreign debt made worse by military mobilization. This civil war has already killed thousands and is now sure to leave millions of the survivors of people impoverished for years to come.
In the face of ever stronger appeals for action and assistance, the world's response has been shamefully muted and restrained. Nations looked first to the implications that a Yugoslav war would have on ethnic nationalist aspirations at home. Britain has to be concerned about the impact on Northern Ireland. Spain nervously watches over the Basques. Even Canadians have looked for parallels. The Canadian government has yet to address the Croatian tragedy in a meaningful way. We heard the minister refer earlier to the hope that once peace reigned in Croatia then we would look for solutions to the Yugoslav problem.
Six months ago I stood in this House and warned that democracy in Croatia was threatened by military rule and military occupation. I called on the Canadian government to recognize whichever form of government was democratically chosen by the people of Croatia. Canada did not recognize Croatia when independence was declared, neither did the rest of the international community, and civil war ensued.
Canada has finally taken the symbolic first step of imposing trade restrictions, but the current implementation strategy places the peaceful republics of Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina at the risk of becoming the principal victims rather than the states actively participating in the war.
The Liberal Party st'ongly supports the imposition and enforcement of a complete oil embf rgo of Yugoslavia by the United Nations. While such an oil embargo will adversely affect citizens in peaceful republics, it is likely to have the greatest effect in the hindrance of the Yugoslav war machine. The highly mechanized Yugoslav army depends largely on the use of aircraft, tanks and heavy equipment, all with great appetites for fuel.

While it is understood that the army will get first call on remaining resources, the political support for war will certainly dwindle when energy shortages become acute. It is time for the federal government to stop paying lip service and show real and effective leadership toward a peaceful solution to the conflict in Yugoslavia.
Members on both sides of this House have on several occasions referred to the words and actions of Lester B. Pearson for guidance in resolving international conflicts by peaceful and humanitarian means.
Earlier the minister adopted a rather defeatist attitude when it came to the racial tensions existing in Yugoslavia. The time has come for the international community to unite as one to achieve a peaceful settlement in Yugoslavia. The human toll is too great to be ignored and too great to be brushed aside by the political rhetoric and diplomatic impotence we heard tonight.
Canada has yet to make any real effort to alleviate critical shortages of medicine and humanitarian supplies. Infection, disease and hospital overcrowding are amplifying the death tolls and the human suffering. Direct shipments of medical equipment and supplies to embattled areas, as the Italians are beginning today, could save the lives of countless Croatians. The $1.5 million initially committed by the Canadian government and the additional $1 million announced tonight by the minister are insignificant when compared to the billions that Canada spends elsewhere in terms of foreign aid and are a trifle when compared to the $600 million committed by this government to military action in the gulf war.
More more people have been left homeless in Croatia than lived in Kuwait when Saddam Hussein invaded. Perhaps the west does not view Croatia as having the strategic importance of an oil rich state in the Persian Gulf, but if the world is to believe that the gulf war was in any respect a humanitarian effort, the west must now act to safeguard democracy and human rights in Croatia.
The Liberal Party supports Canada's involvement in mobilizing an effective UN peacekeeping force and directly participating in that force. With no end in sight to the bombardment of civilians, Canadian efforts must also be directed toward humanitarian relief in ensuring
that Canadian resources and products are in no way fueling the aggressor.
Furthermore, Canada should announce that trade missions will be undertaken to ensure that captured territories and goods will not prove to benefit the army or its backers. The spoils of this war must never be cashed into Canadian dollars.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in her intervention a few minutes ago, the Secretary of State for External Affairs recited events and in reciting the events that she had witnessed and participated in she revealed also the impotence of the policies that she and her government have pursued so far.
It seems to me that the Secretary of State for External Affairs failed to put forward in this debate two questions. The first one is: How long can the Government of Canada continue to deal with the government of a country which submits its own people to bombardment of its own population, to the destruction of its own towns and cities, and to the destruction of the fibre of the very nation?
One must ask for how long the Secretary of State for External Affairs can live under the delusion that Canada and the west can have a leverage in negotiating with Belgrade when Yugoslavia has fallen apart and when the government of that country has lost the moral authority to govern because it started the destruction of its own people. I cannot believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada does not have the intellectual strength to put forward this question for debate tonight. It seems to me that this is one of the key questions that must be approached.
In other words, how long can we in Canada pretend that Yugoslavia still exists? How long can the Government of Canada elude itself that it can negotiate and bargain with a government in Belgrade when that federation which was a dream for two generations since 1945 has suddenly fallen apart and disappeared almost overnight?
The second question it seems to me is: Why has the Secretary of State for External Affairs, despite the urgings and the debate that preceded her intervention, not put forward the principles or at least her views on the proposition made by the member for Winnipeg South

Centre when he proposed earlier the concept of a new ethic for intervention? Obviously one can see the evidence in the global community that the transfer of sovereignty to a higher level is required in order to deal with national situations.
Evidently we are witnessing the fact that international institutions which we have created are not capable of surviving the acid test of internal divisions in a country such as Yugoslavia. Therefore, at the point when we come to that realization I then submit that we have to discuss and elaborate on the concept put forward by the member for Winnipeg South Centre, the concept of a new ethic for intervention. It is the kind of ethic that will be required in order to bring peace to this war tom and desperate nation which is so gifted with human qualities, so rich with history, so rich with architecture and culture, as everybody in this House has already stressed and underlined.
Evidently something is not functioning within the regional or international institution within the security organizations which have so far more or less served us well. We are now entering a new phase.
Canada a few months ago got passionately involved in the question of Haiti, and so it should have. We have a large population in Canada from that country. In Canada we have a large population of Yugoslav origin. I cannot understand why the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not get as passionately involved as she did with the Haitian question. It escapes me why Canada is not really involved in the negotiations in the search for a solution. We have to work at the solution and we cannot limit ourselves in endorsing other country's initiatives. We have to demonstrate that we also have initiatives of our own and that we have a role to play toward the working out of a satisfactory solution.
We know that there was no support for the Czech and German initiative. We know that there is fear in the international community for creating a precedent. Let me explain.
There must be some fear in a number of nations which have minorities within their own borders in intervening in case of an emergency, because if they were to do so they feel they would create an emergency or create a
precedent that would allow minorities within their own boundaries to develop initiatives and activities reminiscent of the situation in Yugoslavia and which then in turn would require and would justify intervention by the international community.
The question has been raised by the member for Victoria: Why has this matter not been resolved? We as Canadians do not understand why it is not being resolved. Maybe part of the answer is that there is a fear of creating a precedent by intervening in the situation in this distressed part of the world.
What we have seen in the last several months is the use of brutal force. This brutal force has destroyed a federation of six republics and two regions which had become the model for many other nations which are functioning as a federation. It had existed for 45 years. It had brought together people of different languages and different backgrounds for that many decades and managed to develop quite a powerful and impressive economy and force in the international scheme.
However, the mutual respect which the federation had brought about has been replaced unfortunately by guns and mortars, naval shelling, guerrillas and the like.
What do the people in power in Belgrade see when they look at Croatia? Obviously it is not just a question of the Serbian minorities there. What they see are waterways, agricultural lands which are beautifully managed, coastal tourism, natural gas. By endeavouring to take over the territory of Croatia, the powers in Belgrade are hoping that they can encircle Bosnia-Herzegovina, thus moving toward the goal of creating this greater Serbia.
In the early stages, and I will conclude, this conflict was allowed by the world community to get out of control. Right wing nationalist movements in both Croatia and Serbia would not have taken over, I submit, if the west had intervened early and if it had intervened firmly.
Now, after 13 cease-fires the situation is disastrous. Passions have led to a tragedy. We must recognize that the west has allowed this to happen. We have failed collectively to give leadership. Therefore, I conclude with the words of the member for Winnipeg South Centre, that we need a new ethic of intervention. We need a manner of approaching the situation in future.

November 18, 1991
This may also happen in other parts of the world. It is an unacceptable situation for the world community from a human, cultural and social point of view.
