speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the hon. member for Don Valley East.
When Vukovar came under siege, the world paid casual notice. This was a small community in the eastern comer of Croatia, but I believe it was only when one of the great treasures of the Adriatic, that wonderful Renaissance city of Dubrovnik came under brutal attack that the world, late, spoke out.
It is tempting to be cynical and say that if oil were involved we would be there. It is facile now to say this is a federal state sorting out its own affairs, to say as Mr. Trudeau said: "Where is Biafra?" Yet Canadians of all origins are insisting that something is dreadfully wrong in the Balkan peninsula. One by one and group by group, they are doing something about it. Young sons of Canadian Croatian families are leaving in increasing numbers to offer up their lives for their European cousins.
In Edmonton tonight a petition bearing 2,000 signatures is being sent to this Parliament imploring Canada to recognize Croatian independence. A semi-trailer truck will leave Edmonton Thursday bound for Montreal where it will disgorge its cargo of food, clothing, medical supplies, wheelchairs and prostheses on to a ship bound for one of the few Adriatic ports not under blockade.
A question is posed about this curious silence from some quarters of the world. Anthony Lewis of The New York Times in an article which my friend from Davenport was kind enough to circulate posed this question: "Suppose at this moment Venice were being shelled and bombed in a civil war, its treasured monuments menaced, its population starved. Would the western world be
silent? Of course not. It would react in outrage. It would intervene to stop such a crime against history and humanity."
"Across the Adriatic today, another historic jewel of a city, Dubrovnik, is being bombed. Its population is being strangled by blockade and where are the world's protests? Where is any effective action to stop the crime?"
In that same article by Anthony Lewis, one of the most distinguished new democrats of eastern Europe, Vaclav Elavel, says that the danger that is coming from Yugoslavia may be deeper and longer than the international community has realized.
In other words, I believe the President of Czechoslovakia may be referring to the seeds of extended conflict, perhaps once again germinating in the Baltics as happened unfortunately in July of 1914.
The Croats have had a different history than that of the Slovenes, although both spent several centuries as part of the Hapsburg Empire. The Croats were able to establish a strong, independent state in the 10th and 11th centuries which included most of Dalmatia.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in 1102 Croatia was joined to Hungary and was governed by an appointee of the Hungarian kings. The triple kingdom of Croatia, Slovenia and Dalmatia was established in the Peace of Zadar in 1358 A.D.
We have here a nation, a people, who have had a cohesiveness and an identity over the centuries. As has been pointed out by many speakers in this debate tonight, there is the intermingling of ethnicity which has the effect of, in a way, hostages existing within the territory of other peoples. There are 600,000 plus Serbs inside Croatia and a million or so Croats outside Croatia.
Of course, we recall the horrendous, horrific events that took place between the years 1941 and 1945 with atrocities on all sides; two million casualties, 10 per cent of the population of Yugoslavia and half those casualties were inflicted by Yugoslav on Yugoslav.
November 18, 1991

In the months that have gone by since June 25 it has become clear that Yugoslavs have not yet been able to solve their differences peacefully. Since late June of this year a dozen successive cease-fires have come and gone without bringing an end to the fighting. The violence and risks spread beyond the Republic of Croatia to other parts of Yugoslavia, even beyond its borders.
I am pleased that from the beginning Canada has made clear its deep revulsion at these methods of resolving political and inter-ethnic differences. On July 4 the Prime Minister pointed out that countries are not held together by tanks or guns but by the will of men and women to live together. The Secretary of State for External Affairs later said that what needs to be understood in Yugoslavia is that peace cannot be imposed by force, nor are violence and aggression a way to address the rightful concerns of minorities. In an urgent appeal for a cease-fire as early as July 3, Canada joined with other members of the Conference of Security and Co-operation in Europe in offering to send assistance and observers to the area.

Since the beginning of the conflict, it was clear the international community could not dismiss the crisis in Yugoslavia as simply an internal matter. The situation in Yugoslavia has a direct impact on international peace and security in the region. The quasi-collapse of any effective Yugoslavian government has intensified the civil conflict and threatens the peace and security of neighbouring countries. At this very moment, Serbs and Montenegrins are in control of what remains of the federal assembly and presidency.
The sovereignty principle, essential to the survival of a State, has been invoked by those who reject all foreign intervention in Yugoslavia. However, sovereignty must observe more fundamental principles. Today, the mindless destruction of human life can no longer be considered a purely internal matter. The federal Yugoslavian authorities in fact recognized the need for international involvement by supporting initiatives like the peace conference in The Hague organized by the European
Community and by allowing EC and Canadian observers, with a mandate from the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, to be stationed in conflict zones inside Yugoslavia.

Canadians have no interest in imposing an external solution. The only lasting solution to the crisis will come from internal consensus. But Canada has acted with other countries in the international community to try to ensure that a workable political arrangement issues from a democratic process that is free from coercion and that includes specific provisions to safeguard the rights of minorities living in the different republics.
When it became clear that some of the players in the Yugoslav crisis had decided to resort to force, Canada joined the other 34 member states of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in an emergency meeting in Prague in early July to appeal urgently for a cease-fire. These states made clear that recourse to the use of force in the Yugoslav crisis was absolutely inadmissible. They offered the assistance of the CSCE in helping to restore peace in the area and proposed the dispatch of observers to Yugoslavia.
On August 28 the Secretary of State for External Affairs renewed Canada's offer to participate in the CSCE mandated and EEC led cease-fire monitoring team. The offer was accepted September 5 and a group of nine Canadians from the Department of National Defence remain on deployment in Croatia at this time. Should it be possible for the international community to play a more active peacekeeping role, for example, by sending more cease-fire monitors or by dispatching peacekeeping forces, Canada has made clear it would be ready to do its part. All we await is a viable lasting cease-fire and the consent of the major parties involved in the conflict.
The Security Council, as we know, met on September 25. It adopted resolution 713 which expressed full support for the peace initiatives of the European community and the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe and called on all parties to abide by the ceasefire.

November 18, 1991
Canada's role has been one of constructive involvement in the international peace process. The situation in Yugoslavia is complex and intractable and there are no easy solutions. Canada is committed to continuing the search with our international partners for means to end the violence. Talks are continuing with all of the parties involved in the fighting.
This week the United Nations is addressing the issues of universal and mandatory oil sanctions and of peacekeeping. Canada remains actively committed to a peaceful and negotiated solution to this tragic conflict. This is one which may find some kind of permanent resolution of peace in an area that has been a tinder-box in European and world history.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague, the member of Parliament for Edmonton Southwest, for allowing me a few moments of his time in this debate this evening.
I do not know whether you have ever had the opportunity to visit Yugoslavia, Mr. Speaker. I have, and I can tell you that it is a wonderful country made up of marvellous and varied peoples. As you know, tens of thousands of people from those varied backgrounds in Yugoslavia have come to Canada over many years and each and every one of them with their families has made just an enormous contribution to our country of Canada. Canada is a much richer place because of them and because of that contribution.
In 1979, in my former capacity as the mayor of East York, one of the cities that make up metropolitan Toronto, I had the opportunity to travel to Yugoslavia, particularly to East York's twin city of Skopje in the Macedonian republic. But Skopje was only one of a number of communities and a number of cities that I visited at that time, including the city of Dubrovnik. Over the last few days I and other Canadians have watched in horror as Dubrovnik and its people have been destroyed and wiped out in a very systematic way.
That is a city that has a long and ancient history. It is a city that has resisted the armies of Napoleon. Now it has been systematically attacked and systematically destroyed by an army which is out of control, as the Prime Minister has said.
Dubrovnik is one of many horrifying examples and one of a vast number of tragedies that we have seen occurring in Yugoslavia over the last many weeks. A son of one of my constituents, a journalist, was killed there just a few weeks ago in a town very close to Zagreb. I know that you, Mr. Speaker, and I and all Canadians want to see an end to the killing and an immediate stop to all of the destruction that is there. We know that Canada has taken a number of steps so far to try to bring that about. This includes raising the matter at the United Nations, the proposal for sending peacekeepers and imposing some sanctions.
But there is more that we can do and there is more that we must do in this dreadful situation. After all, Mr. Speaker, you know and I know that Canada did not shrink in any way from intervening in the crisis in the Persian Gulf and Canada did not shrink in any way from intervening, as many have said, in the internal affairs of South Africa. Surely there are other things that we can do.
Just before I came to the House for this debate this evening I received a call from a friend of mine in Yukon. He suggested that what we should be doing, as he suggested to me before, is proposing that we have a United Nations emergency force.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs tonight has indicated that there are problems with that, problems with the United Nations taking further action in this matter particularly with respect to the possibility of a veto by the People's Republic of China.
If that is the case, surely Canada has an obligation to itself and to Canadians to be speaking out and speaking out firmly and making it quite clear to the public in this country what the difficulties are in making our voice heard and putting the spotlight where it should be put, on those who are blocking intervention on the part of our country and on the part of the United Nations and other bodies around this world.
Earlier today I received a telegram from a good friend of mine and a constituent, Miro Mihelic. It read: "In the forthcoming debate, stand up and demand the immediate recognition of Slovenia. Let Canada be first. Slovenia fulfils all conditions and more. She has democratic government, undisputed borders, necessary infrastructure, its own currency and no enemies. Recognition will improve the prospect for peace. Absence of recognition will imperil the economic survival".

That is a plea for Canada to recognize the independence of Slovenia. I have to say that every day in my constituency office I receive calls from Canadians whose origins are in Croatia calling on Canada to recognize the independence of Croatia as well.
Mr. Speaker, you and I know that in Slovenia, Macedonia, Bosnia and in Croatia all have made declarations of independence. There have been votes in many of those republics. You know as well that in other eastern European countries like Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania there have been unilateral declarations of independence and where those declarations of independence were made and where there was an overwhelming vote for independence on the part of the peoples of those countries and where the necessary safeguards for minority rights were in place, Canada has not shrunk from recognizing the independence of those states and of those countries.
The Prime Minister has indicated that in a week or two's time when there is a vote in Ukraine, if in fact Ukraine opts for independence, Canada will be recognizing it as well.
Surely at the very least Canada must be consistent when it comes to the recognition of independent states.
Fortunately tonight the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not closed the door on this, but in this case the time has definitely come for Canada to fling the door of independence wide open.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note you said 10 minutes so you are aware that I am sharing the time with the hon. member for Regina-Qu'Appelle and I would appreciate some warning as I get near the end of my 10 minutes.
As we speak this evening on this subject, we are speaking in very comfortable surroundings. It is cold outside but we are quite warm in here. We have had our dinner. We can sit here and talk as though it was something that was not really happening at all and not terribly important, but as we speak people are dying. People are being slaughtered by an army and Canada is talking. We are rather proud of the fact that we are talking and saying things that mean little to the people who are being killed.
The minister said that Canadians condemn violence. Mr. Speaker, you and I both know that all of the violence is taking place in one republic, the republic of Croatia. There is no violence taking place anywhere else. It is taking place in Croatia because Croatia has been invaded by an army, a Yugoslav army, which is supposed to be beyond the control of the civilian authorities.
I find that awfully hard to believe. I am not sure whether it can be accepted or not, but we know that an army depends upon its supply line. An army needs food, an army needs clothing, an army needs shelter. It needs supplies to continue fighting. Somebody is filling those supply lines and keeping them open and operating.
It can be nobody other than a government that is doing that. An army left on its own could not continue to battle for any more than hours before it would have to stop. In the meantime, we can feel good and proud of ourselves for the fact that we are condemning violence, knowing all the time that we are condemning it in only one place.
We have called for action on the part of the Security Council. That is great. We have asked for a peacekeeping mission. That too is good. We are going to impose sanctions pretty soon. We will get around to it. We have done all these things, talked about all these things, always in very comfortable surroundings, thousands of miles away from where people are being slaughtered.
We talk about doing these things and we feel good about it. Can we honestly say that all of the things that Canada has done to this point in time, short of the Red Cross donations, that all of the talk has saved one life in Croatia? Can we point to any one person and say that somebody in Croatia has benefited at all from the actions and the talk that we as Canadians have contributed to that is going on internationally?
The fighting is going on in Croatia. That was my father's homeland. He never lived in this place called Yugoslavia because he left there in 1897, long before Yugoslavia was dreamed of. But the fighting is going on in the village from where he came. I have a cousin there, the cousin has a wife. They have a daughter with two young children, a son about my age. The last I heard, the fighting was very near the village of Ozalj, 10 kilometres from Karlovacz. That is where the fighting is going on

and I am wondering whether or not my relations have been wiped out.
This community held its head up high because it stood off the Turks. The Turks never conquered Ozalj. There was a castle there, they were able to get into the castle every time the Thrks approached and they were able to save that village. It was never conquered by the TUrks. They have a proud history. That is the kind of country we are talking about, a nation that was independent for centuries, off and on, conquered by one or another, but a nation that had its own history of independence.
We are talking about giving them $250,000 through the Red Cross. That is great and they need it. We are going to give them another $1 million somewhere down the road. We are not exactly sure when that is going, we have to find it first, like we must with the money that is going to the wheat farmers in the prairies. If we do, it totals $1,250,000. The damage in Zagreb according to newspapers is reported at $110,000,000 a day. In three months, $12 billion worth of damage and we are contributing $1,250,000. Well good for us.
We could and should be doing more. In my opinion, we should be. Yugoslavia is a nation that was created by the allies at the end of World War I. The name Yugoslavia means South Slavs, the union of South Slavic nations, a union of nations. Canada is a nation. In spite of what some people might argue, there is one nation here. We are separate colonies that agreed to come together to form a nation. We got our independence from Great Britain and we formed one nation. Yugoslavia never did agree as a group to form a nation. It was imposed upon them by the allies as a way of stopping the Russians from expanding to the southwest and getting access to the Adriatic. Created for that purpose, power politics, they never agreed to live together and they never wanted to be together. Certainly the Croats never wanted to submit themselves to the rule of the Serbians. They never have in history and they still do not today.
There has been talk about recognition. Recognition is important because there is no other way of stopping this with talk as long as the Serbians are supported by then-own government, the Yugoslav government if you like or the Serbian government. Certainly Serbia is the largest republic, the most populous republic and the one that is controlling the army, the one that is feeding the army,
the one that can stop the army by cutting off supplies at any moment in time. That is where the control is. They have that control.
Recognition would mean that we are saying as a group of nations that we made a mistake when we forced these people to be subjects of the Serbians in this so-called union of South Slavs. We made a mistake when we did that and we are going to correct that mistake. We are going to correct it by saying that we should never have done it in the first place.
We recognize that the Croatians in free and democratic elections-and I was one of the ones privileged to be there and to observe those elections-made a decision to elect their own democratic government and to make their plea for independence.
If anything, the Serbians have proven that they do not have the right to rule people like that. The way in which they have handled the situation in the past three months, they just do not have the right and they should not have the right. There is only one way. All the talk in the world is not going to save one life. As I said, people are being slaughtered there every day.
There is only one way, that is for the United Nations to take action, the kind of action that we should be prepared to take in many parts of the world. The kind of action, as one member said, the United States took when it went into Iraq. There is oil there. Does anyone believe that if there was oil in Croatia that there would not be a war on right now, that the United Nations would not be involved and that the Americans would not be in there? Of course they would if it was important to them. It is not important to them, so they are not.
I believe it should be important to all of us involved in the United Nations. I believe that it should mean recognition of Croatia as an independent state. It should mean that we are prepared to go in there and say we are negotiating a treaty with this independent state and we are going to save these people from the genocide that is now taking place, the genocide that will never wipe out the Croatians. They have had a lot of practice fighting.
The Croatians fought the Germans during World War II. The Serbians fought the Croatians. Croatians were being fought from both sides but they survived. They will survive this as well. But it falls on our heads if we let this fighting go on so long that so many people on both sides

are being killed. It takes action. If it takes recognition first, so be it. Let us get on with it. Let us get beyond the talking and do something that will mean something to the Croatians who are dying right now. They have their own flag, their own anthem. I wish I could sing it. But I can say, Mr. Speaker vivjeli Hrvatski.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. 0. 52   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in this discussion.
When the republic of Croatia had the first free election I was asked to bring a group of members of Parliament together to observe that election and again when the first free election occurred in Bosnia-Herzego-vina, I was asked at that time as well to put a group of MPs from all parties together. We went and we observed the elections.
I will never forget the evening as some of the election results started to trickle in from Croatia, the sheer joy and jubilation, the tears in the eyes of the men and women in the city of Zagreb. It was an experience and a privilege for me to be there that evening to join with them in that experience. There were some things that I discovered that I think are very important that I wish to convey to the House.
As we were there during the election, I had an opportunity of listening to many of their politicians, particularly to the President, Dr. Tudjman. I had an opportunity during and after the election of talking with Dr. Tudjman. In fact, I would say that from that time to the present, I have talked on maybe five or six different occasions with Dr. Tudjman and various members and leaders of the Croatian government.
What struck me was that the government of Croatia realized that if it was to become a more independent- and that is what they wanted-nation, to restore the nationhood they had to do it in a way in order to prevent a civil war from occurring. In fact, the very thing that is happening today.
They want to develop into a western democracy with western values.
They knew that a civil war would impact, would create a tremendous amount of hatred, retribution, violence, terrorism, that would prevent them from accomplishing their goals. They knew and understood this. They tried to
do everything possible to deal with the Serbian minorities within their borders.
On numerous occasions I had discussions with the leadership, and always the question was: how can we accomplish this, how can we achieve our goal of free, liberal democracy that respects human rights. How can we prevent this type of bloodshed and civil war, this type of disaster which is pulling down the Croatian people as well as the Serbian people. It is a situation where there is no winner.
They tried, but part of the blame has to rest with the west, with our government and the Government of the United States of America, and the governments of the countries in Europe, because they failed to send a strong message to the Serbians. I should not say the Serbian people, I should say the group that is in control there now. They failed to send a message that the behaviour that they used is unacceptable in this day and age in a modem world.
Had they sent that message a year ago, we would not have had the killings today. We would not have had the violence. We would not have had the destruction. But unfortunately, that message was not sent and we are now paying the price.
I do not understand the thinking of our western governments. We hailed and applauded when democracy came, and lo and behold, when you give people the ballot, one of the first things they do is vote back the country. Is this amazing? Had Germany won the war and occupied Holland, Belgium, France and 40,50 years later the ballot was reintroduced to Holland, guess what? The first thing the Dutch would do would be to vote back their country, and that is exactly what the people of Croatia have done, and the people of Slovenia and the people throughout the world who have been forced into a union without their consent. Give them the ballot and the first thing they will do is vote back their nation.
Is that surprising? Apparently it is surprising. But surely common sense tells you that this is inevitable. Either we accept democracy or we do not accept democracy, and the people of Slovenia and the people of Croatia have spoken loud and clear: They want their own republic. They want their own nation. They want a nation to live in peace. They want a nation that will protect minority rights. How often have I discussed this with the people in the Croatian government, willing, Mr. Speaker, to bend over backward to guarantee the rights of the

Serbian minorities. They want a society that would respect human rights. They want to be like a western liberal democracy.
They have not succeeded. In fact, some would even say that Dr. TUdjman and the Croatian government, in their attempt to in a sense appease the army by not doing what Slovenia did when Slovenia declared independence, and that is bottle up the army garrisons, allowed the army room to move in the hope of averting this type of situation.
In fact, all it did was encourage the Serbs and the Yugoslavian army to continue their aggression. So we have seen this peace being negotiated. The only people who have benefited from that, of course, have been the Yugoslavs because every time there is a so-called peace declaration or an agreement, they just continue to gobble up more territory.
When are we going to stop fooling ourselves? When I listen to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is she naive? Is the western world so naive? She talks about not recognizing Croatia because it would remove leverage. The opposite is true. If she wants to use a lever and stop the bloodshed, she tells the Serbs that we are going to recognize Croatia. That is what will have some effect, not by saying we are not going to recognize Slovenia and Croatia because we need that as leverage. A leverage on whom? She does not need a leverage on Croatia. She needs a leverage on the Serbs.
Then we hear this rationale about it being an internal matter within Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia does not exist today. Yugoslavia does not have a legal government today. By its own constitution it does not have a legal government. The nation does not exist.
I suggest that if we are going to have some effect we need an international force. Without an international force, the fourth largest army of Europe is going to continue to commit genocide on part of its population. This we cannot accept in the western world.
I would suggest that Canada first of all recognize Croatia and Slovenia. Second, it should declare that the country called Yugoslavia no longer exists and ask its ambassador to go back home. As well it should request that the position of Yugoslavia in the United Nations no longer be there. Third, it should brand the Yugoslav army an occupational army and demand that it withdraw
November 18, 1991
from Yugoslavia. Fourth, if the Yugoslav army does not exit from Croatia, the government or some international body should be prepared to knock out the Yugoslav air force, the Yugoslav navy and the Yugoslav armoured columns. Then I suspect we are going to see an end to the bloodshed finally.
The western world must wake up to a new reality that people have the vote. People are going to use their ballot. We are either going to see peaceful change or we are not. I would suggest that the western world ask for two conditions before any republic or new entity gets recognized: first, that the borders continue to exist as they are and can only be changed through peaceful negotiation and, second, that minority rights be established, recognized and entrenched in the constitutions of these new republics and that a mechanism like our Human Rights Commission be set up and be monitored by an international human rights body.
Then I think we would see the changes occurring and the changes could become peaceful. They are inevitable, but let us hope and pray they will be peaceful. It is not just in what used to be called Yugoslavia but also in what used to be called the Soviet Union and perhaps in many other parts of the world. The countries that were put together by military might or by imperialism can no longer hold together when you give people the ballot. We will see the changes.
Let us set forward some conditions so that these changes can occur in a peaceful way and that minority groups can continue to enjoy their freedom and their rights. Until we do that as a global community we will continue to see that type of bloodshed.
Surely the time for Canada and other countries in the west when we can afford just to say nothing is passed. The time has come to stand up.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I want to make sure the member for Mississauga South gets an opportunity tonight, so I will try to be brief.
As the House will recall from some of my speeches in this House of Commons I have spoken out on this issue before. I am very happy tonight to see this unanimity that we have found together. I am happy that we are working on this problem and finally seeing that maybe through working together we can do something collectively that
November 18, 1991

has not been been done yet. I remind the members that in March of this year when an all-party delegation authorized by the Speaker of the House of Commons went to Yugoslavia to study in-depth the situation, we reported to this House and there was definitely some fear in our report that this very thing would happen.
The members of the committee reported that in their opinion they felt that violence and tragedy would come to Yugoslavia and that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should take note of this and immediately the occasion arose involve the United Nations. That was months ago. We are finally happy to see some movement in that direction but sadly so much tragedy has gone on.
I want to remind the House of the words of Pope John Paul II on November 13 when he personally denounced the destructive fury deployed against the Croatian population. He said: "An end must be put to this tragedy which dishonours Europe and the world. In the last few days there have been attacks of incredible violence all over Croatia, but especially on Dubrovnik and Vukovar. In Dubrovnik a hotel and a hospital full of refugees and wounded have been hit, among others. It is an aggression that must end. I beg the Yugoslavian army to spare the lives of defenceless civilians".
That is the same army that Mr. Milosevic, President of Serbia, told the delegation he was in complete control of and not to be worried. One would wonder about those words said a few months ago about how much control he really has, because his position was diametrically opposed at that time to Tbdjman's position and Tbdjman's position was democratically attained. It was clear by the referendum in Croatia that the people wanted the right to self-determination, they wanted their independence. Although this was against the intentions of the Serbians, it is nonetheless something that Canadians and Canadian governments have always recognized.
I wonder what has happened to that recognition. I would agree that the Canadian government has urged the 38 countries in the CSCE as well as the European community for peace and mediation. I would agree that this is the first time it has had an opportunity to work in this field, and I guess we on the sidelines should applaud its initiatives and energies. Clearly it is out of its depth in this field. Clearly the United Nations should have been
involved from the outset, and now we need it urgently to resolve this crisis and to get on with the recognition that Croatia so justly deserves.
I would like to talk a bit about the people who have helped bring this to the fore here in the House of Commons. I think that Canadian Croatians have done admirable work in bringing this cause forward, although it certainly has been finally brought to all of our attention through the television media, as it so justly deserves, so that all 27 million Canadians can recognize the horror in Croatia today which all of us abhor. We have talked about it well tonight.
I think that these people have done a real service, a real Canadian service to us in the House of Commons to bring this to our attention and to be diligent about it. I think it is incumbent upon the members of this House to stay together on this issue. We must stay together and we must push this government to act responsibly. It is a clear case that the people of Croatia and Slovenia have made their point about their future. It has been known for months that position is against the position of the Serbian government within the framework of what was then Yugoslavia.
This is no time for partisan politics. This is a time when members of this House should act together and responsibly to keep the pressure and the facts clearly before this government and let other parliaments of the world know that we as a group of parliamentarians want action. We want the situation rectified immediately and the democratic rights of the Croatians recognized outside their country by Canada and the other nations that comprise the United Nations. We want the rights for self-determination to be given as soon as possible in a peaceful atmosphere, looked over and supervised by the United Nations, while the rest of the republics have the same opportunity.
Although tonight we are focusing on Croatia and its situation as it has evolved in Yugoslavia, there are other republics democratically seeking the same path and that has not been recognized by this government either. I would say that they have the same right. We are making a terrible mistake here if we do not stay together on this course and be committed as a group of Canadians that will lead this country's position to be one that will recognize the self-determination of the Croatians, the Slovenes, the Macedonians, and all the other republics

November 18, 1991
that when democratically given a chance for self-determination get it.
I would like the member from Mississauga South to finish this off.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in September my colleague from London- Middlesex and I were two of the delegates for Canada at a conference at the European parliament on democracy. We flew to Paris and then drove to Strasbourg. On the way we stopped at Verdun to see the crosses row on row on row that were there because of a war that some say was caused by the murder of the Archduke in Serbiano in 1914.
After that war a country was cobbled together and became known as Yugoslavia. That country had no cohesiveness whatsoever. It was cobbled together to break up the Austrian-Hungarian empire and to take a hunk out of the Ottoman empire and to put together people who really had no decent arrangements among themselves.
They were different peoples but they were cobbled together into a nation. That nation did not succeed. It did not succeed through the last world war. It was again forced together and it is now broken up. It is no longer a nation. Its people and its separate republics have overwhelmingly voted to be separate and distinct.
To suggest that Yugoslavia as a country exists is to dream. Yugoslavia as a country does not exist. To continue to suggest that the ambassador from Yugoslavia occupying premises in Ottawa represents and can speak for the people of Yugoslavia generally is crazy. It just is not so. He cannot speak for them. He cannot speak for a Yugoslav government because a Yugoslav government does not exist. The fact is that we have separate republics, all intending to go their own way and all going their own way. The problem today that we face is that one of those republics has control of the military might that used to be Yugoslavia and that army is the army controlled by Serbia that is now invading and taking over in Croatia.
There have been problems between Serbs and Croats for a long time. It is not of our making and it is not for us to judge how those problems developed and where is the
root of those ills. The fact is that we were part of a western world that tried to cobble together peoples that really did not want to be together to form a country. It is about time we recognized our error and recognized the separateness that these people really want.
The fighting is abhorrent to all of us. We have attempted as Canadians up until now to try to play the even road. We have attempted to go to the United Nations and say: "Let us get the Security Council in and we will even be part of a peacekeeping force to help make the peace". The European common group has helped organize 13 cease-fires and 13 cease-fires have become 13 new wars. I suppose we could have another cease-fire tomorrow and we would have another continuing war.
The fact of the matter is that it is clear to me. I think it should be clear to all of the House here tonight that the cease-fires will not work, that we cannot easily get a situation where the United Nations can come in and just be quiet peacekeeper in the normal course. I think it is important that the countries of the world started recognizing the situation, that the only way we can force peace in this particular part of the world is to recognize the separate republics and cease the recognition of Yugoslavia as a state because that state does not exist any more.
I believe that it is important for the House and for the government to accept that the condition of trying to be the broker between people is not going to work that easily. We are going to have to take a stand. That is not a stand against Serbia and that is not a stand against Croatia. That is a stand for the common sense of the fact that these separate countries are really separate countries and that we ought to recognize them as separate countries. From that point of view we ought to insist that separate countries become apart. If they refuse to come apart then we ought to insist that the United Nations or whoever take compulsory action to stop the fighting without the permission of the parties involved. Clearly the parties involved cannot work out a cease-fire among themselves or an accommodation. So that accommodation will have to be forced on them.
We cannot afford in this world to allow wars to continue. We have a war going on here between people who are hostile to each other that will spread if we do not step in and stop it. That kind of thing will spread and

create the kind of holocaust that created World Wars I and II.
l say that this House has got to direct our government in our speeches and in our common agreement that it is time that the matter in Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia, Herzegovina and Montenegro be ended. We should recognize those countries, if they want to be dependent and independent, as quickly as possible and get on with it.

Mr. Speaker, I am also pleased to stand in this House and speak on this very important subject this evening.
I would just like to comment briefly on the comments of the previous speaker on the government side of the House. I do not think anybody is being partisan here this evening. I think we all have the same interests at heart and that is for peace in the republics, in Croatia and in the others, in what he referred as the former Yugoslavia.
The emergency debate this evening has been long overdue. We on this side of the House have been asking for it. I think those other speakers have not been putting the kind of pressure on their government that we on this side of the House have been.
We have been consistently calling upon this government to address this issue. My colleagues and I have pleaded for the government to use its influence at the UN in mobilizing a peacekeeping force. The senseless, brutal violence against innocent people must stop.
One of my constituents-I hope he does not mind my using his name-Mr. William Viduka made an impassioned representation for an end to the violence in his ancestral homeland of Croatia. He even brought along a video which visually showed the violence that his people in his homeland were having to endure. His message over and over to me was: "Do something. Canada has to do something to stop this violence".
Thousands of Canadians claim Yugoslavia as their homeland. They and all Canadians want this government to live up to its commitment to advocate peace in the strongest of terms. We on this side of the House condemn the Yugoslavian army for its attack on the Croatian people.
I have met with and heard representatives on all sides of this debate. I have participated in committee and I have made comment in this House. My concern is for the protection of human rights and the right to life, for the establishment of a coherent and consistent national and international policy for the protection of the dignity and the rights of people. The issue of human rights should override sovereignty. The precedent has already been set.
Yugoslavia has been a victim of an international double standard. When similar activities were occurring in Kuwait, with Iraq as the aggressor, the international community was quick to respond to the point of going to war.
If true justice, namely the protection of human rights, is to emerge within the international community then there has to be a more consistent and effective response to ongoing and blatant violations of human rights.
The causes of this particular conflict are numerous and complicated, but the right to self-determination for Croatia lies at the core of the problem. Self-determination is a right afforded to peoples through the UN covenant on civil and political human rights. It has been ratified by over 80 countries, including Canada and Yugoslavia.
I have never been to Yugoslavia though a great number of people in this House here tonight indicated they have. However, I have been to other historically beautiful cities in Europe such as Prague. Its architecture is probably very similar to that of Dubrovnik. It is unparalleled and irreplaceable.
The destruction of not only the people of Yugoslavia but also its historic properties will forever be lost to its peoples and the world in such wanton needless waste.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister always say that they make representations on behalf of Canada. Yet it is my belief that Yugoslavia has never been on this government's agenda.
Canadians demand more than behind the scenes rhetoric.
Canada has always carried weight in the international community. Canada has never been a power militarily. However we have been a power diplomatically. What is

November 18, 1991
wrong with this government today that it is unable to take a leadership role in settling this dispute?
Canadians demand the resumption of this role in order to bring an end to the violence and killing. Canada must bring her influence to bear in the international community to see that such atrocities are not repeated ever again in any country in this world.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I seek unanimous consent of the House to move:
That this House recognizes the republic of Slovenia and the
republic of Croatia as independent nations.
Do I have the unanimous consent of the House, Mr. Speaker, to move this motion?

Mr. Speaker, the inability of the peoples of Yugoslavia to get along together peacefully and the inability of the world community to stop the fighting is a tragedy of unspeakable proportions. Thousands have died, tens of thousands of persons have become refugees, friends and neighbours one day have become enemies the next.
Great potential exists for similar conflicts in much of eastern Europe. Most of those states and most of the republics in the Soviet Union are multi-ethnic states. It is for this reason that it is somewhat perplexing to me that Canada has not been vigorously promoting the concept of federalism.
Despite our failings we have gone further than other countries in providing constitutional guarantees to linguistic minorities. Many of these guarantees are found in our federal structure. Unless the world community is prepared to contemplate independence for every ethnic group, federalism is the only answer.

The NDP external affairs critic said that the people of Slovenia and Croatia had opted for independence. That is true, but he did not say that Serbs in Croatia, who represent 12 per cent of the population, want to continue to be part of Yugoslavia.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that Canada wanted a peaceful, negotiated settlement that would protect minority rights. If I understood correctly, she also said that Canada was opposed to any unilateral border changes. However, her statement does not answer the following question: What guarantees will satisfy the Serbs in Croatia? They want to stay in Yugoslavia.

They showed that they are prepared to fight to remain part of Yugoslavia. I am not saying that Yugoslavia or other countries must remain together for an eternity with boundaries or an ethnic composition that may be artificial. There may have to be and probably will have to be adjustments. Professor Oral Brown of the Department of Political Science at the University of Toronto spoke on October 22 to the Standing Committee on External Affairs. I would like to quote him:
What we may best be able to do is to tiy to manage the dissolution of Yugoslavia. This might involve territorial compromises but you cannot have a settlement along purely ethnic lines because geographically it is impossible. So we would have to create some sort of conditions whereby minority rights are guaranteed within states, where there is some adjustment, but there are still minorities.
Note what Professor Brown said. There may have to be some adjustments. This might involve territorial compromise. But he added that we cannot have a settlement along purely ethnic lines because geographically it becomes impossible unless, as I said earlier, we are willing to contemplate independence for every ethnic group or people, or the uprooting of millions of people.
I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that there are some 30 million ethnic Russians who live outside of the Republic of Russia in the Soviet Union.
If we want to preserve peace, the world community and Canadians will have to promote the idea of federalism. We must deal with the present situation. Many Canadians are dismayed that the world community has not acted decisively in dealing with the war in Yugoslavia.
On September 16 I wrote to the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of a constituent who was and is deeply distressed with the inadequate response of the world community in general and the Canadian government in particular to the conflict in Yugoslavia. This constituent believed that the Government of Canada had not done enough to protest or put an end to the killings of hundreds of Croatians. This constituent is of

Croatian origin and all of her relatives, with the exception of her immediate family, live in Yugoslavia. I too have felt that the world community and Canada has not acted decisively enough. I listened to the remarks earlier this evening of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. She mentioned that Canada was the first country to request a meeting of the Security Council but pointed out that China views this as an internal matter, yet hopes that China will stop in its stand.
In spite of her assurances, I do not see the same resolve that existed a year ago when this House and the government confronted the situation in the Persian Gulf. On October 28, our spokesperson for external affairs, the MP for Winnipeg South Centre, asked the minister whether Canada was prepared to publicly support the call for an economic embargo against Yugoslavia. The minister on that day replied that she was concerned that an economic embargo would hurt the people et je termine, monsieur le President, it intended to help and that an economic embargo is not going to stop the attack on Dubrovnik.
Of course, 11 days later on November 8, Canada joined the European Community in imposing economic sanctions. Why the equivocation? Why not demonstrate to Canadians that the government is indeed pleading for action on a daily basis, as the minister stated in her remarks tonight.
I hope the debate this evening will lead to more forceful, visible actions by our government to put an end to the bloodshed in Yugoslavia.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this emergency motion which deeply touches the heart of anyone who cares for humanity.
For the past five months we have been witness to destruction of greatest infamy taking place in the Republic of Croatia, not Yugoslavia. I said Republic of Croatia because on June 25 of this year, Croatia declared its independence from Yugoslavia and reaffirmed its declaration on October 7 at the expiry of the moratorium on independence.
I did not say Yugoslavia because the Yugoslav federation is no longer a functioning federation entity. The Yugoslav army is out of control. In fact, we know that last September the President of Yugoslavia, Mr. Stipe Mesic, ordered the federal forces to cease engaging the Croatian forces. The army has refused to obey their

Commander in Chief, their legally constituted President who heads the eight member presidential committee.
Indeed, the Yugoslav army made death and suffering in Croatia visit us daily on television and in the newspapers, while for others the crisis reaches in to take the lives of family and friends.
People in my riding of Winnipeg North have lost loved ones in Yugoslavia, in Croatia. Canadian youths of Croatian descent have planned to make a voyage to Dubrovnik to lend moral support.
As horrific as the war may be for both sides, Croatia has become a victim and the Yugoslav army the oppressor. The bloodshed and ruin to Croatia, the people, the cities, the country, the spirit, are heinous. It is time for this human bloodshed to halt. It should never have begun. Canada cannot be allowed to stand idly by any longer.
Aside from the large number of people across Canada who have already voiced their concerns over this issue, I have received numerous letters from my constituents in Winnipeg North, expressing distress and asking what the federal government can and is doing to put an end to this situation.
Over 3,000 have died while a hundred times that number are homeless. Today on television I witnessed the surrender of Vukovar, as hundreds of Croatians, shelled for days by Yugoslav army forces, gave up and were marched from their homes. I saw women weeping with babies on their shoulders leaving the city to an unknown future. Croatian defenders dropped their rifles in piles beside the road, leaving themselves at the mercy of the army.
Indeed, thousands of innocent civilians are being wounded as it is always in any war. It was heartbreaking. The demolition of Croatia is truly heartbreaking. The communist dominated army has violated 13 cease-fires already issued by the European Community. It has attacked the entire region along the Dalmatian coast as well as the cities of Dubrovnik, Karlovak, Somobor, Sibenik, Vukovar, Zadar and Zagreb. The vicious attacks on Dubrovnik have been especially devastating. The army has invaded this 14th century city with such onslaught that countless places of worship, hospitals,

November 18, 1991
schools and architectural wonders have been demolished.
Such cultural annihilation is an absolute breach of international law. Can we permit such unabridged and thorough destruction to run unfettered?
We must make a commitment to Croatians and ensure the presence of Canadian peacekeeping forces under the auspices of the United Nations to aid them in their struggle and bring about a rapid conclusion to this profoundly destructive conflict.
We support a strictly imposed oil embargo as my colleague has earlier indicated to this government, the critic for external affairs, the member for Winnipeg South.
Canada must do more and be directly involved in the search for peace in that part of the world.
As I stand before you, Mr. Speaker, this evening and conclude my debate, I hope the government will recognize not only the severity of the situation but also the need to do more decisively. The colossal human carnage in Croatia must stop. What will we as elected members of Parliament do to stop the war?
Allow me to reflect briefly on recent events and relate them to the tragedy in Croatia. The Baltic states were fighting for freedom and independence; the Croatians are doing the same. The Baltic states were battling to rid themselves of oppressive forces; Croatia has been doing the same. The Baltic states voted overwhelmingly in favour of democracy; Croatia at 94 per cent has done the same.
The 94 per cent of Croatians who opted for freedom, democracy and independence simply cannot be dismissed. Canada must answer the question: Shall we allow Croatia to exist as an autonomous republic which has the right to circumscribe its own political future just as we have done with the Baltic states? This is a soul-searching question that demands an equally soulsearching answer.
My city of Winnipeg has given the answer in a resolution passed on November 6 this year and I quote: "Now therefore be it resolved that the council of the city of Winnipeg on behalf of all citizens of the city recognizes the sovereignty of the people of Croatia and the right to exist free from external threat of force of arms. Be it further resolved that this council by adoption of this resolution calls upon the Prime Minister and the House of Commons to recognize the nation of Croatia and to use all diplomatic means possible to stop further military actions against this nation".
There is no more time to waste. The economic sanctions came in late. Let us now not be too late with the ultimate solution.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this important debate.
About 12 years ago I was in Yugoslavia with the Governor General of the day, the Right Hon. Ed Schreyer, the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin, and Mark Rose from the NDP. We were attending the funeral of Marshall Tito. As we waited at the airport to make our way back to Canada we talked about how long it would be before Yugoslavia flew apart. Then when they appointed a president and a council of advisers we again asked how long it would be. Now of course we know the answer. It has taken 12 years for them to break apart.
What we see today in Yugoslavia is the result of a sad and tragic history, a history of distrust, suspicion, recrimination and conflict. Everyone in Croatia and Serbia has bitter memories of the tragic incidents between those two peoples during the Second World War. The communist regime imposed by Marshall Tito at the end of the war did not solve the deep regional and ethnic rivalries. It just kept them under a wrap. Now that Marshall Tito is gone, now that the oppressive system he imposed has lost its grip, the bitter enmity between these two peoples can and is being expressed with a vengeance.
In 1990, when communism was being discarded by the people of eastern Europe, all Yugoslav republics held multi-party elections. Almost without exception, they elected non-communist but strong nationalist governments. Serbia and Montenegro merged nationalism and communism, which they renamed socialism.
After months of unsuccessful negotiations concerning new constitutional arrangements-everything from a confederation to a loose form of associated states-Slo-
November 18, 1991

venia and Croatia unilaterally declared their independence. That was June 25.
On June 27, the federal Yugoslavian army tried, without the full agreement of the Yugoslav federal government, to assert control over Slovenia's external borders. The Slovenian defence forces fought the federal army in a number of violent clashes.
After talks with federal and republican authorities, representatives of Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands announced that the army had agreed to return to their barracks and that two secessionist republics would suspend the implementation of their declarations of independence.
With its failure to take control of the symbols of independence in Slovenia, the army agreed to a ceasefire during a meeting sponsored by the European Community on the island of Brioni on July 7. Eleven days later, the army agreed to withdraw from Slovenia and a team of international cease-fire monitors was deployed in Sic enia to ensure the terms of the Brioni agreement.
A similar pattern of conflict in violence is occurring in Croatia. There are, however, factors which make matters even more complicated than in Slovenia.
When the Croatia nationalist government was elected in May 1990, Serbian groups within Croatia decided to take control of some of the Serbian populated areas of the republic. These groups, now constituted in self-proclaimed Serbian autonomous regions within Croatia, launched an important offensive in July to gain control over larger areas with significant Serbian populations as well as over some other important industrial and transportation sites.
Since then, the Serbians, Croatian and federal governments have negotiated cease-fires, but these cease-fires, as we know, have not worked. They have not worked because Serbia does not completely control the actions of the armed irregular groups in the Serbian controlled parts of Croatia. Croatia does not have the control of all its paramilitary units and the federal army seems to have its own agenda.
I outlined some of this background to the current crisis to show how complicated and tangled the situation is. But it is not the complexity of the situation that we most regret, it is the loss of the life and limb, the wilful destruction of homes and families, the violent settling of
accounts, sometimes over issues of situations that are decades if not generations old.
As we in this peaceful country of ours try to work out our own differences, we had better pay attention to the tragedy unfolding in Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia is a painful reminder of the dangers of ethnic and cultural insularity. It is also a reminder of the virtues of tolerance, openmindedness and flexibility.
Peace, order and good government have been the longstanding principles behind the Canadian Constitution. With the disturbing events in Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia over the past few months, those constitutional principles show the wisdom of the Fathers of Confederation.
I am proud of the way the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have managed Canada's response to the Yugoslav crisis. Though Canada is far from being a powerful force in central and eastern Europe, we have been at the forefront of international action to support efforts for peace and to provide assistance to the innocent victims of this conflict.
In the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, in NATO and at the United Nations, Canada has been an active player in trying to help resolve this crisis. There will always be those who for one reason or another, usually partisan, say that Canada should be doing more and that we should be giving more. In my opinion, we have already been doing a great deal. We have to be realistic. Ask any Canadian and he or she will tell you that Canada cannot single-handedly resolve this crisis. In fact, I would argue that the European community is best positioned to influence the course of events there. That does not mean that Canada should sit back and do nothing or do little. As a responsible active member of the world community, that would be an abdication of our responsibilities.
It does mean however that we have to use our heads and keep a proper perspective on what it is that we can and should do. What the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have been doing is working with other like-minded countries, especially the European Community, to bring pressure on those who are using violence to try and resolve the situation and bring relief to those who have been the targets of violence.

One of the frustrating aspects of this whole situation is the notion of sovereignty. For decades, law and practice in the United Nations have argued against any action which could be seen as intervention in the internal affairs of member states, and there are very good reasons for this. But where do we draw the line? How much bloodshed, brutality, oppression and destruction is required before the international community can intervene?
We would all agree that continued and indiscriminate killing and abuse cannot be justified by nationalism. We can also agree that killing and abuse can no more be justified by the notion of sovereignty. We all hope, sir, that this debate has contributed something to the difficulty faced by Yugoslavia and we continue to bend our efforts to do everything we can to see that we can bring peace and take care of the people involved in this terrible conflict to the best of our ability.
